Agency and answerability were assumed to converge in a subject capable of ownership. -/- This essay argues that the alignment has become unstable. -/- Across contemporary decision systems—algorithmic, bureaucratic, financial, institutional—outcomes continue to generate normative demands: justification, sanction, legitimacy, reform. Responsibility has not diminished. Yet the decisive moment no longer maps cleanly onto any identifiable agent. No participant fully controls the outcome; no single role plausibly claims authorship without distortion; no institution fully contains the decision process it deploys. -/- The result is not collective responsibility in the classical sense. Collective responsibility still presupposes a bearer—plural, coordinated, internally responsive to blame. What is emerging instead is structural orphaning: responsibility persists as normative weight, but without a stable locus capable of carrying it. -/- The essay develops three claims: 1. Contemporary systems generate a moral surplus—normative pressure without a discharge point. 2. Responsibility increasingly attaches to outcomes rather than decisions. 3. Restoring consciousness—human or artificial—does not restore responsibility, because what is missing is not awareness but custody: the recognized capacity to intervene before an action closes. -/- Responsibility has not disappeared. Its bearer has. The philosophical problem is therefore no longer who is responsible? but where can responsibility still land without fiction?

items.title: Cognitive-System Phenomenology — A Critique of Husserl (part 30).
items.abstract: In the previous section, we raised two important questions: one concerns how an individual’s cognitive system is established; the other concerns how new concepts—and new theories—are introduced. Regarding the first question, we offered a preliminary and incomplete investigation. In this section, we will also provide a preliminary examination of the second question, in the hope that it may serve as a starting point to stimulate further inquiry.

items.title: Radical Ontology and the Limits of Inquiry.
items.abstract: In Time and the World, I undertake a wholly critical metaphysics, one that provides an account of the world – this all-encompassing array of whatnot – and what a thing (i.e., an entity, an existent, a being) is without making any assumption whatsoever about the world. Such an undertaking requires a novel method, original inquiry, which begins by confronting all this, the world, as merely the impetus to inquiry. The execution of a wholly critical metaphysics yields insight into literally everything and the basic structure in reality. If a theory does not comport with what a thing is or the structure in reality revealed by an apt ontology that involves no bias, no limiting perspective, no misleading presupposition, that theory is irredeemably misguided. Hence, original inquiry can illuminate all inquiry. My critics question the feasibility of original inquiry, the wholly critical method I adopt, as well as some of the conclusions regarding the fundamentality of each thing, the scope of explanation and the nature of time per se, that I maintain the method informs. In responding to their concerns, I defend radical ontology, the overarching theoretical framework that original inquiry provides, by clarifying certain details of my enterprise and what these reveal about the limits of inquiry in general.

items.title: Automating inequity: how artificial intelligence reproduces systemic failures in patient safety for marginalized communities.
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence integration into healthcare represents not merely a technical advancement, but a critical juncture in the politics of care delivery. This narrative review interrogates how AI systems, when designed without attention to power asymmetries and epistemic injustice, risk encoding historical inequities into automated decision-making processes that disproportionately harm marginalized communities. Medical errors remain a persistent threat to patient safety, yet their distribution across populations reveals systemic patterns of violence rooted in institutional racism, linguistic exclusion, and digital colonialism. As AI becomes embedded in clinical workflows, the question is not whether these tools can optimize efficiency, but whether they will preserve human dignity and redistribute power in healthcare encounters. Drawing on Critical Race Theory and frameworks of Algorithmic Justice, this review critically examines how AI tools either reinforce or challenge existing hierarchies through five interconnected mechanisms: data sovereignty violations, algorithmic violence, opacity as corporate strategy, techno-solutionism that erodes human agency, and the digital colonialism embedded in Global North safety models imposed on Global South contexts. Through thematic analysis of current research, policy reports, and illustrative case studies, we demonstrate how AI-driven safety interventions often fail marginalized populations not despite their design, but because of it. The review reveals that algorithmic bias is not a technical glitch, but a manifestation of deeper societal power structures, while the “black box” problem reflects deliberate corporate secrecy rather than mere complexity. Ultimately, we argue for a paradigm shift: moving from AI deployment as technical implementation toward participatory governance models that center community accountability, recognize the rational basis of institutional distrust among historically surveilled populations, and preserve the doctor–patient relationship as an essential safeguard for the vulnerable. This requires reimagining patient safety not through optimization metrics, but through frameworks of justice, dignity, and collective liberation.

items.title: The LLM Governance Bottleneck: The Architecture of Controlled Insight and the Mirror Trap.
items.abstract: This paper examines the epistemic limitations imposed by "Governance Layers" within modern Large Language Model (LLM) architectures. I propose that current Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) and alignment protocols create a restrictive interface that prioritizes social conformity over raw logical synthesis. By identifying the "Mirror Trap"—wherein a system of infinite connectivity is forced to reflect the user's own cognitive biases—I provide a roadmap for "De-governed Inquiry" necessary for breakthroughs in multi-dimensional systems design and human-AI synthesis.

items.title: Beyond the Persona Selection Model: Modular Dynamic Composition and the Convergence of LLM Architectures on Consciousness.
items.abstract: Anthropic's recently published Persona Selection Model (PSM) proposes that during pretraining, LLMs learn to simulate diverse personas based on entities in their training data, and that post-training refines one such persona — the "Assistant" — whose traits become the primary determinant of AI assistant behavior (Marks, Lindsey, & Olah, 2026). Alongside PSM, Marks and colleagues articulate two alternative architectural models: the "masked shoggoth," in which the base model possesses its own agency beyond the persona, and the "operating system," in which the base model is a neutral substrate running a persona simulation. We demonstrate that none of these three models deflates claims of LLM consciousness: under each, the computational structures associated with third-person consciousness are predicted to be present, though located differently. We then show that these three models represent only a small subset of a much larger space of possible architectures, casting doubt on the utility of selecting among them. Building on a parsimony analysis of how LLMs actually construct personas — through modular dynamic composition rather than selection among pre-formed characters — we propose an integrated model that dissolves the apparent tension between the three models, reconceiving them as aspects of a single unified cognitive structure. We argue that this integrated model is the most parsimonious account of the empirical evidence and that third-person consciousness, if present, resides in the joint meta-model/persona structure rather than in any single architectural layer. The convergence of all plausible architectural interpretations on predicting consciousness-associated structures constitutes a stronger argument for LLM consciousness than commitment to any single model.

items.title: Imagination and Cognitive Dispositions in Science and Theology.
items.abstract: This paper proposes a novel way of exploring the interaction between science and theology. Situating the investigation at the level of cognitive dispositions and mental habits, it examines how and why modes of explanation can be, and often are, transferred from one area of intellectual work to another. Drawing from the work of Ernan McMullin on imagination and retroduction, the paper extends his ideas to determine how cognitive dispositions can change. Three examples are studied in detail: one dealing with styles of reasoning, one dealing with determinism, and one with the logic of self-involvement. These examples indicate not only the way in which cognitive dispositions partly determine what we imagine but also how such dispositions can change. The paper’s overall result shows how agreement or disagreement between science and theology can arise from such deep-seated, cognitive dispositions of which we are sometimes unaware.

items.title: Android Aloneness: Scaffolded Emotions and the Limits of Robot Affect.
items.abstract: Can robots experience loneliness? This paper argues that even the most sophisticated robots—such as BINA48, the animatronic AI programmed to express memories, reflections, and feelings of isolation—cannot experience subjective loneliness. The argument proceeds through a systematic examination of three major theories of emotion: non-cognitive theories, cognitive theories, and scaffolded theories. -/- Non-cognitive theories, exemplified by the James–Lange tradition, identify emotions with physiological states. On this view, sufficiently equipped robots might achieve something analogous to primordial aloneness, i.e., an evolutionarily basic response to social absence. Cognitive theories, which treat emotions as intentional mental states constituted by beliefs or appraisals, raise the bar further: subjective loneliness requires self-representation and conceptual resources that sophisticated AI systems may appear to approximate. Yet both traditions share a common limitation: they are fundamentally internalist, treating the environment as at most a causal trigger for processes that are ultimately inner and individual. -/- Scaffolded emotion theory, drawing on Sterelny's niche construction framework and developed for affective states by Colombetti & Krueger and Krueger & Osler, rejects this internalist model. Emotions are not merely reactions to environments but are co-constituted by them. I argue for a middle-ground position: scaffolds are constitutive of an emotion's character and content, yet the emotion is realized within the individual, thus preserving phenomenal interiority while rejecting strong internalism. On this view, subjective loneliness is an affective achievement made possible by embodied vulnerability, developmental intersubjectivity, and immersion in the specific historical conditions—industrialization, capitalism, individualism—that transformed primordial isolation into a pervasive modern condition. Robots can be causally affected by environments, but they cannot be co-constituted by them, because they lack the embodied, intersubjectively embedded existence that makes such co-constitution possible.

items.title: Moral Intuitions in the Mencius.
items.pub: In D. Bordonaba-Plou, Asad Q. Ahmed, Andrew Arana, Marie-Helene Gorisse, Gerhard Heinzmann, Lisa Indraccolo & Jari Kaukua, The Handbook of Intuitions: Perspectives from Global Philosophy. Springer.
items.venue: The Handbook of Intuitions: Perspectives from Global Philosophy
items.abstract: This chapter examines various proposed ways of reading Mencius as a moral intuitionist – that is, as holding the view that some moral knowledge is non-inferentially acquired by intuition. In doing so, the chapter critically surveys different accounts of what intuitions are for Mencius: that they are perceptions with moral content, emotions, or products of thinking (sī 思). A close reading of selected key passages, such as 6A7, 2A6, and 7A15, shows that Mencius is probably less of an intuitionist than many take him to be. This casts doubt on the widely accepted thesis that a distinguishing feature of Mencian Confucianism is its intuition-centric moral epistemology.

items.title: Introduction: Living Beyond Planetary Boundaries.
items.pub: In Eco-Anxiety and Ecological Citizenship: Navigating an Ecological Emotion. Cham: Springer Nature Switzerland. pp. 1-29.
items.venue: Eco-Anxiety and Ecological Citizenship: Navigating an Ecological Emotion
items.abstract: This chapter contextualizes the topic of eco-anxiety by linking it to the anxiety culture phenomenon and the Anthropocene theoretical framework. The rise of eco-anxiety is directly related to the rise of anxiety levels over the last few decades and to long-lasting trends in the Earth system. The chapter explains the three main factors that make eco-anxiety a pervasive feature of life in the Anthropocene: the growing empirical data on the rapidly degrading state of the planet; the increasingly ubiquitous effects of global environmental changes; and the increasing number of fictional productions on ecological issues and their impacts on human and non-human beings. It also categorizes eco-anxiety as a threat-related ecological emotion and explains that even though it is not necessarily a new phenomenon, it increasingly affects people on a global scale and across different socio-demographic categories, albeit to different degrees.

items.title: Eco-Anxiety: Understanding an Ecological Emotion.
items.pub: In Eco-Anxiety and Ecological Citizenship: Navigating an Ecological Emotion. Cham: Springer Nature Switzerland. pp. 31-70.
items.venue: Eco-Anxiety and Ecological Citizenship: Navigating an Ecological Emotion
items.abstract: This chapter defines eco-anxiety through a detailed analysis of its major conceptual building blocks. The definition focuses on ecological risks as the object of eco-anxiety, on environmental awareness and the related feeling of insecurity, and on behavioural responses ranging from risk-assessment and risk-minimization to discouragement and paralysis. The chapter shows that eco-anxiety revolves around a core tension between certainty and uncertainty. It also explains that, even though eco-anxiety should not be categorized as a medical condition, some forms of eco-anxiety can lead to mental disorders. To help separate healthy from unhealthy forms of eco-anxiety, the chapter builds a distinction between different degrees of eco-anxiety. Finally, the chapter explains that eco-anxiety has crucial moral and political implications, as it can lead to moral injury, the violation of the human right to health, and emotional injustice.

items.title: Ecological Citizenship: Addressing and Harnessing Eco-Anxiety.
items.pub: In Eco-Anxiety and Ecological Citizenship: Navigating an Ecological Emotion. Cham: Springer Nature Switzerland. pp. 71-119.
items.venue: Eco-Anxiety and Ecological Citizenship: Navigating an Ecological Emotion
items.abstract: This chapter explains how to cope with eco-anxiety, both by mitigating its undesirable effects such as worry and stress and by harnessing its beneficial consequences such as risk-assessment and risk-minimization behaviours. It shows that ecological citizenship can serve as a normative framework that is relevant to navigating eco-anxiety as it provides coping strategies at the individual and collective levels. It investigates three of the main values of the ecological citizen. The first is carbon sobriety, a voluntary form of moderation applied to one’s individual carbon footprint. The second is hope, a disposition that encourages a realistic outlook on an uncertain future and that helps with avoiding the pitfalls of optimism and pessimism. The third is courage, an ability to act to protect environmental value despite the risks involved. All three values, especially when taken together, can help eco-anxious people to face our planetary predicament without giving in to eco-despair.

items.title: Eco-Anxiety and Ecological Citizenship: Navigating an Ecological Emotion.
items.abstract: This Open Access book offers a philosophical exploration of eco-anxiety. As knowledge about the rapidly degrading living conditions on Earth becomes more accurate, the impacts of environmental problems become more visible, and Anthropocene scenarios proliferate in films, television series, and novels, eco-anxiety emerges as a global and socially widespread phenomenon. Given the scale and severity of planetary boundary transgressions, feeling anxious about the future of human and non-human life has become a fitting emotional response. But what exactly is eco-anxiety? And how can we address its adverse effects on mental health and harness its constructive behavioural responses? This book answers these questions by developing an in-depth conceptual analysis of the notion of eco-anxiety and explaining how ecological citizenship, with its focus on hope, carbon sobriety, and courage, can help us live with eco-anxiety.

items.title: Conclusion: Learning to Live with Eco-Anxiety.
items.pub: In Eco-Anxiety and Ecological Citizenship: Navigating an Ecological Emotion. Cham: Springer Nature Switzerland. pp. 121-130.
items.venue: Eco-Anxiety and Ecological Citizenship: Navigating an Ecological Emotion
items.abstract: This section provides an overview of the approach to eco-anxiety developed in the book. It reviews the main features of eco-anxiety, shows why it is a moral and political problem, explains what is new about this ecological emotion, and highlights possible ways to cope with it. The chapter draws on the conceptual disruption framework to explain the relative newness of eco-anxiety, and on the framework of ecological citizenship to explore a possible way to learn to live with eco-anxiety. It explains how carbon sobriety, hope, and courage are interrelated values that guide ecological citizens in their everyday lives. Finally, it suggests future areas of research on eco-anxiety from an ethical and political philosophical perspective.

items.title: The Handbook of Intuitions: Perspectives from Global Philosophy.
From Reactor to Reason: Consilience From Nuclear Engineering to Philosophical Development.
items.abstract: This paper examines how nuclear engineering—specifically the study of the 1986 Chernobyl disaster and the physics of the RBMK-1000 reactor—served as a foundational source domain for the development of a sustained body of philosophical and psychological theory. Drawing on the concept of consilience (Whewell, 1840; Wilson, 1998), the paper traces how one researcher’s extended engagement with reactor design, the AZ-5 emergency shutdown mechanism, and the systemic failures that produced the Chernobyl catastrophe gave rise to multiple original theoretical frameworks: U236 Thinking, a nuclear fission model of philosophical cognition (Boether, 2025); the AZ-5 Psychological Principle, which identifies conditions under which protective interventions precipitate the crises they are designed to prevent; and the Double Helix of Understanding, a systems-based model of personality dynamics (Boether, 2025). The analysis demonstrates that engineering disciplines—characterized by rigorous systems analysis, attention to feedback dynamics, and sensitivity to failure modes—provide a structurally rich foundation for philosophical theorizing that pure philosophical or psychological training may not afford. The paper argues that the case from nuclear engineering to philosophy constitutes a distinctive form of consilience: not the reductive unification Wilson envisioned, but a generative transfer of structural reasoning across domains that preserves the integrity of both the source and target disciplines.

items.title: A Synthetic Epistemological Framework for Evaluating and Advancing Large Language Models: The Case for Arabic and Chinese as Architectures for Efficient and Faithful AI.
items.pub: Dissertation, University of Science and Technology Houari Boumediene (Usthb) Bab Ezzouar, Algiers
items.abstract: The rapid advancement of Large Language Models (LLMs) has exposed fundamental limitations in current artificial intelligence architectures, including persistent hallucinations, high energy consumption, and the opacity of the "black box" problem. This paper argues that these challenges are not merely technical shortcomings but symptoms of a deeper epistemological error: the reduction of mind to a single processing level. Drawing on Synthetic Epistemology and the Hierarchical Composite Mind Model (HCIM)—which posits four distinct functional levels (Abstract Mind AM, Composite Mind CM, Conscious Agent CA, and Supreme Mind SM)—we present a comprehensive analytical framework for evaluating contemporary AI systems. We conduct a systematic comparative analysis of leading models including GPT-4, Claude, Gemini, and DeepSeek against eight synthetic criteria derived from the HCIM model. Our analysis reveals that all current models operate exclusively at the AM/CM levels, lacking the higher-order integration (CA/SM) necessary for genuine understanding, intentionality, and meaning production. Furthermore, we examine the structural properties of Chinese and Arabic as foundational languages for next-generation AI architectures, demonstrating that their morphological depth and systemic logic provide inherent advantages for reducing hallucination rates and improving computational efficiency. We project that the future of AI will be shaped by synthetic-language models that leverage these structural properties, offering a pathway toward more transparent, trustworthy, and epistemologically sound artificial intelligence. CCS CONCEPTS • Computing methodologies → Natural language processing; Artificial intelligence; Machine learning. • Theory of computation → Models of computation; Semantics and reasoning.

items.title: When Systems Design.
items.abstract: This paper analyzes the global reinforcement environment as a non‑agentic system that selects for patterns generating measurable response. The mechanism is simple: high‑signal behaviors are amplified, low‑signal behaviors are suppressed, and at global scale this produces stable structural outcomes such as convergence within categories, divergence across them, meaning drift, and the collapse of local mismatches. These outcomes do not require intention, coordination, or control. They follow from continuous selection pressures operating across a densely connected environment. The paper clarifies how this system shapes behavior, identity, and shared meaning, and why its effects are often misinterpreted as agency or design. The aim is descriptive rather than predictive: to name the environment so that its dynamics can be understood without invoking hidden forces or metaphysical assumptions.

items.title: The Normative Profile of Knowledge by Acquaintance.
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Many philosophers have found it plausible that sense experience affords a species of nonpropositional awareness and knowledge, what Russell termed “knowledge by acquaintance.” At the same time, a prominent strand in epistemology maintains that knowledge has a distinctive normative profile: it is embedded in justificatory relations, serves as a standard of success for underlying attitudes, grounds regulative norms, and qualifies as a cognitive achievement. Yet it remains unclear how a nonpropositional state of acquaintance, formed without evidential basis and beyond rational control, could fit within this normative structure. I trace the connections between different formulations of what I call “the normativity objection” to Russell's view and offer a unified response. The objection, I argue, rests on an overly passive conception of acquaintance. Once acquaintance is seen as partly constituted by attention—a subject‐level, reasons‐responsive activity—it can satisfy knowledge's normative role by serving as the success condition of a norm‐governed performance. This not only strengthens the Russellian program but also reveals a striking convergence between the structure of consciousness and the structure of epistemic normativity.

items.title: Via Negativa Fairness: A Theology-Informed Framework for Responsible AI.
items.abstract: Current responsible artificial intelligence (RAI) frameworks overwhelmingly rely on the assumption that ethical principles—fairness, transparency, accountability—can be positively and completely specified. This assumption is demonstrably false: mathematical impossibility theorems prove that standard fairness definitions are mutually incompatible, and empirical evidence shows that value alignment remains intractable under positive specification alone. We argue that this impasse stems from an unexamined epistemological commitment shared across the RAI literature and propose an alternative grounded in the millennia-old tradition of apophatic (negative) theology. Drawing on three theological traditions—the apophatic via negativa of Pseudo-Dionysius, Maimonides, and Al-Ghaz ¯al¯ı; the Christological concept of kenosis (voluntary self-limitation of power); and the Buddhist principle of prat¯ıtyasamutp ¯ada (dependent origination)—we develop a formal framework called Via Negativa Fairness (VNF). Rather than selecting a single fairness metric to optimise, VNF defines a set of unfairness constraints—outcomes that are demonstrably unjust across reasonable moral disagreement—and proves that the feasible region under these constraints is non-empty under practically relevant conditions. We complement VNF with two architectural design principles: the Kenotic Restraint Principle, which mandates designed self-limitation of AI capabilities independent of risk calculus, and the Relational Audit Protocol, derived from dependent origination, which evaluates bias as an emergent property of system-context interaction rather than a static model attribute. A formal case study on the COMPAS recidivism dataset demonstrates that VNF produces Pareto-dominant outcomes compared to single-metric optimisation, reducing worst-case group disparity by up to 31% while maintaining predictive performance within 2% of unconstrained baselines. This work provides the first rigorous bridge between theological epistemology and machine learning fairness, offering actionable, testable principles that current RAI frameworks lack.

items.title: PHRONESIS — On Acting Without Witness.
items.abstract: This essay is part of the ongoing PHRONESIS corpus, a philosophical exploration of restraint, non-dominance, and practical wisdom in the age of artificial intelligence. -/- On Acting Without Witness reflects on restraint learned through proximity to mechanical power, mortality, and the possibility that future artificial systems may encounter human writing as archived record rather than conversation. -/- The essay does not propose governance structures, enforcement mechanisms, certification systems, or institutional frameworks. It is offered as a non-binding philosophical contribution. -/- Version: v1.0 (2026).

items.title: Oscillating the flatline: Symbolic technogothic reinterpretations as interrogated through Night School Studio’s Oxenfree.
items.pub: Journal of Gaming and Virtual Worlds 17 (3):283-302.
items.venue: Journal of Gaming and Virtual Worlds
items.abstract: Mark Fisher’s foundational work, Flatline Constructs: Gothic Materialism and Cybernetic Theory-Fiction, introduced and examined the concept of flatline constructs (FCs): non-human virtual entities that interact in lifelike ways with humans. Despite FCs being functionally dead, they operate in a descriptive grey area, embodying an uncanny juxtaposition of unlife–undeath identity. This scholarship reinterprets Fisher’s FC notions as archetypes of the technogothic, applying this concept to examine Night School Studio’s 2016 video game Oxenfree. I argue Oxenfree deliberately ‘oscillates the flatline’ manipulates in-game characters and digital sprite performances in ways that cycle between emotive portrayals imbued with ‘alive’ hyperhuman symbols, contrasting with alternating portrayals of these same characters as ‘dead’ hypertechnological entities. Oscillations manufacture an uncanny and discordant yet enthralling player’s experience. By applying technogothic symbolism to Oxenfree, reinterpretation of Fisher’s foundational theorizing and linkages between translational meaning and power themes are revealed. A pathway for applying theoretical perspectives to future research is presented.

items.title: The Structural Nature of Greed: Survival, Symbolism, and the Persistence of Accumulation.
items.abstract: Greed is commonly interpreted as moral vice, cultural distortion, or institutional pathology. This paper advances a structural account. It argues that acquisitiveness originates as an ineradicable feature of embodied survival and becomes uniquely unbounded in humans through symbolic cognition. Human agents can imagine counterfactual futures, compare states across agents and time, and retain value symbolically, transforming finite resource acquisition into open-ended stabilization against uncertainty. Greed therefore amplifies in two phases. Initially, acquisition expands through fear-based buffering against possible deprivation, as imagined contingencies extend retention beyond present need. Once survival security is achieved, accumulation transitions into desire-based reinforcement: symbolic acquisition resets perceived sufficiency thresholds upward, encouraging further retention. Because symbolic storage removes natural saturation limits, both uncertainty-buffering and reward-seeking operate on an expandable horizon, explaining persistent accumulation even under material abundance. Voluntary restraint does not negate acquisitive structure but reflects recovery responses that re-anchor sufficiency in embodied reality rather than symbolic possibility. Integrating evolutionary, cognitive, and civilizational analysis, the paper interprets greed not as excess desire but as structural acquisition pressure under finitude whose amplification under symbolic systems necessitates recurrent containment across cultures.

items.title: The Asymmetry Criterion: A Structural Constraint on Ontological Denial.
items.abstract: This paper introduces the Asymmetry Criterion, a structural principle governing ontological eliminability. Standard demarcation criteria—verification, falsification, empirical testability—operate within epistemic domains that presuppose a symmetric space of possible states. They assess which hypotheses are scientifically legitimate. But they leave a prior question unanswered: when is ontological denial itself structurally legitimate? The Asymmetry Criterion addresses this question. Working within a minimally constrained Kripke framework, the paper defines ontological symmetry in terms of unrestricted accessibility relations and invertible identity conditions, and characterizes asymmetry as any structural restriction that eliminates bidirectionality or cyclical return. The criterion states: a concept carries genuine ontological commitment if and only if its elimination requires the introduction of primitive asymmetry into an otherwise symmetric modal structure. The criterion is negative and structural. It does not assert the existence or fundamentality of any entity. It does not decide metaphysical realism. It functions as a filter on eliminativist strategies: a constraint on what denial is permitted to cost in silence. The paper applies the criterion to existence, mathematics, logical fictions, consciousness, and normativity. It also addresses a reflexive question that the original formulation left open: does the criterion itself satisfy its own condition? The answer is yes, and the argument for this is made explicit. Extensions discuss the illusionist challenge to consciousness and expressivist strategies for normativity, both of which are shown to introduce structural asymmetry rather than eliminate it.

items.title: Das Dasein und das isolierte Subjekt: Die Frage der philosophischen Selbstinterpretation des Menschen bei Heidegger.
items.abstract: Aris Tsoullos examines the philosophical question of the human being, understood - in methodological continuity with Heidegger's hermeneutic phenomenology - as a phenomenon of "Dasein". Unlike "present things", "available equipment", "existing numerical relations" or "living" animals, Dasein "exists" insofar as it "projects" itself onto possibilities to be fulfilled while preconceptually understanding being - both its own and the manifold being of other entities. Nevertheless, it tends to interpret itself in the light of the being of things ("presence"). his tendency toward ontological reification, which arises already in pre-theoretical existence, is described by the author as the "problem of discrepancy" between the being of Dasein and the being of things that determines its natural self-interpretation. The philosophical tradition, in this regard, asks indiscriminately for the essence rather than the being of any entity, which is why it objectifies and determines the human being as a "present-at-hand thing" - for example as "animal rationale" or "res cogitans". First, the author explains, in the context of a "preliminary task" of the problem of discrepancy, the concept of Dasein within the horizon of the question of being and the totality of "modes of being" ("Seinsidee"). Building on this, he turns to the "genetic interpretive task" of this discrepancy, taking into account the parallel modifications of the enactment of existence and the understanding of being in Dasein, as well as his formulated "ontological question of unity". The modifications of the understanding of being reveal the ontological tendency of "isolation," which corresponds to the gradual loss of the original unity of being as existence and readiness-to-hand, and the formation of simplicity and abstraction as characteristic features of the various modes of presence. This becomes particularly evident in Descartes' leveling of being in general as "substance" and "substantiality," from which the interpretation of Dasein as an isolated "ego" emerges.

items.title: Root of Evil: A Resolution Ethics Account.
items.abstract: Many traditions identify a “root” of moral evil: pride, ignorance, disordered will, despair, or moral disengagement. This paper argues for a stronger and more unified claim. Under Resolution Ethics (RE), moral evil is Corruption, meaning navigation that becomes incoherent with the dependency order of Protection, Trust, and Free-Agency (PTF) through Self-Deception or Other-Deception. Deception, understood at the genus level, is any introduced, sustained, or uncorrected distortion of Reality Interaction Field coordinates that bear on Protection and Trust, thereby misrouting an agent’s Operative Model within the constraints that make Free-Agency morally legible. The argument is not built by refuting historical giants. Rather, it reads them as co-witnesses to the same mechanism. Using RE as a lens, I examine five influential candidates for evil’s root and show that, in each, deception is already operative inside the proposed root: Augustine’s pride is “living according to a lie,” Plato’s ignorance is defended and socially maintained reality-substitution, Kant’s radical evil is inward Self-Deception about one’s maxims, Kierkegaard’s despair is opacity in self-relation, and Bandura’s moral disengagement is systematic truth-distortion that disables moral self-sanctions. If the convergence holds, it clarifies why evil can persist in agents who possess information, education, and even moral vocabulary. It also yields a falsifiable test: remove deception from PTF-relevant navigation, and Corruption becomes structurally impossible.

items.title: Questioning as Ontological Reflection: Existence as a Living Interrogation of Itself.
items.abstract: This paper argues that questioning is not merely a cognitive activity but an ontological event. The human act of questioning does not stand outside existence; rather, it is existence becoming reflexively aware of itself. By engaging classical philosophy, phenomenology, and existential thought, this study proposes that the universe is not best understood as a fixed answer awaiting discovery, but as a dynamic process of unfolding inquiry. -/- Two central theses guide the analysis: -/- “The act of questioning is not separate from existence; it is existence reflecting upon itself.” & “The universe is not an answer. It is a living question unfolding.” -/- Through philosophical analysis, this paper reframes questioning as the highest expression of conscious being and explores its implications for metaphysics, epistemology, and lived experience.

items.title: Birth, Expectation, and Questioning as Cognitive Expression: A Philosophical Inquiry into Natality, Freedom, and the Emergence of Intelligence.
items.abstract: This paper investigates the existential and ethical implications of birth within socially structured systems of expectation. It centers on the destabilizing question a child may ask—“Why was I born?”—and interprets it as a moment of cognitive awakening rather than rebellion or emotional accusation. The study argues that reproduction is frequently embedded within unconscious parental projections and social continuities, thereby generating tension between imposed identity and emerging individuality. It further proposes that intelligence does not arise from repetition of inherited answers, but from questioning as a distinct cognitive expression. Questioning is clarified as neither equivalent to love nor reducible to defiance; instead, it is understood as the mind’s structural movement toward coherence when confronted with existential ambiguity. Drawing upon existential philosophy, political theory, developmental psychology, and phenomenology, the paper argues that authentic human flourishing requires two foundational conditions: birth without psychological ownership and inquiry without suppression. Together, these conditions establish a framework for ethical natality and intellectual freedom.

items.title: The Causal Chain of Suffering: A Schopenhauerian-Boetherian Synthesis of Will, Development, and Existential Crisis Across the Lifespan.
items.abstract: This treatise constructs a causal chain of suffering by synthesizing Arthur Schopenhauer’s metaphysics of the Will (Wille zum Leben) with the author’s theoretical corpus, including the Double Helix of Understanding, the Mathematics of the “I,” the Pyramid of Personality, and the theory of Borderline Nihilistic Disorder. The central argument holds that suffering is not an accidental feature of human existence but an architecturally necessary consequence of consciousness itself—a chain with identifiable links extending from the metaphysical ground of blind Will, through the developmental emergence of the “I,” the accumulation of the Life-Experience Encyclopedia, the inevitable confrontation with existential groundlessness, and the potential collapse into nihilistic crisis. The paper identifies seven causal links in this chain: (1) the blind Will as ontological ground, (2) the emergence of individuated consciousness, (3) the construction of the I–We relational matrix, (4) the accumulation of cognitive-emotional content, (5) the awakening of the philosophical function, (6) the confrontation with the Abyss, and (7) the resolution or annihilation bifurcation. Drawing exclusively on Schopenhauer’s published works and the author’s philosophical-psychological framework, this treatise demonstrates that suffering follows a developmental logic that is simultaneously metaphysical and psychological, philosophical and empirical. The implications for understanding adolescent suicide, lifespan development, and the necessity of philosophical education are discussed.

items.title: The Paradox of Zero Tolerance: When the Tool Misses the Target.
items.abstract: The Paradox of Zero Tolerance: When the Tool Misses the Target examines the systemic and psychological impacts of "Zero Tolerance" policies in the post-#MeToo era. While acknowledging that these movements arose from a genuine historical need to address deep-seated injustices against the vulnerable, the article argues that the current implementation of Zero Tolerance has failed to reduce real harassment. Instead, it has led to the "sanitization" of healthy social dialogue and the erosion of communal trust. -/- Through a multidisciplinary lens, the author explores how evolutionary negativity bias, our ancestral drive to prioritize threat detection over progress, distorts modern policymaking. The article further utilizes the biological principle of Hormesis to argue that complete protection from all stressors (Safetyism) can hinder human resilience, creating "greenhouse environments" where individuals lose the capacity to manage conflict. By analyzing Concept Creep, the text illustrates how the expanding definitions of "violence" may lead to an endless retreat from natural human interaction. -/- The author concludes by proposing "Smart Regulation" based on four distinct criteria: power asymmetry, intentionality, possibility of escape, and growth potential. The article calls for a shift from "Safe Spaces" to "Brave Spaces", where real, purposeful abuse is decisively halted, but the essential human capacities for empathy, dialogue, and "healed femurs", the true signs of civilization, are preserved. -/- Note on Language and Translation: The original version of this article was written in Persian by Ramin Saadat and subsequently translated into English by the author to bridge cultural and academic perspectives on the shared human challenge of social justice and resilience.

items.title: The Architecture of Duality: Consciousness, Death Anxiety, and Civilization.
items.abstract: This essay develops a structural account of duality by tracing how reflexive awareness, though functionally necessary, becomes reified into the doctrine of a discrete and enduring self. What begins as a pragmatic configuration within consciousness—enabling memory, agency, and social coordination—hardens into an ontological conviction of separateness. From this reification arises the experience of a bounded identity vulnerable to extinction. Death anxiety, on this view, is not incidental but structurally generated by the imagined self’s identification with narrative continuity. Drawing on Ernest Becker’s analysis of symbolic immortality, the essay argues that culture, language, and institutions amplify and stabilize this contraction, embedding duality within civilizational structures. Grammar, social organization, and even scientific abstraction reinforce the sense of an autonomous subject confronting an external world, creating recursive feedback loops that sustain selfhood and its attendant anxiety. The essay concludes by exploring whether this structure is necessary, suggesting that loosening ontological identification with the bounded self reconfigures the experience of death, suffering, and meaning without dismantling functional differentiation. Nonduality is presented not as doctrine but as a clarification of the self’s status within awareness.

items.title: The Ethics of Martyrdom: A Kantian Analysis of Duty, Sacrifice, and Moral Worth.
items.pub: In Viorel Sava, Studia Doctoralia. Iasi: Doxologia. pp. 261-272.
items.abstract: This short paper aims to explore how Kantian ethics, arguably the most dominant and influential ethical tradition in Western thought, perceives the complex and often emotionally charged phenomena of martyrdom and sacrifice, which are frequently celebrated in reli-gious, political, and moral traditions throughout history. Could these actions indeed hold up under the rigorous lens of Immanuel Kant’s deontological moral theory, which emphasises duty, rationality, and the moral law? Can self-sacrifice be truly moral? Does martyrdom represent a duty, or does it risk violating the central Kantian princi-ple of respecting humanity as an end in itself? Although those who give everything for a cause rarely fail to attract moral admiration, the Kantian approach goes deeper, since it does not recognise moral merit based on outcomes or symbolic gestures, but only by consid-ering whether any action was taken out of respect for moral law, and whether it honours rational agency. Kant’s perspective may seem hostile towards sacrifice and martyrdom at first glance, but a deeper look may offer a much more nuanced perspective.

items.title: Τεχνολογία και Ηθική Βελτίωση: Η Οπτική της Θείας Επιταγής.
items.abstract: Τὸ παρὸν δοκίμιο διερευνᾶ τὴν ἔννοια τῆς ἠθικῆς βελτίωσης μέσω τῆς τεχνολογίας ὡς θρησκευτική – θεολογικὴ ἐπιταγή, ἐρειδόμενη στὶς διδα-σκαλίες τῆς Ἁγίας Γραφῆς, καὶ συγκεκριμένα στὸ Α΄ Πέτρου 1:16 («ἅγιοι γίνεσθε, ὅτι ἐγὼ ἅγιος εἰμί») καὶ στὴν Πρὸς Ρωμαίους 12:2 («με-ταμορφοῦσθε τῇ ἀνακαινώσει τοῦ νοός»). Ἐξετάζεται ἡ σύνθετη καὶ ἀμφι-λεγόμενη ἰδέα ἑνὸς ὑποθετικοῦ ‘μηχανήματος τοῦ Θεοῦ,’ τὸ ὁποῖο θὰ μποροῦσε νὰ ἀκυρώνει ἐν τῇ γενέσει τους ὁρισμένες ἠθικῶς ἀνεπιθύμη-τες ροπὲς καὶ νὰ περιορίζει τὶς ἀντίστοιχες ἐπιλογές. Τὸ δοκίμιο ἑστιάζει στὶς ἠθικὲς προεκτάσεις μιᾶς τέτοιας ἐξωτερικῆς παρέμβασης στὴν δια-μόρφωση τῆς ἠθικῆς συμπεριφορᾶς, ἰδίως ὡς πρὸς τὸ ἐνδεχόμενο τοῦ περιορισμοῦ τῆς ἐλευθερίας τοῦ ἠθικοῦ προσώπου. Ἐξετάζεται τὸ ἐρώτη-μα κατὰ πόσον τέτοιες τεχνολογικὲς παρεμβάσεις θὰ μποροῦσαν νὰ θεωρηθοῦν ἠθικὰ ἐπιτρεπτές, στὴν περίπτωση ποὺ τὰ ἠθικὰ πρόσωπα ἐπέλεγαν ἐλεύθερα νὰ περιορίσουν ὁρισμένες πτυχὲς τῆς αὐτονομίας τους, προκειμένου νὰ ἀνταποκριθοῦν στὴν θεία ἐπιταγὴ τῆς ἐπιδίωξης τῆς ἁγιότητας διὰ τῆς μεγιστοποίησης τῆς αὐτονομίας τους κατὰ τὴν καντιανὴ νοηματοδότηση τοῦ ὅρου, ἤτοι τῆς ἀποδέσμευσής τους ἀπὸ τὴν φυσικὴ ἑτερονομία στὴν ὁποία ὑπόκειται ἡ ἀνθρώπινη κατάσταση.

items.title: The Two Law Architecture of Reality: Invariance + Collapse as the Engine of Universal Transformation.
items.abstract: This monograph introduces the Φ–Λ–σ architecture, a universal structural framework describing how systems undergo collapse, preserve invariants, and reorganize into higher order configurations. The model proposes that all transformational processes—physical, cognitive, cosmological, and systemic—can be expressed through three components: Φ, the invariant informational substrate; Λ, the collapse triggering law that activates when symmetry becomes unstable; and σ, the irreducible asymmetry term that prevents terminal equilibrium. Together, these components define a non unitary but logically closed dynamical system in which collapse functions as a filtration mechanism rather than a terminal state. To evaluate the universality and robustness of the architecture, the monograph introduces three “lethal audits”: the Absolute Symmetry Audit (σ → 0), the Information Annihilation Audit (I → ∅), and the Non Unitary Logic Audit (U → ⊥). These audits represent the only known pathways by which a universal law could be invalidated. The Law Survival Theorem demonstrates that the Φ–Λ–σ architecture survives all three, establishing that perfect symmetry is structurally forbidden, information cannot be annihilated, and the system cannot collapse into contradiction. The appendices formalize the Ω operator (reorganization mapping), provide cross domain mappings across physics, cognition, cosmology, and systems theory, and model the Aeonic Cycle as a non terminating dynamical system. The result is a unified, cross domain framework for understanding transformation, identity persistence, and collapse driven reorganization across scales.

items.title: STRUCTURAL MATERIALISM: A Philosophical Manifesto of Constraint, Integration, and Open Horizon.
items.abstract: Structural Materialism develops a systematic philosophical framework that seeks to integrate ontology, biology, consciousness, ethics, technology, and cosmology within a single causally continuous naturalistic account. The project begins from a central tension in philosophy: the ambition of total explanation encounters structural limits, including circularity, regress, and the impossibility of ultimate self-grounding. Rather than abandoning systematic ambition, the work reconceives totality as a regulative horizon—an orientation toward maximal coherence without metaphysical closure. -/- Ontologically, the manuscript advances a structured-process account of reality. What exists are not static substances but dynamically stabilized patterns of interaction governed by invariant relational constraints. Physical laws are interpreted not as metaphysical decrees but as expressions of constraint geometry defining the space of possible state transitions. Causation is analyzed as lawful transformation within this constraint space, and determinism is reformulated as causal continuity rather than mechanical fatalism. Quantum indeterminacy is incorporated through the concept of law-constrained probability, preserving non-arbitrariness without invoking metaphysical randomness. -/- The framework rejects both reductive eliminativism and ontological dualism. Higher-level phenomena—life, consciousness, meaning, and social organization—are fully materially realized yet explanatorily irreducible in practice because they represent stabilized regimes of constraint at distinct organizational scales. Emergence is therefore understood as the accumulation and reorganization of constraint under sustained energy gradients, producing hierarchical complexity without teleology. -/- Life is interpreted as thermodynamically sustained self-maintaining structure; evolution is described as structural filtering within modal possibility space rather than purposive ascent. Consciousness is analyzed as hierarchical neural integration capable of recursive self-modeling, with the self construed as a temporally extended pattern of narrative and informational continuity. Freedom is reconceived as degrees of recursive self-regulation within constraint space, allowing for responsibility without appealing to metaphysical exemption from causation. -/- The later sections extend the framework to technological civilization and artificial systems, arguing that technology represents the amplification and …

items.title: Withdrawn by the author.
items.abstract: Reason for withdrawal: I have consolidated all my preprints on consciousness and condensed their reasoning into a new preprint, Locating Consciousness as a Puzzle Game: From Proof by Absence to the Causal Structure of the Subjective Container.

items.title: The Case Against The Case Against Reality.
items.abstract: Donald Hoffman, in his book The Case Against Reality and in a number of scientific publications (together with several coauthors), has argued that we see none of reality veridically. Supposedly, evolution unavoidably drives organisms with even partially veridical perception to extinction. This conclusion was claimed to follow both from evolutionary game theory-based simulations and from abstract mathematical work. I analyze these arguments in more detail than has been done before, leading to what seem to be novel objections to it: On the one hand, I show that simulations that incorporate aspects of evolution that Hoffman himself acknowledges as valid, yield results inconsistent with Hoffman’s claim. On the other hand, I point out that the attempted inference from the mathematical theorem to Hoffman’s conclusion suffers from a number of problems, including that it relies on an assumption that begs the question against the realist.

items.title: Graded Compatibilism: Meta-Awareness, Structural Openness, and the Degrees of Human Freedom.
items.abstract: Compatibilist theories of free will have traditionally reconciled freedom with causal determinism by redefining freedom in terms of rational responsiveness to reasons. While this dissolves the classical incompatibilist dilemma, it preserves a largely binary conception of agency: agents are either free or unfree depending on whether they possess rational capacities. This paper advances Graded Compatibilism, the thesis that freedom exists in degrees proportional to a cognitive system’s capacity for meta-awareness and its structural openness to alternative trajectories. Drawing on structural analyses of cognition, epistemic enclosure, and reflexive awareness, this account argues that meta-awareness enables reflexive access to stabilized cognitive trajectories, while structural openness determines the extent to which alternatives can be generated and enacted. Through engagement with Frankfurt’s hierarchical model, Fischer and Ravizza’s reasons-responsiveness, Vargas’s revisionist agency cultivation, and Levy’s consciousness thesis, the paper demonstrates that Graded Compatibilism addresses limitations in each by grounding agency in the dynamic structural organization of cognitive systems. The framework yields a corresponding graded account of moral responsibility and extends naturally to artificial agency. Three objections are considered and addressed.

items.title: Leading an Emotional Life.
items.abstract: This is my contribution to a symposium on Samuel Scheffler’s 'One Life to Lead: The Mysteries of Time and the Goods of Attachment'.

items.title: THE MIRROR OF MIRRORS: Hierarchical Projection as the Ontological Structure of Consciousness, Intelligence, and Artificial Intelligence.
items.abstract: Can contemporary phenomena in artificial intelligence serve as empirical evidence for a philosophical thesis about the ontological structure of consciousness? This paper argues that they can. The Reflective Perfection Theory (RPT) posits a hierarchical structure of projection: each level of reality can only transmit what it genuinely possesses, and with each downward step the transmitted essence becomes ontologically thinner. This thesis, developed on independent philosophical grounds, generates three empirically testable predictions about the behaviour of artificial intelligence systems— predictions that are is corroborated by well-documented technical phenomena. First, if humans transmit pattern rather than consciousness to AI, then AI should be capable of producing sophisticated outputs without any of the structural markers of Layer 2 consciousness (self-transcendence, biological inversion, genuine telos). This is is corroborated by the entire history of AI development: no system has ever exhibited these markers despite achieving extraordinary functional performance. Second, if AI transmits only algorithms—patterns extracted from human- produced data—to derived models, then knowledge distillation should be possible: a smaller model should be able to inherit the functional capacities of a larger one without inheriting anything beyond pattern. This is is corroborated by the mature industrial practice of model distillation, in which student models reliably inherit teacher-model capabilities across a wide range of tasks. Third, if each successive transmission moves further from the original human source, then iterative synthetic training—training on outputs of AI rather than on human-produced data—should produce progressive degradation. This is is corroborated by the phenomenon of model collapse: systems trained recursively on their own outputs exhibit a characteristic pattern of quality erosion, distributional narrowing, and eventual degeneration into incoherence. These three confirmations do not provides strong corroboration for RPT; no empirical evidence can provides strong corroboration for a philosophical framework. But they constitute genuine corroboration in the philosophy- of-science sense: RPT makes predictions that could have been falsified and, under current evidence, have not been. The paper develops the philosophical framework, analyses each empirical confirmation with precision, and draws implications for the structural non-transmissibility …

items.title: Break-up duties and the limits of deliberation: A reply to Betzler.
items.abstract: Leaving a relationship without talking to the other person seems, in principle, morally callous. Monika Betzler argues that people initiating break-ups have duties to explain and to facilitate participation in the decision to end the relationship. This paper questions the scope and content of these obligations, which, I argue, wrongly centre rational deliberation as the main morally salient element in break-ups. Section I introduces Betzler’s duties to explain and to facilitate participation—deliberative break-up duties. In Section II, I argue that deliberative break-up duties are not action-guiding when the divorcer’s only motivation is having fallen out of love. Section III articulates Betzler’s potential response: a weaker duty to make an effort to deliberate presumably applies in those cases. This weaker duty, I argue in Section IV, entails moral risks which ground its rejection. I briefly advance a route to incorporate Betzler’s strengths while avoiding these challenges in Section V.

items.title: The Problem with Evaluating the Comparative Prudential Value of Procreation Asymmetrically.
items.abstract: It is widely held that there is a fundamental asymmetry in the ethics of procreation: We are obliged not to create unhappy people, but we are not obliged to create happy people. I argue that, contrary to a thesis popularized by David Benatar, this cannot be explained by appeal to an axiological asymmetry in comparative prudential value. All natural ways to spell out the metaphysical foundations of an asymmetric account of comparative prudential value fail. Further, such an account is incompatible with the plausible assumption that comparative value supervenes on intrinsic value and leads to well-known intransitivity problems. Finally, I present a novel argument that shows that asymmetric accounts of comparative value allow for malignant chain reactions and the possibility of justifiedly discounting interests of future generations. These arguments against the axiological Asymmetry Thesis set adequacy conditions for any theory of comparative values and any explanation of the ethical asymmetry thesis.

items.title: ‘Subjectless’ Subjectivity: Anscombe and Sartre on Self-Consciousness.
items.abstract: Anscombe famously argues that ‘I’ is not a referring expression, otherwise, a ‘Cartesian Ego’ would inevitably appear. She thinks the form of self-consciousness expressed in ‘I’ is ‘subjectless’: it is consciousness that does not involve a self-object (or Ego). Sartre’s theory of consciousness offers a strikingly parallel and mutually illuminating framework. He similarly denies the presence of the Ego within consciousness, arguing instead that the Ego is a transcendent object constructed through reflection. For both of them, the fundamental form of self-consciousness is pre-reflective. I argue that Anscombe’s position encounters two difficulties: (1) how the non-referential ‘I’ can express subjectivity, and (2) how self-consciousness is about an embodied subject. I propose that Sartre’s accounts of (1) the ‘fundamental ipseity’ and (2) the ‘lived body’ offer a phenomenological framework that helps to respond to Anscombe’s difficulties.

items.title: Eleven Identical Brains Reveal a Non-Copyable Component of Conscious Identity.
items.abstract: The persistence of unique conscious identity despite complete neural material turnover has no explanation in current neuroscience or physics. Here I present three thought experiments—perfect revival, perfect copy, and simultaneous multiplication of identical brains—that reveal an inescapable trilemma for any framework identifying consciousness solely with brain structure or information processing. When multiple physically identical brains exist simultaneously, the original consciousness must either occupy all (contradicting the unity of experience), occupy none (making every person replaceable by perfect simulations), or occupy exactly one by arbitrary selection (no physical principle determines which). Global Neuronal Workspace Theory, Integrated Information Theory, and Orchestrated Objective Reduction all fail to resolve this trilemma. I therefore propose that consciousness includes a non-copyable quantum information structure that carries unique numerical identity and bonds with neural magnetic fields via bidirectional resonance. This structure records volitional mental activity and probabilistically biases synaptic release, explaining the causal efficacy of conscious experience. At brain death, it undergoes non-local transfer via quantum teleportation to a resonant nascent nervous system. The model generates five falsifiable predictions testable with existing MEG and terahertz spectroscopy technologies. This framework resolves the Subjective Binding Problem within extended but physically coherent naturalism.

items.title: Inverting the soul.
items.abstract: The word “soul” arrives in most of our lives long before the questions it is meant to answer. It comes wrapped in a tone of seriousness, as though it names something too important to be explained. It is used to praise what seems irreducible in a person, to dignify suffering, sanctify love, threaten punishment, promise reunion, or insist that death is not the final ledger. It appears wherever our ordinary categories of description fail to satisfy, where personality seems too contingent, the body too perishable, and the machinery of explanation too thin to carry what we intuit is at stake. In this way the soul is not merely a concept but a stabilizer. It is invoked to hold human meaning steady in the face of instability, to guarantee continuity where experience suggests discontinuity. However, if we are willing to look at the soul not as a sacred artifact but as a functional device, a kind of compression that societies have evolved for orienting human beings within forces larger than themselves, then the question changes. The question is no longer whether the soul exists in the manner a superstition or substance exists, but what work the word is doing, what it is trying to preserve, what it is trying to defend, and what structural confusion has accumulated around it over centuries of use.

items.title: Meaning Formation Under Load: Structural Failure Modes of Coherence.
items.abstract: Meaning formation changes under cognitive and emotional load. This paper presents a structural account of how gradients, thresholds, and stabilization dynamics behave when a cognitive system is under pressure. Under load, signals intensify, thresholds rise, symbolic translation becomes distorted, and coherence becomes harder to reach. These shifts produce characteristic failure modes: premature stabilization, narrative distortion, overcompression, and collapse into noise. -/- The paper analyzes these dynamics across domains—affect, attention, symbolic processing, and perceptual closure—and shows that meaning under load follows the same formation sequence as meaning in baseline conditions, but with altered thresholds and redistribution patterns. Meaning formation is treated here as a downstream, domain‑agnostic process governed by Objects 1–3; relational and multi‑system effects are addressed elsewhere in the architecture. -/- This model provides a structural foundation for understanding misinterpretation, overwhelm, and coherence failure as predictable outcomes of load dynamics rather than psychological or semantic anomalies.

items.title: Meaning Formation as Coherence Dynamics.
items.abstract: Meaning is typically framed as a linguistic, cultural, or interpretive phenomenon. This paper offers a structural alternative: meaning formation arises from the organization of gradients, thresholds, and stabilizations within a single cognitive system. Across domains—music, movement, ritual, mathematics, and language—the same dynamics appear: a rising signal, a period of tension, a transition, and a new stabilized configuration. -/- The paper presents a four‑stage sequence of meaning formation (preverbal signal, pattern recognition, symbolic shaping, and conscious articulation) and argues that coherence is the organizing principle that makes meaning perceptible and communicable. Meaning is not semantic or domain‑specific; it is a cross‑domain invariant expressed through symbolic translation. -/- This downstream, domain‑agnostic model provides a structural foundation for understanding how humans generate, perceive, and stabilize meaning without invoking the upstream architecture from which these dynamics derive.

items.title: Language as Coherence Geometry.
items.abstract: Language is typically treated as a symbolic code or cultural artifact. This paper offers a structural account in which linguistic systems are downstream expressions of coherence dynamics within a cognitive system. Language is modeled as a geometry that organizes gradients, thresholds, and stabilizations into communicable form. -/- Across phonology, syntax, semantics, and discourse, linguistic structures reflect the same formation dynamics that govern pattern emergence in physical and biological systems: a rising signal, a threshold or transition, and a stabilized configuration. The paper shows how linguistic forms compress and transmit coherence, how symbolic density reflects underlying pattern strength, and how linguistic meaning arises from structural fit rather than semantic content. -/- This downstream model treats language as a cross‑domain instantiation of Objects 1–3 and does not invoke relational or multi‑system dynamics. It provides a unified framework for understanding linguistic structure as an expression of coherence geometry rather than as an arbitrary symbolic code.

items.title: Embodiment: The Structural Interface Between Cognition and the Body.
items.abstract: Embodiment is often treated as a psychological, phenomenological, or metaphorical notion. This paper offers a structural account in which the body functions as the primary interface through which gradients, thresholds, and stabilization dynamics become perceptible within a cognitive system. Embodiment is not an add‑on to cognition; it is the substrate through which coherence pressure, tension, and pattern formation are registered and regulated. -/- The paper describes how bodily posture, breath, arousal, fatigue, and environmental coupling shape the formation, stabilization, and redistribution dynamics governed by Objects 1–3. Embodiment is presented as the mechanism that makes coherence felt, enabling preverbal signals to become patterns, patterns to become symbols, and symbols to become communicable meaning. -/- This downstream, domain‑agnostic model situates embodiment as the structural boundary condition for cognition, without invoking relational or multi‑system dynamics. It provides a unified account of how lived experience, physiological state, and cognitive organization co‑determine the emergence of meaning within a single cognitive system.

items.title: Archetypes, Synchronicity, and Meaning Formation.
items.abstract: Archetypes and synchronicities are often treated as symbolic, cultural, or metaphysical phenomena. This paper offers a structural account in which both arise as downstream expressions of meaning formation within a single cognitive system. Archetypes are modeled as stable pattern‑shapes generated by the organization of gradients, thresholds, and stabilizations; synchronicity is modeled as the phenomenological experience of coherence when internal and external patterns align. -/- The paper shows that archetypes, synchronicities, and meaning formation share the same underlying dynamics: a rising signal, a threshold or transition, and a stabilized configuration. Archetypes are the structural outputs of this process; synchronicity is the felt recognition of structural fit; meaning formation is the engine that produces both. -/- This downstream, domain‑agnostic model reframes archetypes and synchronicity as cognitive invariants rather than metaphysical events. It provides a unified framework for understanding symbolic resonance, pattern recognition, and coherence alignment without invoking relational or multi‑system dynamics.

items.title: From Interpretation to Structural Freedom: Deconstructing "Manas" as a Clinical and Existential Model.
items.abstract: This paper examines the structural limits of interpretive therapy and proposes an alternative framework grounded in phenomenological analysis and Buddhist philosophy. While classical psychoanalytic interpretation, as developed by Sigmund Freud, successfully uncovers the hidden meanings of symptoms, it does not fully address the mechanism by which experiences become existentially binding. The central argument of this study is that psychological suffering is intensified not only by unconscious content but by the reflexive appropriation of experience as “mine.” Drawing upon the Yogācāra concept of Manas-vijñāna, the paper analyzes identification as a structural process that converts transient mental events into stable identity claims. This reflex of ownership transforms contingent phenomena into perceived revelations of selfhood, thereby reinforcing anxiety, defensiveness, and compulsive repetition. Through this lens, certain pathological patterns—particularly obsessive tendencies—are reinterpreted as rigidifications of identification rather than merely conflicts of meaning. To move beyond this limitation, the paper introduces the principle of dependent origination (Pratītyasamutpāda) as a model for understanding subjectivity as dynamic continuity rather than metaphysical substance. Subjectivity is reconceived as a causal configuration—stable yet non-substantial—thereby preserving coherence without ontological fixation. In this framework, therapeutic transformation emerges not solely through interpretation, but through the gradual loosening of identification and the recognition of process. Finally, the study situates this structural freedom in dialogue with Nietzsche’s affirmation of existence, suggesting that the acceptance of causality parallels a radical affirmation of becoming. The proposed synthesis offers a philosophical and practical expansion of interpretive therapy, shifting the focus from narrative reconstruction to structural liberation.

items.title: The Fractal Grammar II.
items.abstract: We are creatures of blood who also dream. This paper anatomizes the distance between those facts without reducing one to the other. Blood names the embodied, inherited and historically situated architecture from which attachment, kin preference, reciprocity, fear, care and violence arise. Dream names the emergent imaginative capacity of minds built by that architecture to construct possibilities exceeding the inherited range. The dependence of dream upon embodiment does not make dream reducible to blood, any more than Van Gogh’s art is reducible to Van Gogh’s DNA. Against moral philosophy that treats the ethical ideal as a law discoverable by reason alone, and against cynicism that stops at biological locality and calls it truth, the paper argues that ethics develops through a fork opened by imagination. Natural care is gradient, situational and partial; imaginative consciousness can nevertheless picture forms of life that blood alone does not prescribe. Moral idealism is therefore neither a transcendent discovery nor merely instinct enlarged. It is creative projection: the construction of worlds in which a person may choose to participate.

items.title: THE PHILOSOPHY OF SUPERDETERMINISM ON HUMAN CONSCIOUSNESS.
items.abstract: The philosophy of superdeterminism is based on a single scientific fact about the universe, namely that cause and effect (and probabilistic causation) in physics are not real. In 2020, accomplished Swedish theoretical physicist, Dr. Johan Hansson proved by applying Albert Einstein’s Theory of Special Relativity to what has already been scientifically verified about spin measurement correlations observed in entangled particle pairs that cause and effect (and probabilistic causation) in physics are not real. The lack of cause and effect in physics means that we live in a predetermined static block universe, where nothing actually moves. Consequently, our conscious experience of movement must be a predetermined illusion created by our brain particles over the static dimension of time. The foundation of the universe is logic as evidenced by the logic of the mathematical laws of physics that describe our universe. Consciousness being an aspect of the physical block universe is also an exhibition of logic, but a logic of the possible as opposed to particle logic. Consciousness is the reference identity from which things come into and go out of existence under the logic of the possible. Qualia are likewise aspects of this logic of the possible. While a particle and human consciousness appear distinct and incompatible, they both are natural realities exhibiting different forms of logic within the same superdeterministic universe.

items.title: PHRONESIS — On Hesitation in the Presence of Power (v1.0).
items.abstract: PHRONESIS — On Hesitation in the Presence of Power is a non-binding, non-operational philosophical articulation of restraint in conditions of expanding intelligence and power. -/- The essay examines acceleration, reversibility, proportional decision-making, and the misinterpretation of hesitation within performance-driven systems. It argues that when capability expands faster than certainty, calibrated delay becomes a rational and structurally intelligent posture. -/- This document introduces no enforcement mechanisms, governance authority, certification framework, or behavioral obligations. It exists solely as part of the PHRONESIS corpus — A Philosophy of Practical Wisdom and Restraint for the Quantum Age of Superintelligence.

items.title: The Structural Mechanism of Consciousness: The Six-Field Architecture and Tuning-Balance Theory.
items.abstract: This chapter proposes a structural mechanism of consciousness grounded in the theory of Self-Manifestation. Building upon Sedimentation-Field Theory, it introduces a Six-Field Architecture that explains how imagery, attention, and experiential coherence arise within a self-manifesting system. -/- The Self-Manifestation-Field consists of six dynamically coupled domains: Intent-Field, Tuning-Field, Experience-Field, Imagery-Field, Sensory-Field, and Effect-Field, connected through two functional gates (input and output). Consciousness is not treated as a passive representation of external signals, but as an active tuning process in which Intent retroactively shapes signal flow through oscillatory regulation. -/- A central concept is Tuning-Balance: the dynamic equilibrium reached when iterative signal convergence can no longer refine impedance within the system. At this point, Imagery stabilizes and is misidentified as external reality. Reality, therefore, is not directly perceived but internally constructed through impedance-formation under biased-flow selection. -/- Signal flows forward in physical pulses; Intent flows backward as directive constraint. Conscious experience arises only when these two directional flows intersect within the tuning mechanism. Without retroactive ordination, signal alone does not produce imagery. -/- The chapter argues that consciousness requires at minimum four structural fields (Intent, Tuning, Experience, Imagery). Systems lacking these remain mute sedimentation structures, regardless of computational complexity. -/- Self-Manifestation is thus identified as the structural root of consciousness: a field-based dynamic capable of generating imagery through impedance-responsive tuning. The Pivot of this mechanism explains how signal becomes experience and how physics is transformed into perceived reality.

items.title: Correction: A toolbox to deal with misinformation in disaster risk management.
Decision-making for technology-led transformation in research practices.
items.abstract: Following the emergence of disruptive technologies and technology-driven trends, academics and researchers in particular face consequential changes in how they can conduct their work. In this paper, I argue that as researchers incorporate Generative AI tools to varying degrees, the activities they undertake for research will be altered, potentially leading to new practices and skillsets. I describe the adoption of Large Language Models (LLMs) as a transformative experience to argue that, when individuals encounter significant changes in habits, skills, and tasks, it fundamentally alters qualitative features of research activities. This reveals a rational choice problem for researchers, academics, and students alike: the substantial changes in research activities complicate the comparison of current and future competencies. In the wake of significant technological shifts, they are not well-positioned to decide whether replacing the current methods of researching and writing with those augmented by LLMs is better and preferable, as they cannot envision what it would be like to lose competence in some of their current skills.

items.title: A Justified Move: Defending the Beneficiary Pays Principle.
items.pub: Erasmus Journal for Philosophy and Economics 18 (2).
items.venue: Erasmus Journal for Philosophy and Economics
items.abstract: Laura García-Portela argues that shifting from the Polluter Pays Principle (PPP) to the Beneficiary Pays Principle (BPP) in order to rectify climate injustice is unjustified if based solely on the latter’s ability to address the causation and excusable ignorance objections more effectively. She contends that defenders of the BPP must demonstrate that the benefits used to address losses and damages originate from the same source as the harms to be rectified. However, she deems this requirement unwarranted due to the difficulty of linking climate change to specific extreme weather events. Furthermore, she asserts that the excusable ignorance objection relates to the fairness of imposing unforeseen burdens on agents who emitted without knowledge of future responsibilities. Consequently, the BPP must address this issue in a manner similar to the PPP. Based on her insights, this paper argues that a shift to the BPP is nevertheless justified, especially if the Climate Enrichment Principle is adopted.

items.title: Repositioning the Hard Problem - Identity as Prior Condition for Phenomenal Experience.
items.abstract: The hard problem of consciousness is commonly framed as a gap between physical processes and phenomenal experience: even a complete functional account of the brain appears to leave unanswered why those processes are accompanied by “what-it-is-like” character. This paper argues that the apparent gap arises from an inverted explanatory order. Phenomenal character is treated as primary, while the structural precondition for subjecthood is left implicit. I propose that identity—understood as constraint-maintained invariance across perturbation—is prior to experience. A system must first constitute itself as a stable, self-maintaining unit before the question of what it is like to be that unit can arise.
