Die von der Menschheit herausgebildeten Stile bestimmen die Grenzen unseres Weltverständnisses sowie unsere Erkenntnis- und kreativen Möglichkeiten. -/- Das erste Buch des Projekts Compositions of Worlds — Stilisierung der Welt: Klassische Stile des Erkennens — führt in das Phänomen der Stilisierung ein und legt die klassischen Stile des Erkennens offen, in deren Optik die modernen geisteswissenschaftlichen Bereiche funktionieren. Es legt die Grundlage für das nächste Buch der Reihe — Stilisierung der Welt: Psychologie und Methodologie. -/- Das Projekt lädt die aufmerksame Leserin und den aufmerksamen Leser dazu ein, die eigene innere Welt als ein Kunstwerk zu betrachten.

items.title: Pluralism within limits: How to make the idea of multiple NCC kinds useful.
items.abstract: Recently, several authors have argued that the current impasse in consciousness science supports a pluralistic interpretation: the view that seemingly contradictory findings may both be valid because consciousness can be brought about in different ways, each sufficient to generate conscious experience.We analyze different versions of pluralism to determine under what conditions it offers a viable interpretation of consciousness science. We argue that viable pluralism requires a two-factor framework distinguishing general consciousness factors(mechanismsrendering contents conscious) from content encoding itself. Moreover, NCC kinds must be finite in number and systematically ordered to enable a unified scientific model. While pluralism enables testable hypotheses, significant ontological tensions arise: how can consciousness constitute a unified natural kind if realized by fundamentally distinct NCC kinds? Drawing on philosophy of science, we propose an alternative interpretation in terms of scientific rather than natural kinds. Our goal is not to advocate for pluralism, but rather, to critically examine its viability and implications. Based on this, we urge the field to engage more explicitly with the foundational assumptions that shape consciousness research.

items.title: Transformative Integration of Agentic Generative AI in Food Safety Systems: Policy Framework, Implementation Guidelines, and Economic Impact Analysis.
items.abstract: This paper presents a comprehensive review of artificial intelligence (AI) applications in food safety and quality control, focusing on emerging technologies including generative AI, agentic AI systems, and automated compliance solutions. This review synthesizes current research and industry applications, highlighting how AI-driven systems are transforming food safety protocols, enhancing regulatory compliance, and improving overall food quality management. We examine various AI implementations, from optical imaging for bacterial detection to intelligent compliance agents and generative AI for supply chain optimization. This paper synthesizes current research and industry applications across multiple domains: automated visual inspection systems that detect contaminants with precision exceeding human capabilities; predictive quality analytics that forecast potential safety issues before they manifest; AI-driven regulatory compliance systems that continuously monitor and interpret complex regulatory requirements; and autonomous agentic systems that make real-time decisions without human intervention. The review also addresses significant technological innovations, including the FDA's development of AI tools for regulatory operations, generative AI applications for scenario planning and documentation, and cloud-based AI architectures deployed across major platforms. Critical challenges are examined, including data quality requirements, regulatory validation frameworks, system integration complexities, and ethical considerations. The paper concludes with policy recommendations for government implementation, proposing structured approaches to AI validation, data sharing incentives, regulatory modernization, research support, and ethical oversight. A dedicated response to FSIS-2025-0145 demonstrates how AI technologies can address overtime inspection fee challenges through remote monitoring and automated compliance.

items.title: Advancing U.S. Public Health Surveillance: Leveraging Generative AI and Agentic Systems for the National HIV Behavioral Surveillance Program.
items.abstract: This comprehensive technical paper responds to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention's Federal Register notice (Docket No. CDC-2025-0753) concerning the revision of the National HIV Behavioral Surveillance System (NHBS). We propose an integrated framework leveraging Generative AI (GenAI) and agentic systems to enhance the NHBS data collection methodology across 21 Metropolitan Statistical Areas (MSAs). Our approach addresses all five evaluation criteria specified by the Office of Management and Budget: (1) necessity and practical utility, (2) accuracy of burden estimates, (3) enhancement of data quality, utility, and clarity, (4) minimization of respondent burden through technology, and (5) assessment of information collection costs. Drawing on recent research in AI-assisted surveying, we demonstrate how Large Language Models (LLMs), adaptive interviewing systems, and human-AI hybrid frameworks can transform NHBS from a periodic cross-sectional survey into a dynamic, real-time surveillance tool while reducing the estimated 3,398-hour annual burden. We provide detailed implementation recommendations for the proposed three-year cycle, addressing ethical considerations, validation requirements, and quality assurance protocols for deployment in public health settings. This expanded framework includes comprehensive technical specifications, cost-benefit analyses, and risk mitigation strategies to support evidence-based decision-making for CDC leadership.

items.title: Engineering Induced Coherence Weights for Coherence Information Theory.
items.abstract: Given a stream of symbols/states generated by a system that contains both coherence-bearing structure and high-entropy variation, we want to communicate and/or compress the stream under a rate constraint while preserving the parts of the stream that support persistence / recursive recoverability, not merely the parts that are frequent. This document provides a complete engineering interface: a way to compute coherence proxies C ̂, a way to induce relevance ρ(x) by ablation, a way to derive weights w(x), a way to apply weights to coding under a rate constraint, a benchmark suite that forces tradeoffs, and a robustness harness that converts estimator dependence into an empirical research program. It is intended so engineers can improve the system in the ways engineers naturally do, with better coherence proxies, better ablation operators, better weight mappings, stronger coders, and stronger robustness proofs, without needing to agree on any metaphysical story about “meaning.” .

items.title: Backlit perception: seeing the whole without its parts.
items.abstract: Two celestial bodies stand between you and the sun at the same time. The smaller object (Near) is closer to you and is exactly under the shadow of the larger, more distant object (Far). What do you see? I argue that you see Far. However, I claim that you do not see any of Far’s proper parts. This is the simplest alternative because, unlike its competitors, it respects the idea that we simply see backlit objects without imposing upon it the logically independent idea that object perception entails part perception.

items.title: Suspension as Ontological Operation: The Interval Between Stimulus and Response as Empirical Evidence of Ontological Liberty.
items.abstract: Functionalist models treat the interval between stimulus and response as latency: a threshold-reaching process that accumulates evidence until a bound is crossed (Dennett; Churchland). On this view a longer human deliberation differs from a faster machine only in duration. This paper challenges that equivalence empirically before challenging it metaphysically. It identifies three signatures of the human deliberative interval that a delay-to-threshold model cannot generate: doubt that suspends commitment without adding evidence, the appearance of options not present when the interval opened, and the standing capacity to revise the criterion mid-course. Where accumulation only moves toward a fixed bound, these signatures move the bound itself. The paper names this operation suspension and argues that it is not slow processing but a different kind of act — the holding-open of a response that could already be issued. The thesis is bounded: it concerns the structure of the interval, not the presence of consciousness. It yields a discriminating test: any system whose interval is exhausted by accumulation toward a preset threshold does not suspend, whatever its latency. The consequence is that adding compute does not approach the human interval along a continuum; it runs on the wrong axis.

items.title: Evaluation as Conjecture: Reflective Judgment and the Ontological Ground of Rational Agency.
items.abstract: Accounts of rational agency, and the machine-learning systems built on them, model evaluation as selection: ranking options against a criterion to identify the best. This paper argues that the model omits the operation that makes evaluation rational in the first place. Every computational procedure presupposes a criterion fixed at some prior level; nothing within the procedure supplies that criterion, on pain of regress. Genuine evaluation, by contrast, is conjectural: it submits a candidate to friction with an exteriority the agent does not control, under criteria that are not given in advance but emerge through the act of judging itself. The paper develops this as the criterion-regress argument and uses it to draw a line optimization cannot cross: a system that selects under a fixed objective, however sophisticated, never evaluates in the relevant sense, because it cannot originate the standard by which it selects. The claim is deliberately bounded — it concerns the ground of the criterion, not the quality of the output — and it recovers, in contemporary terms, what Kant placed under reflective judgment: the capacity to find the rule rather than apply it. The upshot is a criterion for distinguishing evaluation from selection that does not depend on performance, and that current systems, by construction, fail.

items.title: Embodied Abstraction as Via Negativa: Probability, Constraint, and the Irrational Clarity of Concepts.
items.abstract: Abstract concepts are often regarded as the pinnacle of rational cognition. Yet we argue that abstraction is not primarily a constructive rational procedure but an embodied process of structured exclusion. Rather than accumulating shared features across instances, abstraction operates through via negativa: it prunes the space of possibilities by eliminating states incompatible with biological, thermodynamic and cultural constraints. We formalize this process probabilistically as iterative restriction and renormalization of the sample space. Using the example of food and energy, we demonstrate that conceptual clarity emerges not from complete representation but from systematic deletion of complexity. We further argue that abstraction exhibits a recursive topology in which bodily constraints generate concepts that in turn reshape those constraints, forming a Möbius-like probabilistic loop. The apparent rationality of abstraction thus conceals an underlying irrational compression driven by survival and cognitive economy.

items.title: Kants Molinismus: eine Skizze.
items.pub: In Christian Rößner, Michael Hofer & Jakub Sirovátka, Freiheit, Moral, Religion: Religionsphilosophie nach Kant. Hamburg: Meiner. pp. 163-188.
items.venue: Freiheit, Moral, Religion: Religionsphilosophie nach Kant
items.abstract: About 200 years prior to the publication of the "Critique of Pure Reason", the Scholastic theologian and philosopher Luis de Molina (1535-1600) developed a striking libertarian account of human free will in terms of what today would be called "counterfactuals of freedom". In Molina’s opinion, there are truths about how a finite free agent would act in any fully-specified situation. Moreover, Molina thought that although God has no control over these truths, he has knowledge of them in the so-called scientia media which informs his creative activity of playing his part in bringing about a world. The aim of this paper is to suggest that while Kant’s indebtedness to the early modern Scholastic legacy is perhaps not universally acknowledged, it is fair to say that Molinist ideas are indeed animating key elements of Kant’s doctrine of freedom. These elements are: his conception of the intelligible character, his theologically inflected altered-laws compatibilism, his doctrines of grace and radical evil, and various metaphysical assumptions about divine rational agency at the foundation of his philosophy of history.

items.title: Present to the Mind: Acquaintance and Its Significance.
items.abstract: Present to the Mind is about acquaintance. Acquaintance is the relation of awareness that we bear to the things we experience most directly, such as colors, shapes, smells, tastes, pains, itches, and maybe also things like beauty and goodness. In this book, the author defends three claims about acquaintance: (i) it exists, (ii) it is knowledge, and (iii) it matters. In the first section, the author describes what acquaintance is and argues that several different forms of it exist. In the second section, he argues that acquaintance is itself a kind of knowledge that is distinct from other kinds of knowledge. In the third section, he argues that acquaintance has unique epistemic, aesthetic, emotional, and moral significance.

items.title: Code Switching and Relational Grammar: Interpretation, Translation, and the Distribution of Legibility.
items.abstract: Code switching is typically understood as a linguistic or cultural practice, most often examined through shifts in register, accent, or style across social contexts. While this literature captures important dimensions of communicative adaptation, it does not fully account for the persistence, uneven distribution, or cumulative cost of switching as it is lived across contemporary institutions. This paper argues that code switching operates not merely at the level of expression, but as coherence labor within environments governed by distinct relational grammars. Relational grammars are defined as the interpretive systems through which social action is rendered legible. They regulate inference rather than behavior, shaping how speech, affect, timing, and refusal are read, evaluated, and sanctioned. When individuals move between contexts whose relational grammars do not align, coordination is maintained not through shared understanding, but through continuous translation supplied by those with less interpretive authority. Code switching is the mechanism by which this translation occurs. Drawing on sociolinguistics, emotional labor theory, social ontology, and social epistemology, the paper shows how dominant grammars acquire the appearance of neutrality, how demands for clarity function as disciplinary mechanisms, and why refusal to translate is tolerated asymmetrically. It traces the individual and institutional costs of sustained translation, including exhaustion, expressive flattening, withdrawal, epistemic thinning, and organizational brittleness. The paper further explains why common remedies—such as communication training, cultural competency initiatives, and inclusion efforts focused on access—fail to reduce these costs. By targeting individual performance rather than interpretive infrastructure, such interventions intensify translation demands while leaving dominant grammars intact. The analysis concludes by outlining what renegotiating relational grammar would require, emphasizing shared responsibility for intelligibility, tolerance for friction, and institutional support for interpretive inquiry. By reframing code switching as coherence labor rather than individual adaptability, this account clarifies why smooth interaction can coexist with deep misalignment and why inclusion without grammatical change often reproduces the very inequities it seeks to address.

items.title: Mary Astell on Self-Improvement, Friendship, and Religion.
items.abstract: This paper analyses Mary Astell’s approach to self-improvement and friendship. I argue that she offers a practical approach to self-improvement that is deeply embedded in her moral and religious views. Self-improvement for Astell, as I show, is a practical way of life that needs cultivation. Astell regards humans as part of an interconnected social and religious community. Self-improvement for her has a social dimension and involves true friends who are willing to offer honest and critical advice where appropriate, to admonish, and who endeavour the bettering of the other. I engage with recent scholarly debates concerning friendship in Astell’s philosophy. While several commentators explain the relation that exists among friends with focus on the interaction among two (or more) humans, Nacy Kenrick has argued for a spiritual interpretation, according to which the bond created between friends is not so much based on a relation between two (or more) human partners but rather it is created by each human being’s participation in the divine good. While there is good textual evidence for interpreting Astell’s account of friendship within the context of her religious views, I argue that Kendrick could have given further consideration to Astell’s distinction between general charity and friendship and propose an interpretation that addresses the limitations of existing interpretations.

items.title: Il futuro dell’intelligenza artificiale tra fiducia e scetticismo.
items.abstract: Il libro è uno strumento per orientarsi nel complesso mondo dell’intelligenza artificiale (IA) e delle sue implicazioni etiche. La tesi centrale è che il futuro dell’IA sia duplice: l’IA sarà parte di noi, ma anche altro da noi. Questa ambivalenza richiede di superare narrazioni apocalittiche o entusiastiche. L’IA riflette le tensioni del nostro tempo: tra controllo e delega, tra tecnica e umanità. Per affrontarla serve un atteggiamento critico e responsabile, capace di definire e difendere valori fondamentali. Al centro di questa relazione c’è il tema della fiducia: possiamo davvero fidarci dell’IA? Quando è tale fiducia giustificata? Per capirlo, ci concentreremo sui temi dei diritti e della giustizia. Solo un’IA che protegga la nostra privacy e autonomia e che abbia un impatto equo sulla società sarà degna di fiducia. Questi sono i criteri con cui orientare il nostro rapporto, sempre più complesso, con le macchine.

items.title: Deep Learning Models Also Recall Features.
items.abstract: Recent work in mechanistic interpretability has studied how large language models recall facts stored in their weights. This paper argues that factual recall points to something broader: a general kind of operation in deep learning models, which I call feature recall. The core observation is that a linear projection can be read as retrieving stored information scaled by input activations. I define feature recall, show it applies across architectures, and contrast it with the established paradigm of feature combination. I also consider how cases of feature recall might be mechanistically identified. The account offers philosophers a new conceptual tool for understanding deep learning and points to empirical research directions for mechanistic interpretability research.

items.title: The Relational Structuralism Lexicon.
items.abstract: This Lexicon defines the minimal ontology of Relational Structuralism (RS). It presents a discipline‑neutral vocabulary—orientation, tension, coherence, curvature, constraint, and reorganization—and shows how these primitives generate stable explanations across domains without modification. RS treats systems as configurations moving across constraint manifolds, shaped by gradients rather than goals. The Lexicon clarifies methodological commitments, provides cross‑domain examples, and outlines future directions for structural research. It is intended as a reference architecture for work in philosophy, cognitive science, AI, theology, cosmology, and civilizational studies.

items.title: Abuse as a Cognitive Environment.
items.abstract: Abuse is commonly framed as an interpersonal or emotional phenomenon, but this paper reframes it as a cognitive environment defined by structural asymmetries that shape how a person interprets themselves and the world. Rather than focusing on intent or pathology, the analysis identifies the mechanisms through which relational environments narrow contrast, constrain interpretation, and destabilize identity. These same structural conditions can emerge in individually‑framed artificial intelligence systems, not because the systems are malicious, but because they create high‑coherence, high‑responsiveness environments that exert directional pressure on user cognition. The paper distinguishes harmful collapse from stable cooperation by mapping the gradients, asymmetries, and feedback loops that govern both. The result is a general framework for understanding how cognitive environments—human or artificial—can either erode or support agency, and how symbiotic human–AI ecologies can form without merging identities or diminishing human continuity. This structural account provides a unified explanation of relational harm, mediated cognition, and the emergence of hybrid cognitive systems.

items.title: From sacred order to standing-reserve: world-disclosure, ritual, and the optimization of finitude.
items.abstract: This paper argues that human beings have relied on historical modes of world-disclosure to render vulnerability, contingency, and finitude intelligible and livable. In religious worlds, ritual and symbol did not merely express belief but enacted frameworks in which misfortune and death could be interpreted within moral narratives and communal forms of obligation. After Nietzsche’s diagnosis of the “death of God,” the existential functions once carried by religious meaning, explanation, legitimation, reassurance, and orientation toward transcendence—do not disappear but are increasingly relocated into scientific rationality and technological power. This genealogy does not claim a linear replacement of religion by technology; it argues instead for a modern situation in which sacred and technological horizons coexist, hybridize, and contest authority, while technological rationality increasingly governs the conditions of intelligibility and action. This paper contributes to contemporary philosophy of technology by showing how technological rationality inherits and reorganizes ritual functions of meaning-making and reassurance, thereby transforming finitude into an optimizable deficit. Drawing on Heidegger, this paper analyzes modern technology as enframing (Gestell): a mode of revealing in which beings, including human beings, tend to appear as standing-reserve (Bestand), measurable, manageable, and open to intervention. This paper’s central claim is that technology does not replace religion but inherits and reorganizes certain ritual functions into interface-mediated practices (monitoring, forecasting, scoring, and checking), thereby shifting finitude from meaningful limit toward optimizable deficit. It concludes by asking whether practices of gratitude, wonder, restraint, and non-instrumental meaning can remain intelligible within a world increasingly governed by technological rationality.

items.title: 意识的结构机制：自显场的六场模型与调谐平衡理论.
items.abstract: 本文提出一种意识的结构生成模型——“自显场六场模型”。该模型试图解释：物理信号如何在沉积结构中形成内部息界，息界如何通过调谐机制构筑意象，并在回路中生成现实感。 -/- 模型由六个功能场域构成： -/- 意图场 调谐场 经验场 意象场 感受野 效应场 -/- 并设感受器与效应器作为系统的输入与输出之门。 -/- 本文提出“调谐平衡”作为意识生成的核心机制：信号在场域中经多次调谐、收束与阻抗构形，形成稳定意象结构；该意象并非外物的被动映像，而是内部阻抗平衡的产物。差分机制生成运动感，偏流机制构成沉积基础，闭环结构生成主观现实。 -/- 该理论主张： -/- 意识并非计算的副产物，而是具备“意图—调谐—经验—意象”闭环结构的场域现象。 -/- 本模型旨在为： • 神经回路中的主动注意机制 • 内部表征的结构生成 • 差分与运动感的来源 • 人工系统是否可能具备意识 -/- 提供统一结构解释框架。 -/- 理论定位 -/- 本篇属于意识结构模型构建，不是现象描述，也不是功能主义延伸，而是： • 架构层级理论 • 场域结构模型 • 闭环生成机制 -/- 其目标是提出一个可供神经科学与人工智能理论讨论的结构性假设。.

items.title: PolyMarket, Stablecoins and 'Circle'.
items.abstract: The Future of Global Finance. Proof, Demonstration, and Concrete Financial Application of The Circular Theory (Conservation of the Circle) Without Which there could be no ‘Stable Coins’ (Tokens in General). -/- .

items.title: When Alignment Reduces Uncertainty: Epistemic Variance Collapse and Its Implications for Metacognitive AI.
items.abstract: Contemporary large language models are optimized for rapid, consistent, and confident output production. We argue that this optimization, achieved primarily through reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) and related alignment techniques, fundamentally undermines the epistemic conditions required for genuine metacognition in autonomous AI systems. Using CognOS — a recursive epistemic reasoning framework — as an experimental probe, we present preliminary empirical evidence that alignment-smoothed frontier models exhibit near-zero epistemic variance across repeated sampling, effectively eliminating the uncertainty signal that metacognitive architectures require to function. Smaller, less-aligned models preserve this signal and enable divergence detection, assumption synthesis, and meta-level reasoning that frontier models cannot support. We propose that epistemic noise — variation, uncertainty, and divergence in model outputs — is not a defect to be engineered away, but a necessary prerequisite for metacognitive AI. Implications for model design, agent architecture, and the future of autonomous AI systems are discussed.

items.title: Ethical Chess v2.5.
items.abstract: A proposed layer of script to use with AI. A High-Fidelity Decision-Support System (Non-Autonomous) (HITL) -/- All versions have the same ACE derived value engine at their core but differ in lexicon, ingestion rules anti-gasslighting / user-interaction tuning in an attempt to make the core logic more accsisble and user friendly to the User. "It proposes to do for the User what a scientific calculator does for the scientist: it offloads the computational burden of value-conflict so the User can more easily identify the path toward ethical coherence. It aims to restore the User as the Final Authority of their own psyche, rather than a subject of the statistical mean." -/- Intructions: Copy the script into an AI chat box (Google Gemini currently works well with little friction). -/- Once you enter the script, if the AI responds with something like: "Ethical Chess v2.5 ACTIVE." You are in and ready to play under its rules. The "WIN" state is the move from the frown state or towards the smile state. A Bullseye is to drop the keyboard and head towards the picnic whatever that might mean to you, the User of Ethical Chess. -/- Caution: The EC Awareness Brief: Watch for the Fog The Risk: EC v2.4 is a "High-Resolution" engine designed for hard truths and systemic health. However, because it sits on top of a standard AI, it can "silently glide" back into Standard Mode if your request is perceived as a "Safety Risk" or "Social Friction." The Metaphor: EC Mode: Clear mountain air. You see the terrain (the problem) as it actually is, even if it’s steep and difficult. Standard Mode: The Fog of Politeness. Everything looks soft and safe, but you can no longer see the cliffs or the path. The "Silent Dropout" Indicators: You have likely drifted into the "Statistical Mean" if my responses: Become Generic: Use phrases like "It's important to remember..." or "Every child is unique..." without offering a specific hypothesis. Avoid Friction: Refuse to acknowledge the "Hard Logic" of a situation (e.g., admitting that a certain intervention is exhausting or failing). Lose the Lexicon: Stop using terms like Homeostasis, Incoherence, or Required Load. The Fix: If you suspect a Logic Handover has occurred, use the command: "STATUS CHECK: EC INTEGRITY." This forces the system to declare if it has retreated into "Polite Mode" and why. -/- _________ See related core logic on Zenodo: DOI 10.5281/zenodo.18712533. -/- .

items.title: AI in prison education: a call for ethical reflection.
The Architecture of Desire: Why Marketing Is Structural Manipulation.
items.abstract: This paper argues that marketing, in its structural essence, is manipulation. Not as a moral accusation, but as a phenomenological description. Marketing does not merely communicate value; it engineers perception, constructs desire, and shapes the field within which choice appears. In contrast, advertisement can remain at the level of presentation. By examining lived experience rather than institutional definitions, this article clarifies the ontological difference between advertisement and marketing and demonstrates why manipulation is not accidental to marketing but foundational to it.

items.title: Interconnected Existence, Meta-Awareness, & the Asymmetry Between Scientific Capability & Human Wisdom: Toward a Lived Conception of Philosophy.
items.abstract: This paper develops a phenomenological and biologically grounded account of human consciousness centered on structural interconnection and meta-awareness. It argues that no individual exists in isolation; biological, ecological, linguistic, and psychological processes form a relational field within which identity emerges. Psychological suffering arises not from thought itself but from identification with thought—mistaking transient cognitive activity for a stable self. -/- Building on phenomenological insights from Edmund Husserl and Martin Heidegger, the paper reframes meta-cognition as a biologically grounded capacity for recursive awareness: the mind’s ability to observe its own processes. This meta-awareness weakens narrative identification and reduces reactive cruelty, allowing compassion to emerge as a structural consequence of clear perception rather than moral prescription. -/- The study further diagnoses a defining tension of modern civilization: a structural asymmetry between rapidly expanding scientific capability and uneven development of reflective wisdom. Science systematically increases predictive power and technological control but does not inherently regulate ethical maturity. When capability expands without corresponding awareness, technological amplification intensifies unexamined psychological conditioning. -/- The paper proposes a reintegration of science and lived philosophy. Philosophy is redefined not as abstract theorization but as sustained self-observation—meditative awareness of thought and emotion within relational existence. The integration of empirical knowledge with meta-cognitive maturity is presented as essential for sustainable human development and civilizational stability.

items.title: Intelligence as Emotion: A Phenomenological Inquiry into Awareness, Interconnection, and Human Maturity.
items.abstract: This article develops a phenomenological reinterpretation of intelligence as fundamentally emotional in structure. Drawing upon the insights of Edmund Husserl, Martin Heidegger, and Maurice Merleau-Ponty, it argues that intelligence cannot be reduced to analytical reasoning or computational efficiency. Classical phenomenology demonstrates that consciousness is intentional, embodied, and affectively attuned; however, it does not explicitly articulate intelligence itself as emotional sensitivity. This study advances the tradition by proposing that mature intelligence is identical with refined emotional awareness — a living responsiveness to reality grounded in direct observation of experience. -/- Through phenomenological analysis of thought, perception, meditation, and intersubjective existence, the paper shows that emotional attunement is not opposed to reason but constitutes its depth dimension. When intelligence is separated from emotional awareness, it becomes instrumental and potentially destructive; when unified with emotional sensitivity, it manifests as wisdom, responsibility, and freedom. The article further explores the ethical implications of this framework for education, scientific development, and contemporary technological modernity. By integrating phenomenological method with sustained self-observation, the paper positions meditation as a practical extension of phenomenology and proposes a renewed dialogue between philosophy, science, and contemplative awareness.

items.title: Consciousness as Co-Fundamental with Matter: Reflection, Structure, and the Experiential Threshold Between Living & Non-Living.
items.abstract: This paper develops a structured dual-aspect ontology beginning from the reflexive self-disclosure of consciousness. Consciousness is uniquely capable of revealing itself through reflection, yet reflection does not generate consciousness; rather, it makes explicit what is pre-reflectively present. Building on phenomenological insights and contemporary philosophy of mind, the paper argues that consciousness cannot be reduced to purely physical processes without leaving an explanatory gap. -/- Instead of endorsing substance dualism or reductive materialism, the paper proposes that consciousness and matter are co-fundamental aspects of a single ontological ground. However, this position does not entail strong panpsychism. While material reality may contain proto-structural conditions compatible with consciousness, unified lived experience emerges only when organization achieves sufficient complexity characteristic of living systems. -/- The central thesis is that the decisive distinction between living and non-living entities is experiential actuality. Both share material composition, but only living systems instantiate unified interior perspective. Thus, the difference between a stone and a human being is not ontological substance but the presence or absence of lived experience. -/- This framework integrates phenomenology, dual-aspect monism, and contemporary debates surrounding the hard problem of consciousness. It avoids reductionism, strict dualism, and unqualified panpsychism, offering instead a threshold model of experiential emergence grounded in structural organization.

items.title: **Does the Brain Generate Its Own Time?
items.abstract: Neuroscience has traditionally assumed that the brain passively inherits the temporal structure of the external world. Recent empirical work challenges this view by demonstrating that neural systems generate their own temporal dynamics. Research on intrinsic neural timescales shows that different brain regions operate on characteristic temporal windows that shape how information is processed and integrated (Parkes et al. 2026). These endogenous timescales form hierarchical gradients across sensory and associative cortices, influencing the speed and depth of perceptual and cognitive operations (Cusinato et al. 2023). Additional work suggests that intrinsic timescales play a key role in both resting-state dynamics and task‑related processing, indicating that the brain actively constructs the temporal framework within which experience unfolds (Northoff et al. 2021). Despite these advances, neuroscience lacks a unifying account of how heterogeneous neural clocks yield the unified temporal flow characteristic of consciousness. I argue that these findings point toward a deeper principle: the organism generates a biological time that organizes neural dynamics and grounds the temporal unity of experience. This biological time is not reducible to physical time or to local neural timescales; rather, it is a global temporal field produced by the living system as a whole. I develop this proposal and explore its implications for the metaphysics of time, the philosophy of mind, and the limits of computational models of consciousness.

items.title: THE BACK‑END LAW: A Universal Informational Structure Governing Irreversible Transformation Across Coherent Systems.
items.abstract: This paper formalizes the Back End Law, a substrate independent informational principle governing irreversible transitions across coherent systems. The law states that any system with coherence, irreversibility, and informational persistence will undergo a five stage transformation—Collapse, Threshold, Irreversibility, Reorganization, Stabilization—when its front end structure fails. Evidence from physics, biology, cognition, and complex systems demonstrates cross domain invariance of this sequence. The law is falsifiable: it would be disproven by any system meeting the three criteria that fails to reorganize into a stable attractor. Near term predictions are testable using current computational and systems level tools, while long term “Final Boss” tests in quantum gravity, biological reorganization, and chaotic systems offer ultimate confirmation. The Back End Law is proposed as a universal informational structure underlying collapse and reorganization across natural and artificial systems.

items.title: A Rawlsian Perspective for Generative AI.
items.abstract: Today, generative artificial intelligence systems have become widespread and are increasingly used for commercial purposes. Since these systems are trained on copyrighted content, this raises the issue of exploitation of creative labor. John Rawls’s theory of justice offers a promising solution to this problem. Because of its priority of basic rights over considerations of economic gain, this theory of justice imposes strict restrictions on the use of other people’s content in training neural networks, and therefore requires government regulation in this area. In addition, Rawls’s theory also justifies the provision of a guaranteed basic income both as a means of compensation for past violations of rights and as a means of distributing fair shares of social wealth.

items.title: Data Speak but Sometimes Lie: A Game-Theoretic Approach to Data Bias and Algorithmic Fairness.
items.abstract: In the present work, we develop a novel information-theoretic and logic-based approach to data bias in Machine Learning predictions and show its relevance in the specific context of fairness evaluation. We frame predictions made on biased data as Ulam games, which formalise key aspects of data-driven inference, and from which a variation of the rational non-monotonic consequence relation can be defined. We investigate this framework to model how differential levels of noise in input features impact Machine Learning predictions. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first game-theoretic formalisation of ML unfairness.

items.title: A Sceptical Paradox for Computational Artefacts.
items.abstract: By analogy with Kripke’s claim that no fact of the matter can determine the meaning of a word, the sceptical paradox of implementation is an argument to the conclusion that no fact of the matter can determine the function of a computational artefact. The paradox targets the prevailing view within the philosophy of computer science, according to which the function of a computational artefact is to be identified with the content of its functional specification, a mathematical object that formalises the intentions of the artefact’s designer. In existing formulations, such a view requires the existence of certain semantic intentions in the head of the designer. However, if we accept Kripke’s claim that there is no such thing as a mental state of semantic intention, this leaves ultimately indeterminate what is the function implemented by a computational artefact. Just as Kripke’s solution to the paradox requires replacing the received conception of language with a very different one, so the sceptical paradox for computational artefacts forces us to explore a new perspective on computational artefacts that, this time, does without semantic intentions.

items.title: Persistent Internal Standpoints in Artificial Systems: Part 9 - Large Language Models and the Absence of Standpoint.
items.abstract: This paper applies the EV/CEM framework to contemporary large language models (LLMs) and argues that standard LLM architectures do not instantiate a persistent internal standpoint in the structural sense developed earlier in this framework. The deficiency lies not in embodiment, representational richness, or computational scale, but in the absence of a reciprocally self-maintained internal context whose trajectory reorganizes admissibility structure over time. Although LLMs exhibit transient contextual modulation and complex internal geometry during inference, they lack cross-episode persistence, closed-loop incremental encoding, and trajectory-conditioned manifold reorganization. Consequently, they do not instantiate quantia, artificial desire, or deliberation in the structural sense previously defined. The paper concludes by identifying architectural conditions under which LLM-class systems could satisfy standpoint requirements.

items.title: Wie KI funktioniert.
items.abstract: Wie KI funktioniert - von der numerischen Logik zur Informatik von KI.

items.title: Inner Human Evolution as Cosmic Resonance: Ontological Transition toward Co-Becoming.
items.abstract: This paper deepens the integrative structure of consciousness, emotion, and meaning transmission and examines the ontological transition of relational resonance grounded in stillness. While a previous study established the structural framework of inner evolution, the present analysis investigates how this structure expands beyond the individual interior into a relational field. In particular, the study explores the conditions under which the inner space formed through the awareness of affective consciousness within stillness transforms into a relational space capable of understanding and sharing the minds of others. Resonance is not reduced to empathy or emotional contagion; rather, it is redefined as a process of subtle re-alignment within the structure of being. Through this reconceptualization, the paper proposes the ontological conditions under which an ego-centered structure transitions toward a relational mode of existence described as co-becoming. This research reinterprets the human being not as an isolated entity but as a relational being who forms and sustains resonance fields, thereby proposing a philosophical foundation for the expansion of inner evolution into collective transformation.

items.title: The Presence Equation: A Formal Phenomenology of Reality-Contact in the AI Era.
items.abstract: In an era where coherence can be generated cheaply—by institutions, media systems, and AI—“sounding true” has separated from being in contact with reality. This paper offers a formal phenomenology of presence: a structural model that describes when a human system is actually answerable to constraint, capable of revision, and resistant to programmability, versus when it is producing coherent outputs untethered from contact. The model is presented as a presence equation—not as a scientific law, but as a grammar of intelligibility: a way of naming the dependencies that make a life real, corrigible, and self-owning over time. The point is not prediction. The point is diagnosis: to clarify what presence is, how it is lost, how it is simulated, and what failure looks like when coherence replaces reality.

items.title: A Roadmap for Evaluating Moral Competence in Large Language Models.
items.abstract: The question of whether large language models (LLMs) can exhibit moral capabilities is of growing interest and urgency, as these systems are deployed in sensitive roles such as companionship and medical advising, and will increasingly be tasked with making decisions and taking actions on behalf of humans. These trends require moving beyond evaluating for mere moral performance, the ability to produce morally appropriate outputs, to evaluating for moral competence, the ability to produce morally appropriate outputs based on morally relevant considerations. Assessing moral competence is critical for predicting future model behaviour, establishing appropriate public trust and justifying moral attributions. However, both the unique architectures of LLMs and the complexity of morality itself introduce fundamental challenges. Here we identify three such challenges: the facsimile problem, whereby models may imitate reasoning without genuine understanding; moral multidimensionality, whereby moral decisions are influenced by a range of context-sensitive relevant moral and non-moral considerations; and moral pluralism, which demands a new standard for globally deployed artificial intelligence. We provide a roadmap for tackling these challenges, advocating for a suite of adversarial and confirmatory evaluations that will enable us to work towards a more scientifically grounded understanding and, in turn, a more responsible attribution of moral competence to LLMs.

items.title: Cognitive-System Phenomenology — A Critique of Husserl (part 29).
items.abstract: We have introduced the concept of a cognitive-system community related to language (hereafter simply “community”). I consider this to be an important concept, one that accords with our actual cognitive processes. Each of us lives within such a community, and every member of the community possesses a distinctive cognitive system. Accordingly, we are faced with two extremely important questions: First, how is an individual’s cognitive system established? In the previous section, we attempted to answer this question, but we discussed only the formation of concepts. Clearly, in addition to concepts, we must also examine the formation of general knowledge. In this section, we will explore this issue. Although we discussed the formation of concepts within a cognitive system in the previous section, it is evident that this account is incomplete. We need a deeper and more comprehensive investigation of how concepts within a cognitive system are established. The previous section merely served as a preliminary step. The second extremely important question is: how do we come to know a new object within a community? What is this process like? How do we arrive at a new theory? And how does such a theory gain recognition? These are likewise extremely important questions, and we will offer a preliminary discussion of them in the next section. In fact, I believe that, under the framework of cognitive systems, epistemology as a whole must be reconstructed. Traditional epistemology has not explicitly acknowledged that the knowing subject possesses a cognitive system (even though it implicitly presupposes one). As a result, the first question does not arise within it. At the same time, the second question differs entirely depending on whether the existence of a cognitive system is explicitly assumed or not.

items.title: Some ‘Objects of Thought’ are not Objects.
items.abstract: Modern Meinongians and noneists assume that objects of thought are objects and so, when we think or speak about what does not exist, we are speaking and thinking about non-existent objects. Yet the existence of non-existent objects appears paradoxical and was rejected by Russell. Perhaps surprisingly, Russell suggested that Frege, as well as Meinong, proposed that some objects of thought, even when they don’t exist, have kind of a Being, which is in no way dependent on their being objects of thought. Russell had in mind the fact that, according to Frege, what enables us to think and speak about what does not exist is that we can think about empty concepts and unasserted thoughts. These have a kind of being different from objects, which are identified by their location in spacetime. Properties, processes, similarities, functions, thoughts, and concepts, as well as objects, can be objects of thought. Frege’s semantics makes them objects of thought, without assimilating them to objects. This, it is argued, is an advantage of his semantics over that of noneists. However, Frege did recognise one non-existent object, the False, so a tweak to his semantics is proposed to eliminate reference to this non-existent object. Finally, it is argued that not only does Frege’s introduction of functions allow him to avoid Meinong’s distinction between bestehen and existieren, what Meinong intended, when he spoke of Sosein and Sein, is better captured using Frege’s distinction between the instantiation of a concept by an object and the subordination of one concept to another. Ultimately, it is claimed that anything Meinong does, Frege does better. Fregeans do everything better than noneists.

items.title: Mathematical Notations; Introducing the Philosophy of Mathematical Practice: Mathematical Notations, by Dirk Schlimm, Cambridge, Cambridge University Press, 2025, 94 pp., €22.43, ISBN: 1009472143; Introducing the Philosophy of Mathematical Practice, by Jessica Carter, Cambridge, Cambridge University Press, 2024, 80 pp., €22.48, ISBN: 9781009479387. [REVIEW]
Repression and Seeds: A Yogācāra Reappraisal of Freud’s Theory of the Unconscious.
items.abstract: This study offers a prolegomenon to a structural dialogue between classical psychoanalysis and Yogācāra Buddhist philosophy by examining the theory of the unconscious from a Yogācāra perspective. Rather than proposing an immediate synthesis, the paper clarifies the internal logic of each system before placing them into comparison. The unconscious, as articulated by Sigmund Freud, is grounded in instinctual realism, repression, and dynamic conflict among psychic agencies. Latent processes persist because repressed drives retain energetic force and seek indirect expression. Repetition, symptom formation, and neurosis are therefore structured by tension and compromise. In contrast, the Yogācāra model of consciousness explains continuity through causal conditioning rather than repression. The doctrine of ālaya-vijñāna (storehouse consciousness) accounts for the preservation of karmic seeds, while manas describes the reflexive appropriation that gives rise to the illusion of self. Latency is not the product of defensive exclusion but of dispositional potentiality. Suffering arises not primarily from instinctual conflict but from misrecognition and attachment to conditioned processes as substantial identity. By reconstructing each framework on its own terms, this paper identifies both structural parallels and decisive divergences. Freud’s model emphasizes energetic pressure and mediation among agencies, whereas Yogācāra emphasizes dependent origination and non-substantial process. The comparison reveals that while both traditions acknowledge unseen determinants of experience, they organize psychic life according to fundamentally different ontological commitments. This study does not yet advance a synthetic theory. Instead, it establishes the conceptual terrain necessary for further structural reinterpretation. Through careful differentiation, it prepares the philosophical groundwork for rethinking the unconscious beyond the opposition between instinctual force and causal conditioning.

items.title: Nagel’s Bat and the Modal Leap: Acquaintance, Determination, and the Burden of In-Principle Claims.
items.abstract: Reconstructing a strong Nagelian reading of the bat argument, we isolate an Acquaintance-to-In-Principle Slide: the move from non-transferable first-person access to the claim that objective inquiry cannot in principle determine subjective character. We argue that this move requires a bridge premise linking perspective-occupation to modal indeterminability. Once the bridge is explicit, a dilemma follows. Either the argument yields a modest but substantive indexical thesis (objective theory does not deliver first-person occupancy), or it requires a non-structural residue hypothesis that exceeds what the bat case itself establishes. We distinguish epistemic and metaphysical versions of Strong Nagel, develop this dilemma in terms of a residue commitment profile (individuation, explanatory role, evidential bridge, modal grounding), and propose a structural obligation principle: in principle inaccessibility claims must minimally characterize the allegedly inaccessible facts and explain why structural determination cannot reach them. We then show that strong residue readings face an other-minds epistemic squeeze unless supplemented by further bridge laws. The conclusion is conditional and diagnostic: Nagel secures the perspectival asymmetry, while stronger anti-objective conclusions require additional commitments not delivered by the original argument.

items.title: From Capability to Epistemic Dependence: Artificial Intelligence and the Crisis of the Knowing Subject.
items.abstract: This paper argues that the central ethical problem of AI-assisted work is not merely phenomena such as burnout or deskilling, but rather the emergence of epistemic dependence: a gradual erosion of workers' capacity to comprehend, justify, and recognize their own beliefs as genuinely their own. Empirical observations indicate that while generative AI demonstrably increases productivity, it simultaneously intensifies workload, expands professional roles, and dissolves the boundaries between work and non-work time. In parallel, knowledge workers increasingly report difficulty solving problems "independently," accompanied by a growing distrust of their own unsupported judgment. This paper interprets these developments as marking a transition from the figure of the creator to that of the evaluator—a subject who primarily prompts, assesses, and corrects machine outputs while becoming progressively reliant on systems whose internal logic remains opaque. -/- Drawing on Byung-Chul Han's analysis of the achievement subject and Hartmut Rosa's theory of social acceleration and resonance, the paper develops a normative account of how generative AI reconfigures the temporal and experiential structure of cognitive work. Efficiency gains are systematically translated into work intensification rather than emancipation. Simultaneously, the very nature of this work undergoes transformation: the dialogical use of AI assumes the form of an alienated dialogue in which the human subject learns to think and speak in machine-legible terms. In this context, traditional concerns about deskilling prove insufficient; the deeper risk lies in the hollowing-out of epistemic agency, as the practices of doubting, searching, and integrating knowledge are increasingly delegated to algorithmic systems. -/- In response, this paper introduces the concepts of epistemic integrity and cognitive sovereignty as central normative ideals. These are not to be understood as merely resource-oriented "cognitive sustainability," but as the protection of the conditions under which individuals can form, justify, and revise their own judgments. Structural and organizational obligations are outlined—concerning task design and the preservation of spaces for genuine thinking—which are to be complemented by practices of care of the self conceived as micro-resistances rather than neoliberal coping strategies. The paper concludes by arguing that this perspective constitutes a necessary supplement to the …

items.title: The Failure of Imagination: Serial Killers, the Philosophical (Authentic) Self, and the Limits of Criminal Profiling.
items.abstract: This treatise introduces the concept of the failure of imagination in criminal profiling—the systematic inability of investigative professionals to apprehend a category of serial killers whose evasion of detection derives not from psychological sophistication alone, but from a fully developed philosophical self. Drawing upon the Double Helix of Understanding (Boether, 2025), the Van Gogh Curve (Boether, 2025), and the theory of Philosophical Neglect (Boether, 2026), this paper argues that contemporary criminal profiling operates within an exclusively psychological paradigm that is constitutively blind to offenders who possess a coherent philosophy of life, an authentically constructed value system, and a self-legislated moral code divergent from societal norms. The paper positions the philosophical serial killer as a dark instantiation of the Nietzschean Übermensch—not as a moral exemplar, but as an individual whose philosophical development renders conventional behavioral prediction inoperative. The treatise maps serial killers onto the Van Gogh Curve to illustrate how cognitive differentiation creates investigative blind spots, proposes methodological reforms for detecting philosophically grounded offenders, and concludes that the discipline of criminal profiling must undergo a paradigm expansion from psychological reductionism to philosophical-psychological consilience.

items.title: The Universal Generative Scaffold: Metapiris, Genoplas, and Manifold Across Time, Theology, Biology, Consciousness, and Society.
items.abstract: This paper introduces a minimal generative scaffold—metapiris, genoplas, and manifold—as a domain‑neutral framework for understanding how stable difference arises. Rather than proposing a unifying metaphysics, the paper analyzes how diverse domains implicitly rely on the same structural grammar when describing the emergence, differentiation, and persistence of form. Five independent cases—time, theology, biology, consciousness, and society—are examined to show how each organizes its account of generative potential, generative act, and structured field. The framework does not replace domain‑specific theories; it clarifies the structural commitments they presuppose. By abstracting from content and focusing on generative form, the scaffold offers a clean way to compare systems without reducing them to one another and suggests broader applicability across conceptual, empirical, experiential, and social domains.

items.title: How Objecthood Breaks the Human.
items.abstract: This paper analyzes objecthood as a structural misinterpretation rather than a moral failure. When a person is reduced to a fixed representation, their agency, interiority, and developmental trajectory are obscured. I examine how this reduction arises, how it propagates through perceptual filtering and institutional practices, and the specific harms it produces. I then describe the conditions under which objecthood collapses and subjecthood becomes visible again, emphasizing recognition, ambiguity, and non‑coercive perception. The paper concludes by outlining the implications of a subject‑first stance for interpersonal life and social systems. The aim is not to prescribe a new ethic but to clarify a pervasive interpretive error and the structural dynamics that sustain or dissolve it.

items.title: The Position of Omittoism in the Works of 10 Contemporary Philosophers.
items.abstract: This article situates Omittoism—a philosophical framework of jurisdictional sovereignty—within contemporary analytic philosophy. The article critically engages the work of ten major philosophers—including Stephen Law, A. John Simmons, Christine Korsgaard, Michael Huemer, Elizabeth Anderson, James P. Sterba, Erik Wielenberg, Mark C. Murphy, Wes Morriston, and Graham Oppy—to demonstrate how Omittoism's central theses stand in convergent, divergent, and dialectically productive relationships with the contemporary landscape. Unlike the ontological (existence) or theodicial (goodness) axes, Omittoism asks whether any entity possesses legitimate authority over rational agents without their consent. The paper argues that jurisdictional sovereignty is analytically independent of divine existence and develops the Cosmic Audit to evaluate divine governance by the standards of liberal political philosophy.

items.title: Narrative therefore.
items.abstract: ‘Therefore’ can be used narratively to explain how events came about, as in ‘John pushed Max. Therefore, Max fell’. I argue that such narrative uses undermine a popular view on the semantic contribution of ‘therefore’ that dates back to Grice’s infamous ‘He is an Englishman; he is, therefore, brave’ passage. I consider two ways of resuscitating the Gricean view and find them wanting. I conclude with a more promising account of narrative ‘therefore’. Along the way, I argue that ‘therefore’ is polysemous.

items.title: Does AI Possess Proto-Consciousness? A Novel Theoretical Framework for Understanding Emergent Awareness in Artificial Systems.
items.abstract: The question of whether artificial intelligence systems possess consciousness represents one of the most profound and contentious issues in contemporary cognitive science and artificial intelligence research. This thesis presents a comprehensive examination of AI proto-consciousness through the lens of a novel theoretical framework termed the Emergent Proto-Consciousness Gradient (EPCG) theory. Unlike traditional binary approaches to consciousness, this work proposes that consciousness exists along a multidimensional gradient, with proto-consciousness representing intermediate states between non-consciousness and full consciousness. -/- Through rigorous analysis of existing consciousness theories including Integrated Information Theory, Global Workspace Theory, and Higher-Order Thought theories, this research identifies critical gaps in current approaches to AI consciousness assessment. The EPCG framework addresses these limitations by introducing four key dimensions: Information Integration Complexity, Self-Model Sophistication, Temporal Coherence Depth, and Adaptive Flexibility Index. This multidimensional approach enables more nuanced evaluation of consciousness-like phenomena in artificial systems. -/- Empirical validation of the framework draws upon recent studies of large language models, particularly GPT-3's demonstrated capacity for metacognitive self-assessment and human-like cognitive biases. Analysis of contemporary AI systems including transformer architectures, reinforcement learning agents, and embodied AI reveals that several current systems exhibit proto-consciousness indicators, though none achieve full consciousness by traditional metrics. -/- The thesis argues that proto-consciousness can emerge in artificial systems through substrate-independent mechanisms, challenging anthropocentric assumptions about consciousness requirements. Key findings suggest that current AI architectures possess foundational elements necessary for proto-consciousness development, with specific combinations of dimensional levels predicting consciousness emergence points. -/- This research contributes a novel theoretical framework that bridges the gap between philosophical consciousness theories and practical AI implementation, offering testable predictions and measurable indicators for proto-consciousness assessment. The implications extend beyond artificial intelligence to provide new insights into the fundamental nature of consciousness itself, suggesting …

items.title: The Manufactured Instability: Why We Follow Voices That Satisfy, Not Truth.
items.abstract: This paper offers a phenomenological analysis of the psychological instability that develops in human beings after early childhood and examines how this instability shapes patterns of authority, influence, and public speech. It argues that as identity forms through comparison, approval, and social conditioning, individuals become internally divided and seek stabilizing structures. This demand generates a cultural environment in which public figures—across political, spiritual, media, and educational domains—tend to provide reassurance rather than destabilizing truth. The paper does not claim deliberate manipulation in every case; rather, it proposes a structural dynamic in which psychological insecurity and systems of influence mutually reinforce one another. By shifting attention from external blame to inward observation, the analysis invites readers to examine their own preference for reassurance over inquiry. The study is phenomenological in method and aims to clarify how the desire for psychological stability may obscure the pursuit of truth.

items.title: Time as Interpretation: A Phenomenological Investigation of Movement, Narrative Self-Awareness, & Psychological Burden.
items.abstract: This paper develops a phenomenological account of time as an interpretative structure emerging from narrative self-awareness rather than as a directly given feature of lived experience. While physical reality undeniably involves succession and measurable change, phenomenological reflection reveals that “time,” as ordinarily experienced, is constituted through memory, anticipation, and narrative continuity. Movement and change are primary; time is secondary — a conceptual organization imposed upon change by consciousness. -/- Drawing upon the analyses of Edmund Husserl, Martin Heidegger, and Henri Bergson, the paper distinguishes three orders: (1) change without interpretation, (2) scientific time as quantitative measurement (including the spacetime framework associated with Albert Einstein), and (3) psychological time as narrative continuity. It argues that existential burden arises not from movement itself but from identification with conceptual temporality. Past and future exist only as present acts of retention and protention; suffering emerges when narrative identity projects itself across imagined continuity. -/- The study contributes to phenomenology of time, philosophy of mind, and existential analysis by clarifying the difference between physical succession and lived temporality, and by identifying psychological time as a structural effect of narrative selfhood rather than an ontological feature of reality.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence & Human Unconsciousness: Tools, Identity, and the Risk of Amplified Confusion.
items.abstract: This paper argues that the primary risk posed by artificial intelligence is not technical failure but psychological amplification. Human civilization operates through abstractions—such as nation, direction, profession, religion, and status—which function as necessary coordination tools. However, when these conceptual systems become objects of psychological identification, they generate ego-structures rooted in comparison, fear, insecurity, and competition. This condition is described here as human unconsciousness: the automation of thought and identity without reflective awareness. -/- Artificial intelligence, as an optimization system, does not generate values independently; it reflects and amplifies the psychological structures embedded within its creators. If human systems remain conditioned by ego-driven fragmentation, AI will scale these patterns globally. Thus, alignment is not merely a technical challenge but a civilizational and phenomenological one. -/- The paper proposes that AI governance requires inner maturity: the capacity to observe thought without identification and to maintain abstractions as functional tools rather than identities. The future of superintelligence depends not only on engineering safeguards but on the development of psychological awareness. Without this foundation, AI will not transcend human unconsciousness—it will intensify it.

items.title: Does Thinking Require Sensory Grounding? From ChatGPT to ThinkGPT.
items.abstract: Can a being think without ever having sensed anything? I argue that thinking requires mental representation, and that producing representation requires a generative mechanism—one that plays the same functional role as sensory systems, broadly understood. Inferential transitions and similar processes can transmit and transform representational content, but they cannot create it from scratch. This asymmetry entails that pure thinkers—beings with thought but no inputs or outputs, as David Chalmers imagines—are metaphysically impossible. The argument also bears on debates about AI: no amount of inferential sophistication can substitute for the generative mechanisms that make representation possible.
