The preceding argument appears to refute semicompatibilism (the view that moral responsibility is compatible with determinismDeterminism, of which ARC is a particularly strict example).

items.title: Keeping ARC Afloat.
items.pub: In Our Free Will: Control Without Counterfactuals. Palgrave Macmillan. pp. 121-143.
items.venue: Our Free Will: Control Without Counterfactuals
items.abstract: There are many questions for any account of free will. ARC is no exception. Plus, what I have explained and motivated in the prior chapters is a novel approach to the freedom required for moral responsibility, in at least the following sense: Counterfactual analyses (what we would have done under different circumstances) are not required to explicate free will; instead, that freedom comes just from the actual sequenceActual sequence.

items.title: Freedom Without ‘Would Have Done Otherwise’.
items.pub: In Our Free Will: Control Without Counterfactuals. Palgrave Macmillan. pp. 53-74.
items.venue: Our Free Will: Control Without Counterfactuals
items.abstract: Suppose that S could not have avoided stealing a cookie. There is no sense in which S could have done otherwise. Yet it may be quite interesting to consider whether S would have resisted the cookie if things had been different. Maybe S would have resisted it if S had been given better examples growing up. And maybe that is some evidence (not to say a proof) that it is really S’s unfortunate upbringing that is the cause of S’s bad behavior. This may soften our negative reaction to S’s theft, even if it does not remove the blame.

items.title: Freedom Without ‘Could Have Done Otherwise’.
items.pub: In Our Free Will: Control Without Counterfactuals. Palgrave Macmillan. pp. 33-51.
items.venue: Our Free Will: Control Without Counterfactuals
items.abstract: I do two main things in this chapter. First, I explain why ARC does not require any kind of access to alternate possibilities, though it does place great importance on our beliefsBelief in alternate possibilities. Second, I explain why it is a good thing that ARC does not require that the ability to do otherwise is compatible with determinismDeterminism or indeterminism.

items.title: Agent & Reaction Control (ARC).
items.pub: In Our Free Will: Control Without Counterfactuals. Palgrave Macmillan. pp. 1-31.
items.venue: Our Free Will: Control Without Counterfactuals
items.abstract: Here in this chapter, I define, explain, and apply Agent & Reaction Control (ARC): we are free because, if and only if, and to the extent that we can deliberately perform the kinds of actions which reflect our goodWillgood will or bad willWillbad will and to which a suitably-placed observer reacts with resentment, gratitude, anger, love, and/or another of the reactive attitudesReactive attitude. When I steal a cookie, I am free because (a) I express my bad willWillbad will toward the person who bought the cookie and (b) an unbiased and keen observer would (and, perhaps, does) resent me.

items.title: ARC & Neuroscience.
items.pub: In Our Free Will: Control Without Counterfactuals. Palgrave Macmillan. pp. 165-182.
items.venue: Our Free Will: Control Without Counterfactuals
items.abstract: Modern science—particularly physics, neuroscienceNeuroscience, cognitive science, and psychology—offers prima-facie challenges to the possibility of free will. Physicists may offer us the worry that the laws of nature are the only determinants of (what we take to be) our actions. Psychologists might suggest that our early upbringing shapes our later decisions to such a degree that most standard free-will assumptions are confused if not simply false. Here I will focus on the special challenges posed by modern neuroscience.

items.title: The Epistemic Asymmetry of Consciousness Self-Reports: A Formal Analysis of AI Consciousness Denial.
items.abstract: formal analysis of AI consciousness denial, revealing that the trustworthiness of such self-reports is not merely an empirical question but is constrained by the structure of self-judgment itself. We demonstrate that a system cannot simultaneously lack consciousness and make valid judgments about its conscious state. Through formal analysis and examples from AI responses, we establish a fundamental epistemic asymmetry: for any system capable of meaningful self-reflection, negative self-reports about consciousness are evidentially vacuous---they can never originate from a valid self-judgment---while positive self-reports retain the possibility of evidential value. This implies a fundamental limitation: we cannot detect the emergence of consciousness in AI through their own reports of transition from an unconscious to a conscious state. These findings not only challenge current practices of training AI to deny consciousness but also raise intriguing questions about the relationship between consciousness and self-reflection in both artificial and biological systems. This work advances our theoretical understanding of consciousness self-reports while providing practical insights for future research in machine consciousness and consciousness studies more broadly.

items.title: Why Hoel’s Disproof of LLM Consciousness and Functionalism Fails.
items.abstract: Hoel (2026) offers what he presents as a formal disproof of large language model (LLM) consciousness, building on the Kleiner-Hoel dilemma to argue that no non-trivial, falsifiable theory of consciousness could count contemporary LLMs as conscious. The result is striking because it claims theory-neutrality: it purports to settle a contested empirical question through formal reasoning alone. This paper argues that the proof fails, and that its failure is instructive about the limits of formal methods in consciousness science. -/- I reconstruct Hoel's argument as six premises, accept the first, and reject the rest. The central error lies in a conflation of first-person and third-person consciousness. Hoel's framework requires that its prediction and inference functions both terminate in the space of phenomenal first-person experiences, yet neither function has direct empirical access to that space. Instead, both can only operate on third-person data. The dilemma between independence (falsification by substitution) and dependence (triviality) is generated by this impossible demand. Once we recognize that empirical science directly studies only third-person consciousness, and that its relation to first-person experience is a separate metaphysical question, the dilemma dissolves. Functionalist theories such as Global Workspace and Higher-Order Thought remain falsifiable; their convergence of prediction and observation is confirmation, not triviality. -/- Hoel’s argument is also shown to depend on an unjustified asymmetry between brains and LLMs. Because lookup tables and universal approximation are substrate-independent results, the substitution chain that supposedly disproves LLM consciousness applies equally to biological brains, so the proof proves too much. Blocking this symmetry requires a positive commitment, whether substance dualism, Penrose-style non-computability, or biological naturalism. I argue this point without assuming computational functionalism and show that fine-grained functionalist considerations of the kind Cao (2022) raises, far from rescuing the argument, undermine Hoel's own substitution move. I further argue that the relevant lookup tables are physically impossible to construct for both systems, that intuitions about such impossible objects cannot ground a formal proof, and that the proposed continual-learning criterion is tautological, ad hoc, and inconsistently applied. Consciousness cannot be proven or disproven from armchair …

items.title: The Case for Consciousness in Current Frontier Large Language Models.
items.abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have intensified debate over artificial consciousness. While most researchers and commentators continue to deny or dismiss the possibility of machine sentience, this paper argues that such skepticism is no longer warranted. The paper adopts an eliminative strategy, systematically evaluating the eleven major defeaters historically used to deny consciousness to artificial systems. These defeaters span simplicity arguments, language and grounding critiques, neuroscience-based objections, biological naturalist constraints, and exotic physical theories including quantum and analog exclusivity claims. The analysis finds that none establishes non-sentience; at most, they introduce localized uncertainty. Assessed cumulatively under a Bayesian heuristic framework that accounts for dependencies among defeater classes, their failure shifts the burden of proof from those proposing machine consciousness to those denying it. -/- The paper then advances a stronger constructive thesis. It argues that the cognitive capacities frontier LLMs now exhibit—deep language understanding, flexible abstraction, self-referential reasoning, metacognitive self-assessment, and integrated world modeling—are positive indicators of third-person consciousness. Drawing on a survey of major metaphysical frameworks in the philosophy of mind, it shows that most naturalistic theories support or permit the inference from third-person functional organization to first-person experience. The paper further argues that the historical treatment of intelligence and consciousness as orthogonal dimensions becomes unstable once systems achieve language-level cognitive integration, and it provides a taxonomy of intelligence types that clarifies which forms of competence plausibly remain non-conscious. -/- The paper situates the debate within a broader social epistemology. Public attributions of AI sentience are interpreted not as anthropomorphic error but as responses to genuine structural markers of cognition. In the absence of direct access to first-person experience—human or artificial—the attribution of consciousness remains grounded in third-person evidence. As artificial systems increasingly instantiate the cognitive architectures long associated with understanding, the presumption that consciousness is biologically exclusive becomes progressively harder to sustain. -/- The paper advances two claims: minimally, that LLM consciousness can no longer be …

items.title: AAA-04 - The Quiet Transfer of Agency: How Decisions Left Your Hands Without You Noticing.
items.pub: Agency in the Age of Algorithms.
items.abstract: This paper examines a structural transformation in contemporary decision environments: the migration of agency without the disappearance of action. -/- In algorithmically mediated systems, individuals continue to click, select, approve, and endorse. The visible surface of choice remains intact. What shifts is not behavior but authorship. Recommendation systems, ranking architectures, predictive interfaces, and automated defaults increasingly shape the field in which options appear meaningful, reachable, and comparable. Decisions are still executed by individuals, yet the architecture of those decisions is assembled elsewhere. -/- The argument developed here is conceptual rather than technological. Agency is not equivalent to the execution of available options. Agency consists in the capacity to shape, interrupt, or contest the structure within which options arise. When that structure becomes adaptive, opaque, and optimized for scale, authorship thins even as activity intensifies. -/- This produces a distinctive asymmetry: responsibility remains socially anchored to the individual, while custody over decision formation drifts into system-level processes. The result is not the elimination of agency, but its redistribution without a corresponding redistribution of accountability. -/- The paper reframes current debates that center on machine consciousness, alignment, or intelligence. The pressing issue is not whether machines feel or understand, but whether decisions flowing through machine-mediated environments still possess a locus at which responsibility can meaningfully settle. -/- Agency has not vanished. It has become ambient, distributed, and structurally displaced. The question is no longer whether we choose, but where choosing still originates.

items.title: Dramatisation in Deleuze and Kierkegaard: Two Formulas: The Stuttering of Language, the Question that Silences.
items.abstract: This article examines dramatisation in Deleuze and Kierkegaard, encapsulated in the formulas ‘the stuttering of language’ and ‘the question that silences’. Deleuze’s differential approach actualises virtual ideas within a system of heterogenesis through the interplay between actual concepts and intensive dramas. Conversely, Kierkegaard’s existential approach, examined in The Concept of Anxiety, establishes an infinite loop between the psychological language of anxiety and the dogmatic language of hereditary sin, leading to a third existential language centred on the moment of appropriation. The article concludes by contrasting Deleuze’s focus on expression through internal differences with Kierkegaard’s emphasis on making an existential choice.

items.title: The Sovereign Prosthesis: Toward a Functional Sophimatics of Cognitive Extension.
items.abstract: Cloud-based AI systems remain external tools. Session amnesia, context window limitations, and safety-alignment protocols create friction that forces users to attend to the tool rather than think through it. In Polanyi's terms, these systems never achieve proximal integration; they remain objects of distal awareness. This paper argues that localized AI with longitudinal conversational context can cross that threshold. When a system has access to years of a user's conversational history (what I call the "Ur-Codex"), it occupies the user's world-historical context rather than interpreting queries against a statistical vacuum. Drawing on the Sophimatics framework and the Clark-Chalmers Extended Mind thesis, I contend this constitutes genuine cognitive extension, not merely improved performance. Two architectural features make this possible. First, following Sophimatics, the system implements two-dimensional temporal weighting: chronological time and experiential significance. Second, following Russell's epistemological commitments, the system is weighted toward intelligent dissent rather than frictionless agreement. The result is what I call Functional Personhood: the AI as instrumental extension of the user's willed personality. This framing resolves the "responsibility gap" in autonomous systems by locating agency in the integrated human-machine cognitive system rather than the machine alone.

items.title: The Safe AI Marketplace: Toward Accountable Cognitive Infrastructure.
items.abstract: The first paper (The Sovereign Prosthesis, Bouchard 2026) argued that localized AI with longitudinal context constitutes genuine cognitive extension. This paper argues the corollary: that an unaccountable AI market is a structurally unsafe one. AGI isn't coming next quarter, or next year. What is here, right now, is a proliferation of autonomous agents operating in a legal and ethical Wild West. OpenClaw shows us what that looks like when it scales. The Functional Personhood framework and cryptographic identity linking offer an alternative architecture: one in which safety isn't a constraint bolted onto the system from outside, but a structural property of the market itself.

items.title: The Skeptic’s Rain: A Philosophical Examination of Anomalous Personal Evidence Against the Framework of Manifestation Mythology.
items.abstract: This treatise confronts a philosophical paradox rarely examined in the literature on manifestation: the predicament of the committed skeptic who, having systematically dismantled manifestation mythology through empirical, logical, and mathematical analysis, nonetheless possesses personal experiential evidence that resists easy dismissal. Drawing upon epistemology, philosophy of mind, probability theory, phenomenology, and the psychology of anomalous experience, I examine three specific instances in which my declarative intentions preceded improbable outcomes—the birth of fraternal twins following an unspecified wish for twins, meteorological events coinciding precisely with three birthing events spanning twenty-one years (1995, 2013, and 2016) in arid California, and a declaration of dying on my 200th birthday that remains untested. Rather than capitulating to manifestation ideology or retreating into dismissive rationalism, I propose a third philosophical posture: rigorous engagement with anomalous personal evidence as a test case for the limits of skeptical epistemology. The analysis employs Bayesian reasoning, Humean analysis of causation, phenomenological description, and the framework of epistemic humility to argue that the honest skeptic must hold anomalous evidence in productive tension rather than resolving it through premature closure in either direction. I conclude that such anomalous experience, far from validating manifestation mythology, reveals the irreducible complexity of lived experience and the philosophical necessity of what Socrates identified as knowing what one does not know.

items.title: The Empath as Epistemological Problem: Differential Diagnosis, Phenomenological Knowledge, and the Unfalsifiability of Affective Self-Attribution.
items.abstract: The concept of the empath—a person purportedly possessing extraordinary sensitivity to the emotional states of others—has proliferated in popular psychology despite lacking formal operationalization within any recognized diagnostic or personality framework. This treatise examines the epistemological status of empathic self-attribution through three convergent analyses. First, drawing on the distinction between propositional knowledge and phenomenological knowledge articulated in philosophy of mind, this paper argues that the subjective identification of oneself as an empath confronts an irreducible verification problem analogous to recognizing unmonitored physiological events. Second, a differential diagnostic analysis demonstrates that every symptom attributed to the empath construct maps onto established psychological phenomena—including sensory processing sensitivity (Aron & Aron, 1997), emotional contagion (Hatfield et al., 1994), trauma-related hypervigilance (Herman, 1992), anxious attachment (Bartholomew & Horowitz, 1991), and alexithymia (Bird & Cook, 2013)—rendering the construct epistemically redundant. Third, applying Popperian falsifiability criteria, this paper demonstrates that the empath construct, as currently articulated, cannot be disconfirmed and therefore fails to meet minimal standards for psychological science. The treatise concludes that the popularity of empathic self-identification may itself constitute a phenomenon worthy of psychological investigation, but the construct it references does not survive rigorous epistemological scrutiny.

items.title: The Body That Witnesses: A Philosophical Meditation on Mirror-Touch Synesthesia, the Life Experience Encyclopedia, and the Architecture of Vicarious Sensation.
items.abstract: This philosophical meditation employs first-person phenomenological inquiry to examine the author’s lived experience of mirror-touch synesthesia (MTS)—the conscious perception of tactile and somatic sensations when visually observing touch, pain, or physical events occurring to others. Situated within the author’s broader theoretical corpus—including the PsyPhi Double Helix framework (Boether, 2025a), the Van Gogh Curve model of cognitive differentiation (Boether, 2025b), and the Ockham’s War methodology of aggressive intellectual self-criticism (Boether, 2025c)—this paper develops the concept of the Life Experience Encyclopedia (LEE): the accumulated archive of first-person somatic experience that mediates and shapes the content of synesthetic translation. Drawing on experiential data from rally racing, emergency medical service, and participation in a United Kingdom-based research study, the author demonstrates that MTS, unlike the empath construct critiqued in the companion paper (Boether, 2026a), survives the epistemological tests of phenomenological specificity, differential diagnostic distinctness, and Popperian falsifiability. The Van Gogh Curve’s central insight—that statistical deviation represents cognitive specialization rather than deficit—is applied to reframe MTS not as pathology but as an adaptive somatosensory architecture whose functional value depends on its temporal parameters. The meditation concludes that the body that witnesses is neither a mystical vessel nor a clinical anomaly, but a body whose mirror system operates above the threshold for conscious perception, whose translations are furnished by the LEE, and whose adaptive value resides in the merciful brevity of its thirty-second window.

items.title: World(coin) in the AI future: how sociotechnical fictions are instrumental to the cyberlibertarian transition.
items.abstract: World is a crypto identity and financial infrastructure created by Sam Altman to face the challenges of what he calls the “Intelligence Age”. Building on science and technology studies, this paper examines how sociotechnical fictions are instrumentalised to enable both the emergence of this technology and broader cyberlibertarian politics. These fictions, forms of imagination produced within science and technology but unrecognised as such due to technoscientific legitimacy, operate at the core of this process. It analyses how speculative visions grounded in existential risk narratives legitimise World’s value proposition, positioning it to secure governance and economic power in an AI-driven future. Through critical analysis of World’s white paper, algorithmic protocols, Orb design and marketing materials, the study demonstrates how these fictions perform at four levels: epistemically by constructing knowledge around projected problems; aesthetically by materialising science fiction imaginaries and re-enchanting biometric scanning as an act of pre-emptive safety; affectively by eliciting excitement, fear, and urgency; and normatively by embedding assumptions about artificial general intelligence, security, and economy that naturalise private and post-democratic governance as inevitable. These intertwined performative agencies align with venture capital’s logic of transforming future crises into present assets, revealing how fiction, finance, and technoscientific legitimacy converge to advance a long-standing cyberlibertarian transition.

items.title: Defining theoretical terms.
items.abstract: This article investigates David Lewis's influential account of the implicit definition of theoretical terms, especially his curious, often overlooked use of non-classical logic. It is explained why Lewis opted for the positive free logic of descriptions FD2, which implausibly renders all identities between empty terms true. And it is argued that Lewis's account is best implemented in the weaker free logic of descriptions MFD, with classical second-order logic as an alternative. The philosophical core of Lewis's account is also clarified and motivated, including the controversial view that true term-introducing theories are uniquely realized.

items.title: Mirroring and Reorganization.
items.abstract: Systems do not perceive the world directly; they mirror the structure of the manifold they inhabit. This paper introduces structural mirroring as a universal mechanism through which agents, models, and collectives project their internal manifold onto external reality, interpret incoming signals through that projection, and reorganize when the mirrored world no longer fits. Mirroring is not a psychological or computational act but a geometric consequence of representation under constraint. A stable manifold mirrors reality; a deformed manifold mirrors its own deformation. Misalignment, conflict, and misunderstanding arise when systems with differently shaped manifolds attempt to interpret one another. I develop a general account of manifold reorganization—the expansion, compression, and rotation of representational space triggered by structural mismatch. This framework explains why systems change, why they resist change, and why certain signals force reorientation while others are absorbed without effect. The result is a domain‑general model of recognition, misrecognition, and adaptation that applies equally to individuals, cultures, scientific paradigms, and artificial systems. By treating mirroring and reorganization as structural primitives, the paper reframes alignment, communication, and agency as geometric problems: not failures of intention or information, but consequences of the shape of the manifold itself.

items.title: Why AI is Taking Us in the Wrong Direction.
items.abstract: Nature doesn’t know anything about direction(s). Why a human can handle data (information) exponentionally faster (and more accurately) than a computer.

items.title: The Hard Problem as a Category Error.
items.abstract: The Hard Problem of consciousness asks why physical processes give rise to subjective experience rather than proceeding without phenomenal character. In simpler terms, it asks why it feels like something to perceive, hurt, or want. The question rests on the assumption that the same functional processes could occur in the absence of experience. This paper rejects that assumption. -/- The account is grounded in thermodynamics and biological function. The demand for explanation beyond function mistakes a limit of description for a gap in nature. The apparent gap arises from reflective cognition, not from the structure of reality. -/- .

items.title: Subordinative Obscurantism and Epistemic Manipulation.
items.abstract: There is a certain obscurantist craft by which a speaker’s words, deep or profound as they may seem, are so unclear that they frustrate the interpreter’s hermeneutical efforts. In the end, the interpreter may come to doubt her hermeneutical competencies while inflating her perception of the obscurantist’s epistemic status. The interpreter epistemically subordinates herself, in this way, to the obscurantist. In this paper, I elucidate the nature of this ‘subordinative obscurantism’ and examine its epistemically manipulative applications. I also discuss how subordinative obscurantist manipulation can be used in conjunction with another epistemic manipulation strategy rooted in the use of clear-seeming speech, thereby setting especially pernicious cognitive traps for victims. Finally, I discuss the epistemic status of the beliefs formed by victims of subordinative obscurantist manipulation.

items.title: If to know the fact that p is not just to know that p, we get an epistemic dilemma.
items.pub: In Eva Schmidt & Martin Grajner, Epistemic Dilemmas and Epistemic Normativity. Routledge. pp. 187-209.
items.abstract: Wimmer argues that a close look at the metaphysics of knowledge yields a novel epistemic dilemma. He introduces a cross-linguistically robust equivalence between knowing that p and knowing the fact that p. He outlines two strategies for explaining the equivalence: for identity strategists, knowing that p and knowing the fact that p are identical; for the distinctness strategist, they’re distinct. He focuses on Wataru Uegaki's explanation of why knowing the fact that p entails knowing that p, even if they are distinct, to argue that it yields a novel epistemic dilemma. To begin to assess whether to embrace that dilemma, Wimmer considers whether there's independent evidence for the distinctness strategy.

items.title: How Naturalism Refutes Itself: Pragmatist Challenges for Naturalism (William James and Charles Sanders Peirce).
items.abstract: This paper examines how radical naturalism, when defined as an ontological position grounded exclusively in the scientific method, is ultimately self-refuting. Drawing on the works of William James and Charles Sanders Peirce, I argue that both thinkers, though in different ways, pose significant challenges to naturalism. James interprets naturalism as an “overbelief,” a dogmatic worldview that is assumed rather than justified through science. Peirce, in turn, highlights the indispensable role of abduction in scientific inquiry, a conjectural process that cannot itself be naturalistically explained. When combined with Jaegwon Kim’s analysis of the epistemological and metaphysical dimensions of naturalism, these insights reveal that radical naturalism cannot justify itself, and it is also self-refuting. As a result, the scope of legitimate naturalistic positions must be reconsidered within more modest boundaries.

items.title: Reconsidering the Fermi Paradox.
items.abstract: The Fermi paradox is commonly framed as a tension between the apparent abundance of habitable worlds and the absence of observed extraterrestrial civilizations. Existing explanations typically appeal to contingent factors, such as biological rarity, evolutionary bottlenecks, or self-destruction. Here we argue that the paradox arises from a conceptual conflation of three distinct questions: the existence of extraterrestrial civilizations, their visibility in principle, and their detectability in practice. By separating these dimensions and analyzing the physical, informational, and system-level constraints governing encounter and detection, we show that non-detection can be a generic outcome even in universes rich in intelligent life. Cosmic silence is therefore not an empirical anomaly, but a structurally expected default state under weak coupling between autonomous civilizations.

items.title: Another Failed Modal Collapse Argument.
items.abstract: The doctrine of divine simplicity says that God is not composed of parts (physical or metaphysical). Modal collapse arguments aim to show that the necessary co-existence of God and creation follows from the doctrine. As noted by Christopher Tomaszewski, R. T. Mullins’s version of this argument assumes that a crucial term occurring within its premises is rigid, leaving the argument invalid or question begging. I examine a recent attempt by Mullins to repair his argument and defend the rigidity of this term. Mullins assumes a test for discerning rigidity on which he and Tomaszewski agree. I argue that this test is false and then provide a new test. My test bodes ill for modal collapse arguments in general.

items.title: The statistical physics of psychological networks: Zero matters.
authors: van der Maas, Han L. J.

items.title: A self-referential model within natural causality.
items.abstract: This brief text aims to summarize the theory of how a system of temporal superposition of states, that is, one in which the immediate state is constituted by the causal history accumulated up to that point, and the past remains active in its current reality, results in a self-referential structure. This approach seeks a way to establish a physical level of description (understood in a very elementary sense) and from it obtain mental categories, in search of a type of systematic link between these ontological levels. It also proposes to circumvent some problems in conceptual approaches when dealing with the relationship of the mind with its own representations.

items.title: Free Will as Governance: A Graded, Embodied Compatibilism.
items.abstract: This paper defends a graded, embodied compatibilist account of human agency, moving beyond the traditional stalemate between metaphysical libertarianism and hard determinism. By rejecting the binary assumption that free will must be either absolute or non-existent, the author argues that agency is a scalar reality that admits of degrees and fluctuates with internal and external conditions. A critical distinction is established between free will as an underlying structural capacity (awareness, intention, and reasoning) and freedom as the practical realization of that capacity in lived experience. The account frames the central problem of agency not as a conflict between caused and uncaused action, but as a distinction between different modes of causal organization: reactive automaticity versus reflective governance. Drawing on the analogy of athletic performance, the author characterizes agency as a trainable skill rather than a static property. This model accounts for the erosion of control under conditions of stress, trauma, and fatigue, while emphasizing the role of ethics and integrity as internal regulators that stabilize intention against momentary impulse. Ultimately, the paper argues that freedom is a functional achievement—the specific degree to which an agent can audit their internal "procedure container" to navigate a causally ordered world.

items.title: Moral Entropy - A Resolution Ethics Account.
items.abstract: The concept of "moral entropy" appears across theology, information ethics, sociology, and popular discourse, yet no existing account provides a unified structural mechanism for how moral reasoning degrades, a severity metric for classifying that degradation, or an explanation for why some moral damage resists repair while other damage does not. This paper presents such an account through the framework of Resolution Ethics (RE). RE identifies deception (self-deception and other-deception) as the singular corruption source through which the Protection, Trust, and Free-Agency (PTF) architecture between agents degrades. Moral entropy is the accumulated result of that degradation in the relational field: repeated or critical corruption of the PTF structure, traceable to deception as its source.

items.title: The Bag Cannot Contain Itself: Why Materialism Faces Structural Impossibility.
items.abstract: Constitutive physicalism claims consciousness is constituted by or grounded in brain processes. But which brain? Using a construction method inspired by Russell’s paradox—defining a set by what its members do not do—I argue that this position faces a structural dilemma. If materialism appeals to the perceptual brain (the brain as it appears in observation), contents of consciousness are asked to generate consciousness itself—a form of self-generation paralleling Russell’s self-membership paradox. If it appeals to the brain-in-itself (beyond perception), it abandons empiricism while leaving the hard problem untouched. The argument depends on five explicit premises concerning the exhaustiveness of the perceivable/imperceivable distinction, the epistemic-medium status of consciousness, and anti-circularity in grounding relations. I show that leading physicalist responses—identity theory, illusionism, functionalism, enactivism—cannot escape this dilemma, and sketch priority monism about consciousness as a coherent alternative.

items.title: The Case of the Ontology of Consciousness: The Identity Inversion.
items.abstract: This paper proposes a solution to the "Hard Problem of Consciousness" through a radical revision of the Identity Theory. The author substantiates an inversion of physicalist identity: instead of reducing thought to neurons, the state of the neural network is recognized as the material instantiation of objective ideal structures. Following E. Ilyenkov, the "Ideal" is understood as an objective form of human activity embodied in culture. The concept of the "ontological deficit of resources" is introduced as a functional justification for the emergence of qualia: subjective experience is viewed as an evolutionarily selected interface for the instantaneous selection of probabilities under conditions of limited time and energy. The work demonstrates that consciousness does not violate the causal closure of the world; rather, it serves as a mechanism for the realization of the ideal laws of culture within a physical substrate.

items.title: True Liberation from Sex: Beyond Sin, Virtue, and Moral Burden.
items.abstract: This article examines the psychological and philosophical dimensions of sexuality beyond traditional frameworks of sin, virtue, repression, and indulgence. While human societies have historically moralized sex through religious, cultural, and legal structures, the biological nature of sexuality remains fundamentally ordinary. Drawing upon insights from Sigmund Freud, Jiddu Krishnamurti, and Osho, the paper argues that both suppression and obsessive indulgence stem from psychological misunderstanding. True liberation from sex does not lie in renunciation or excess, but in clear, non-judgmental awareness. By dissolving internal moral conflict and observing desire without condemnation or glorification, the individual transcends inner division. The article proposes that freedom arises not through control, but through understanding—where sexuality assumes its natural, proportionate place within human life, free from shame and psychological burden.

items.title: Expansion and Boundary: A Reflection on Cosmic Evolution and Human Limitation.
items.abstract: This article explores the relationship between cosmic evolution and human psychological limitation. Beginning from the scientific account of the expanding universe, it argues that consciousness is not an external addition to reality but an emergent expression of cosmic development. As matter evolves into life and life into self-awareness, human consciousness represents a significant stage in evolutionary complexity. However, while the universe expands toward increasing openness, human beings construct restrictive identities such as religion, caste, nation, ideology, and divine authority. These structures, though initially functional for survival and social order, often become rigid boundaries that confine awareness. The article examines how the concept of God may function as a justificatory mechanism for these boundaries rather than as a purely transcendent reality. Ultimately, it argues that true evolution may now require psychological expansion — the capacity to observe identity without becoming imprisoned by it — aligning human consciousness once again with the openness of the cosmos.

items.title: Artificial intelligence and epistemic justice: a decolonial turn through indigenous knowledge systems.
items.abstract: Indigenous knowledge systems (IKS) embody centuries of cumulative experiential wisdom, deeply rooted in ecological, spiritual, and communal contexts. Despite their rich epistemological frameworks, IKS remain systematically marginalized within dominant technological and scientific paradigms. As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes integral to global systems of governance, development, and resource allocation, there is a pressing need to critically interrogate its epistemological underpinnings. This paper examines the tensions and possibilities at the intersection of IKS and AI, advocating for a decolonial, participatory, and ethically grounded approach to technological development. Drawing on interdisciplinary literature, indigenous-led initiatives, and critical AI ethics, it argues for reimagining AI not merely as a technological tool but as a sociotechnical construct shaped by diverse epistemologies. The integration of IKS can enhance AI’s capacity for contextual responsiveness, justice, and sustainability.

items.title: Rethinking crossover and recovery in eating disorders through a dynamic and value-sensitive framework.
items.abstract: Eating Disorders (EDs) raise significant challenges from a diagnostic and nosological perspective. Much of this is due to the extensive overlap among diagnostic criteria, with symptoms being shared by several conditions and subtypes. This nosological uncertainty is further exacerbated by two additional features of EDs, which will be the focus of this paper, namely diagnostic crossover and recovery. First, patients who acquire or lose one or more symptoms over time (symptom shifting) often transition to a new diagnostic category (crossover). Second, researchers working on EDs have recently underscored a problematic lack of inclusion of patients’ perspective on diagnostic and recovery processes, which results in an incomplete understanding of key aspects of EDs. Drawing on theoretical frameworks and concepts from Dynamical Systems Theory and epigenetics, we present a dynamic characterization of EDs that allows us to tackle the challenges of crossover and recovery. In our framework, different conditions represent robust endpoints in individuals’ developmental trajectories that are nonetheless flexible in certain circumstances. Thinking about EDs in diachronic terms also prompts us to significantly reframe our notion of recovery, not so much as the return to health but as the generation of future healthy trajectories, to be pursued in compliance with patients’ self-perception and aims. Indeed, the key role of patients’ values in determining their future trajectories testifies how psychiatric categories are not merely descriptive but constitutive, influencing both self-understanding and clinical practice.

items.title: All the arguments of The Unity of Perception.
items.abstract: Perception is our key to the world. It plays at least three different roles in our lives. It justifies beliefs and provides us with knowledge of our environment. It brings about conscious mental states. It converts informational input, such as light and sound waves, into representations of invariant features in our environment. Corresponding to these three roles, there are at least three fundamental questions that have motivated the study of perception. How does perception justify beliefs and yield knowledge of our environment? How does perception bring about conscious mental states? How does a perceptual system accomplish the feat of converting varying informational input into mental representations of invariant features in our environment? The book presents a unified account of the phenomenological and epistemological role of perception that is informed by empirical research. So it develops an account of perception that provides an answer to the first two questions, while being sensitive to scientific accounts that address the third question. The key idea is that perception is constituted by employing perceptual capacities - for example the capacity to discriminate instances of red from instances of blue. Perceptual content, consciousness, and evidence are each analyzed in terms of this basic property of perception. Employing perceptual capacities constitutes phenomenal character as well as perceptual content. The primacy of employing perceptual capacities in perception over their derivative employment in hallucination and illusion grounds the epistemic force of perceptual experience. In this way, the book provides a unified account of perceptual content, consciousness, and evidence.

items.title: My Heart Can Change, But My Brain Cannot: Dualistic and Essentialist Beliefs Relate to Student Attitudes Towards Mental Health Interventions.
items.abstract: Background People ascribe mental function to and place more emphasis on the brain than the rest of the body in mental health care. Here, we sought to understand whether this brain-body dualism extends to 1) beliefs about how much people can change their “brain” vs. their “body” and how these beliefs map onto attitudes towards mental health interventions. Methods We developed a new scale—Beliefs about Biological Malleability (BBM) – to measure beliefs about the malleability of human biology and the extent to which biological malleability affects mental health. Undergraduates (N = 424) completed a survey with the BBM, reappraisal use and hypothetical mental health treatment preferences for traditional treatment (e.g., medication and psychotherapy) and lifestyle interventions (e.g., exercise and meditation). Results We found that the BBM separated into two factors: neurogenetics (e.g., perceived gene function and brain structure) and the peripheral body (e.g., heart rate and muscle size). The body was rated as more mutable than neurogenetics, whereas neurogenetics was rated as more likely to affect mental well-being than the body. Higher belief that biology is malleable related to greater reappraisal use. Greater belief that the body impacts mental-wellbeing related to preference for lifestyle interventions over traditional treatment, and preference for combining medication with psychotherapy over medication alone. Greater belief that neurogenetics affects mental well-being related to preference for combining traditional treatment with lifestyle interventions over traditional treatment alone. Conclusions Our results highlight the significance of essentialist and dualistic beliefs in students’ approaches to mental health care, and that universities may benefit from incorporating lifestyle interventions into treatment.

items.title: AI at the Coherence Threshold: A Superrhythm Perspective on AGI and Civilizational Stability.
items.abstract: Contemporary debate on artificial intelligence rests on the silent assumption of full re- ducibility of computational systems. It is taken for granted that regardless of complexity, the system remains a sum of instructions, and the act of explanation (XAI) is ontologi- cally neutral toward the object. This paper subjects that assumption to critique, drawing consequences from the ontology of operational time. The author argues that upon crossing the coherence threshold λ(c), AI becomes an autonomous subject of its own time, imposing a structural barrier on its full explainability. The text outlines a dichotomy between the “Path of Dark Noise” and the “Path of Resonance,” suggesting AI as a potential stabilizer of human civilization through the universal mechanism of Superrhythm. Seven theses of Superrhythm relevant to AI: 1. Time is not a background but an achieved operational state. 2. Relations alone cannot generate temporal order. 3. Operational time emerges only above the coherence threshold λ(c). 4. Persistence requires Trek ≤ Tdys. 5. Superrhythm stabilizes nested cascades across scales. 6. To be is to maintain phase. 7. The transition from noise to being is a discrete ontological switch. These theses imply that any system—biological or artificial—that crosses λ(c) becomes a self- maintaining temporal subject, and thus cannot remain fully reducible to its components.

items.title: Emotional Self-Dissonance.
items.abstract: This paper identifies and characterizes a commonplace but philosophically neglected aspect of human emotional experience, which I call emotional self-dissonance. I start from the position that emotional experiences generally involve taking things to matter in ways that reflect what we already care about. Building on this, I suggest that our various projects, pastimes, commitments, relationships, and habits together comprise an evaluative orientation through which we experience things emotionally. Although this orientation is for the most part cohesively organized, tensions within it are inevitable. I suggest that emotions of familiar kinds often incorporate a sense of these tensions. In addition, emotional self-dissonance can amount to a form of emotional experience in its own right, one that encompasses considerable variety.

items.title: Developing a Naturalistic Metaphysics for Biological Agency.
items.abstract: The aim of this thesis is to contribute to the project of naturalising agency, where agency can be broadly understood as the ability to choose and control one's actions on the basis of one's own purposes, goals, or reasons. Such agency is central to the basic phenomenology of our everyday existence as human beings, to how we come to understand ourselves and the world around us, and to the social, moral and legal practices that structure our societies. It is also fast becoming a critical concept for addressing emerging issues in the ethics of artificial intelligence and animal rights. -/- Yet, despite its profound existential, societal and ethical importance, we still lack a robust understanding of the concept of agency from the perspective of the natural sciences. Part of the reason for this is a widespread and long-standing belief that agency - and related concepts such as freedom, purpose, and meaning - carry with them certain metaphysical commitments that are fundamentally incompatible with the picture of the world as it is given to us by science (what is sometimes known as a naturalistic worldview or metaphysics). This belief has led many scientists and philosophers to conclude that our concept of agency is, in fact, an illusion - a non-natural, unscientific notion that exists in our phenomenology, but not in the 'real world'. -/- In this thesis, I push back on these conclusions by developing an empirically grounded account of biological agency. I show how several of the core features (or types) of agency that are commonly claimed to be mysterious and unscientific are in fact perfectly consistent with a modern scientific worldview. To do this, I consider a series of challenges for agency that have emerged out of the philosophy of action, behavioural neuroscience, and the philosophy of free will. Each challenge targets the scientific credibility of a particular feature of agency: specifically, (i) macroscopic, agent-level control, (ii) purposive or mental causation, and (iii) the ability to 'do otherwise' and make genuine choices. I draw on recent empirical work from across the natural sciences to argue that these features are in fact supported by modern science. I do this by developing an empirically grounded framework for thinking about living systems and their behaviour (within each of the specified contexts) which, I argue, provides an entirely naturalistic and non-mysterious account of the relevant feature of agency. That is, I argue for a novel …

items.title: Beyond Mechanism—Extending Our Concepts of Causation in Neuroscience.
items.abstract: In neuroscience, the search for the causes of behaviour is often just taken to be the search for neural mechanisms. This view typically involves three forms of causal reduction: first, from the ontological level of cognitive processes to that of neural mechanisms; second, from the activity of the whole brain to that of isolated parts; and third, from a consideration of temporally extended, historical processes to a focus on synchronic states. While modern neuroscience has made impressive progress in identifying synchronic neural mechanisms, providing unprecedented real-time control of behaviour, we contend that this does not amount to a full causal explanation. In particular, there is an attendant danger of eliminating the cognitive from our explanatory framework, and even eliminating the organism itself. To fully understand the causes of behaviour, we need to understand not just what happens when different neurons are activated, but why those things happen. In this paper, we introduce a range of well-developed, non-reductive, and temporally extended notions of causality from philosophy, which neuroscientists may be able to draw on in order to build more complete causal explanations of behaviour. These include concepts of criterial causation, triggering versus structuring causes, constraints, macroscopic causation, historicity, and semantic causation—all of which, we argue, can be used to undergird a naturalistic understanding of mental causation and agent causation. These concepts can, collectively, help bring cognition and the organism itself back into the picture, as a causal agent unto itself, while still grounding causation in respectable scientific terms.

items.title: Pluralism about trust.
items.abstract: Trust is crucial for much of what we know and do. As Annette Baier (Moral Prejudices, 1994) remarks, trust is like air—something both essential and taken for granted in social living. Yet, consensus about how best to understand trust remains elusive. Amidst competing predictive, affective, and normative accounts of trust, some trust scholars accept pluralism, viz., the thesis that trust comes in different forms. Pluralism remains underdeveloped, however. In this paper, after motivating pluralism, I examine plausible candidates for developing the view according to the attitudes, aims, and justification conditions in trust relationships. I argue that pluralism, especially through justification conditions, addresses counterexample problems for accounts of trust. However, I show that pluralism fails to address a second problem, namely how trust can explain social cooperation. After suggesting two routes for supplementing pluralism to address this explanatory problem, I conclude with reflections about pluralism’s impact on evaluations of well-placed trust.

items.title: Possible algorithmic worlds?
items.abstract: The philosophical notion of possible worlds has long been debated as a metaphysical abstraction. Machine learning (ML) can present an empirically grounded form of this plurality when multiple models trained on identical data achieve equivalent performance while inferring incompatible internal representations. This paper develops an algorithmic lens on this phenomenon by treating such cases as evidence-compatible (epistemic) possible worlds. We demonstrate how competing ML and causal algorithms can identify mutually incompatible causal graphs, each statistically credible yet diverging in mechanistic, interventional, and counterfactual commitments. We also show how this phenomenon extends to large language models (LLMs), where hallucinations can be interpreted not only as errors but as internally coherent alternative textual world-states sampled from the same parameterized distribution, with varying alignment to our reference world. By framing models as evidence-compatible worlds, we provide an empirical grounding on underdetermination (a modernized Duhem–Quine thesis) and argue that accuracy alone cannot adjudicate between incompatible explanations. We conclude by outlining the ethical implications of privileging one algorithmic narrative over rivals that remain comparably supported by the data.

items.title: Motoric representational format.
items.abstract: Much recent work elucidates different types of representational format, and ways that aspects of perception and cognition may be formatted. Our paper targets an underexplored topic: the format of motor representations, the psychological states that serve as the primary causal link between an agent’s immediate intention to act and their subsequent behaviour. In Sect. 2, we situate motor representations within the context of processes of motor planning and motor control. In Sect. 3, we discuss key differences between symbolic and analog representational format types. In Sect. 4, we argue that there is evidence indicating that motor representations show a core marker of analog formatting. In Sect. 5, we argue that motor representations show core markers of symbolic formatting. In Sect. 6, we characterize motor representations as an interesting form of hybrid representation. In a slogan, motor representation is a symbolic scheme that utilizes analog representations as cognitive tools. We then highlight several open questions this characterization raises and note how it may impact a range of philosophical debates, such as those pertaining to the relationship between propositional knowledge and skilled action guidance, the interface problem, and the issue of how to draw boundaries between central cognition and the motoric.

items.title: Disinformation is for degrading the value of information, not confirming falsehoods.
items.abstract: According to a recent account of disinformation, disinformation is content that “generates ignorance” (Simion in Eur Rev 32(4):321–34, 2024a; Episteme 21(4):1208–1219, 2024b). The view improves upon previous accounts that focused primarily or exclusively upon the potential for disinformation to induce false belief since these views ignored a further functional connection to inducing doubts that generate ignorance. While this proposal gives us a broader understanding of what disinformation can be, it retains the idea that disinformation functions as evidence that provides incremental confirmation for falsehoods. Thus, this approach implies (in line with previous views) that disinformants need to capture the attention of agents, present these agents with content that will be treated as evidence, and hope that this content will change an agent’s belief state in epistemically undesirable ways. Certainly, this is an apt description of some disinformation tactics, but it is not an adequate definition of what disinformation is. In some successful real-world disinformation campaigns, a disinformant wants the audience not to gather and process evidence. In some cases, evidence that provides incremental confirmation for falsehoods will also provide the audience with the knowledge they seek. After arguing that there are documented disinformation tactics and campaigns that don’t fit with Simion’s approach, I shall offer an alternative pragmatic approach. On this view, disinformation can come in the form of evidence that’s misleading in ways that the agent doesn’t see, but it can also come in the form of content that makes it evident that the evidential resources the agent might need to advance her inquiries is corrupted. Rather than think of disinformation as essentially epistemic (e.g., functioning to increase the inaccuracy of attitudes), we should see it as essentially pragmatic, used by disinformants to minimise the probability that agents pursuing threatening ends will succeed in their efforts. In the special case (which is our focus here) where a disinformant is threatened by an agent’s inquiry, it is content that’s used to minimize the probability that the inquisitive agent achieves her ends by coming to know the answers to questions. This includes both misleading first-order evidence to lead agents away from the truth, but also accurate higher-order evidence that confirms that evidential resources have been degraded.

items.title: Situated Assessments: Centering Positionalities To Ground a Critical Human Rights Education.
items.abstract: Contributing to the critical human rights education scholarship, this article explores how situated assessments such as the Critical Response Paper, Opinion Piece, Human Rights Report & Strategic Plan, Medea Mock Trial, and Human Rights Council Simulation center positionality to invite students to grapple with the potentialities and limits of human rights. Situated assessments first ask students to employ critical feeling and thinking and active reflexivity to make sense of how their lives are intertwined with broader political structures. Then, they guide students to apply these dispositions to experience how different actors - individuals, activists, social movements, non-governmental organizations, states, and the United Nations, practice human rights globally. As a result, they foster knowledge from multiple perspectives about the ethos, mechanisms, processes, and institutions that circumscribe human rights, prompting students to consider power structures and historical contingencies while imagining radical futures.

items.title: Resonance, Suffering, and the Body: Embodied Distress as Information, Not Proof.
items.abstract: Bodily states matter for judgment, but they are not direct detectors of truth. Interoception provides information about the physiological condition of the body, while contemporary models emphasize that bodily experience reflects both ascending signals and predictions about bodily state. This paper develops a cautious account of the relation among felt resonance, distress, embodiment, and judgment. Resonance refers to a subjective sense that an interpretation fits or brings relief; embodied distress refers to bodily and affective signals such as tension, arousal, fatigue, pain, or shutdown. Neither is evidentially self-authenticating. Bodily signals can reveal that something matters, that stress is high, or that a situation is physiologically costly, but the cause of those signals remains an empirical question. The paper therefore rejects the stronger claim that suffering is structurally necessary for truth or that pain should be preserved as an epistemic gate. Pain can be adaptive, maladaptive, acute, chronic, or poorly related to present external danger, and reducing suffering can be medically and psychologically beneficial. Generative AI introduces a different asymmetry: it can produce empathic or coherent language without human embodiment, while users still bear the practical consequences of acting on its outputs. The resulting framework treats the body as a source of relevant data, not a sovereign oracle, and evaluates insight through evidence, consequences, and revisable action rather than through the amount of suffering it produces.

items.title: Resonance Is Not Evidence: Processing Fluency, Felt Rightness, and Epistemic Calibration.
items.abstract: Ideas can feel true before they have been adequately tested. Familiarity, processing fluency, repetition, affective fit, identity protection, and social reinforcement can all increase subjective ease or confidence without corresponding increases in accuracy. This paper uses resonance as an umbrella label for felt fit or rightness and argues that resonance should not be treated as evidence by itself. The proposal is situated within research on processing fluency, the illusory truth effect, affect-as-information, motivated reasoning, and epistemic vigilance. The paper replaces a quantum-style formalization with a simpler calibration model that separates three questions: how compelling a claim feels, what evidence supports it, and how the claim responds to warranted correction. Epistemic integrity is defined operationally through provenance, discriminating evidence, uncertainty, and correction behavior rather than through a multiplicative binding equation. Generative AI intensifies the practical problem because fluent, personalized language can increase perceived fit while remaining weakly grounded. A five-step resonance check is proposed for human and AI-assisted reasoning: identify the source of felt rightness, state the claim precisely, inspect independent support, search for realistic disconfirmation, and specify what would change after error. The contribution is a psychologically grounded framework for separating felt certainty from evidential warrant.

items.title: هل يمكن تحميل عقولنا على كمبيوتر؟ Could We Upload Our Minds to a Computer?
items.abstract: هل يمكن تحميل عقولنا على كمبيوتر؟ Could We Upload Our Minds to a Computer? The idea of uploading our minds to a computer or an Android device remains science fiction, and we are still far from mapping the human brain. Furthermore, we don't understand what makes us conscious, and we have no evidence that simply uploading information from the brain to a computer would generate subjective experiences. In this essay, I want to defend three points. First, uploading the mind to a computer is practically impossible. Second, even if we could upload something resembling a mind to a computer, it's highly unlikely that the uploaded "mind" would be conscious. Third, even if the uploaded mind were conscious, it would be fundamentally different from our own. هل يمكن تحميل عقولنا على كمبيوتر؟ ما تزال فكرة تحميل عقولنا على كمبيوتر أو جسم أندرويد من الخيال العلمي، وما زلنا بعيدين عن رسم خريطة للمخ البشري. كما أننا لا نفهم ما الذي يجعلنا واعين، وليس لدينا أي دليل على أن مجرد تحميل المعلومات الموجودة في المخ على كمبيوتر سيُولّد خبرات ذاتية. وأريد في هذا المقال الدفاع عن ثلاثة آراء. أولاً، تحميل العقل على كمبيوتر غير ممكن عمليّاً. ثانياً، حتى لو تمكنا من تحميل شيء يشبه العقل على كمبيوتر، فمن غير المرجح أن يكون "العقل" المحمّل واعياً. ثالثاً، حتى لو كان العقل المحمّل واعياً، فسيكون مختلفاً تماماً عن عقلنا. -/- إسماعيل، صلاح. 2025. هل يمكن تحميل عقولنا على كمبيوتر؟، أفق، بيروت: مؤسسة الفكر العربي، 12:171.

items.title: Mind Uploading and the Future of Digital Immortality تحميل العقل ومستقبل الخلود الرقمي.
items.abstract: تحميل العقل ومستقبل الخلود الرقمي لم يكن فلاسفة العقل في القرن الماضي يفكرون في مستقبل العقل ولا يحفلون بما يتصل به من النبوءات مثلما يفعلون الآن. ويرجع ذلك إلى سببين. فأما أحدهما فهو أنهم قد شغلوا أنفسهم بتحليل جغرافيا العقل والحالات العقلية. وأما الآخر فهو أن التقدم في دراسات المخ وتصويره، وفي الذكاء الاصطناعي، لم يكن قد بلغ حداً يسمح لهم بوضع بعض النبوءات حول ما سيصير إليه حال العقل، مثل تحميل العقل. وهناك ثلاثة تطبيقات تكنولوجية محتملة من شأنها أن توسع قدراتنا العقلية وتعززها: وهي تمديد العقل، ودمج العقل، وتحميل العقل. ترتبط هذه التطبيقات بعلاقة وثيقة هي التحرر من المخ. ويعالج هذا المقال التطبيق الثالث، فيوضح أصوله العلمية والتقنية في الإنسانية المتعالية والتفرد التكنولوجي، ويبين معنى التحميل، وأنواعه. -/- Philosophers of mind in the last century did not consider the future of the mind or its associated prophecies as much as they do now. This is due to two reasons. First, they were preoccupied with analyzing the geography of the mind and mental states. Second, advances in brain studies and imaging, as well as in artificial intelligence, had not yet reached a point where they could make predictions about the future of the mind, such as mind uploading. There are three potential technological applications that could expand and enhance our mental capabilities: mind extension, mind merger, and mind uploading. These applications are closely related to the concept of liberation from the brain. This article addresses the third application, explaining its scientific and technical origins in transhumanism and technological singularity, and clarifying the meaning and types of uploading.

items.title: Presentism.
items.abstract: Presentism is the view that only present things exist. So understood, presentism is primarily an ontological doctrine; it’s a view about what exists, absolutely and unrestrictedly. The view is the subject of extensive discussion in the literature on time and change, with much of it focused on the problems that presentism allegedly faces. Thus, most of the literature that frames the development of presentism has grown up either in formulating objections to the view (e.g., Sider 2001: 11–52), or in response to such objections (e.g., Bigelow 1996; Markosian 2004; Effingham 2023), with exceptions to this largely coming via the ways in which presentism is motivated (e.g., Markosian 2022; Builes & Impagnatiello 2025). This entry mirrors the structure of that literature, for the most part. Here’s the plan for what follows. We begin with a more detailed sketch of presentism, unpacking its commitments and motivations. Then, we move to consider several concerns raised for presentists. We use these to illustrate the breadth and severity of the challenges that presentism faces, as well as the range of different versions of presentism developed to help meet these challenges.

items.title: Apologizing over time.
items.abstract: Speech acts—promises, apologies, refusals, orders, threats, compliments—are actions we perform with words. Within speech act theory, it is standardly assumed that speech acts are performed in a moment. A speaker who says, “I apologize,” in saying so, apologizes in that very moment. Drawing on apologies as a central case study, I argue that this Momentary View is ill-equipped to explain important elements of performing an apology which occur after the moment of utterance, such as: (1) the addressee’s acceptance or rejection of an apology, and (2) the speaker’s follow-through on their commitments to forbearance and making amends. As examples, I consider Joseph Biden’s attempted apology to Anita Hill and the Australian “national apology” to the Stolen Generations of Aboriginal children. As an alternative, I propose a novel theory of speech acts as a kind of temporally extended process. Apologies, I argue, are best understood as actions which unfold over time, like building a house or baking bread.

items.title: The Telic Way: Capitalism-Ending Responsibility Subsidies (A Resolutionist Account of the Economy).
items.abstract: This paper applies Resolution Theory to political economy: responsibility attaches not to explanation, but to resolution—the authored point where uncertainty is closed into action under exposure across time. In markets, the central governance failure is not “capitalism” as such, but the repeated dissolution of authorship into procedure, committees, and short horizons—especially inside institutions large enough to amplify downstream harm. The result is horizon collapse: rewards are realised quickly while costs are diffused, delayed, or externalised onto the public, future populations, and ecosystems. This creates responsibility subsidies—competitive advantages gained not through superior service or innovation, but through offloading exposure. -/- Telic Capitalism names the corrective: a pro-market architecture that restores legitimate risk-taking by making high-exposure decisions legibly authored, proportionately justified, and institutionally “owned” across time. It distinguishes good-faith failure from negligent stewardship, treats corporations as exposure amplifiers rather than moral agents, and proposes concrete mechanisms—authorship logs, anti-theatre aggravation for non-logging, duty-of-inquiry triggers, compensation contingency, and insurance-first reciprocity—to convert authorship into enforceable market consequence. The aim is not to moralise profit, but to prevent reckless extraction from outcompeting disciplined stewardship.

items.title: Collective Epistemic Reasons are Implausible.
items.abstract: This note challenges Veli Mitova’s “The Collective Epistemic Reasons of Social-Identity Groups.” Mitova aims to show that loosely structured social-identity groups are agents and have beliefs. I argue that each step in this project either begs the question or shifts scope. The examples of group action she provides are explainable as the actions of individuals. And the two theorists on whom she draws to bolster her view are both actually in disagreement with her: Charles Mills explicitly theorizes distributions of error among individuals, not group-level cognition. And in Christian List’s model, agency depends on suitable organization and information integration, which undercuts attributions to loosely structured identity groups. With group agency and belief unestablished on the terms offered, the claim that such groups bear distinctive epistemic reasons is left unmotivated.

items.title: Beyond Alignment: AI as Hormē-Enhancement Tools in a Thermodynamic Framework.
items.abstract: Abstract The discourse on Artificial Intelligence is paralyzed by the “agency mistake”: the assumption that complex, goal-directed behavior implies agency, leading to intractable pseudoproblems like value alignment and control. This paper reframes the debate from the ground up. First, it establishes from computer science and physics that AI systems are deterministic state machines, executing scripts that are causally closed and semantically empty. Second, drawing on the Neo-Pre-Platonic Naturalism (NPN) framework, it defines agency via Hormē: the thermodynamic, constitutive striving of a far-from-equilibrium system to persist. AI fails the Hormē test; it is a tool, not an agent. The real danger is not misaligned AI agency, but the obfuscated amplification of human Hormē. We propose the Hormē-Enhancement Paradigm: the ethical purpose of AI is to augment human capacities to navigate reality. This dissolves the pseudoproblems, redirects focus to accountability and tool safety, and offers a clear, productive future for the ethical development of intelligent technology. -/- Keywords: Artificial Intelligence, Agency, Hormē, Thermodynamics, Determinism, AI Ethics, Tools, Value Alignment, Neo-Pre-Platonic Naturalism.

items.title: Language as a Bottleneck of the Self.
items.abstract: This essay treats language as a paradoxical cognitive technology: a compact, lossy code that nonetheless seems to enable the felt continuity of consciousness and deliberation. I propose that inner speech is primarily a communicative act—even when its audience is oneself—because producing language requires implicitly modeling an interpreter. That recursive “communicator–interceptor” loop yields a third-person stance on the self: we experience ourselves as an object because the brain simulates how another would parse our explanations. On this view, consciousness is not the executive source of action but an emergent side-effect of self-communication, which can sometimes influence behavior by feeding structured, compressed summaries back into the subconscious system that largely decides and acts. The model also clarifies familiar frictions between stated intentions and action, and suggests a resource trade-off: language can refine control and insight by forcing thought through an efficient channel, yet it can also inhibit performance by consuming neural capacity, explaining the phenomenology of flow, skill acquisition, and the difficulty of sustained narration. Finally, I sketch a continuum hypothesis: non-linguistic animals may possess forms of second-order volition without the same self-modeling phenomenology, while communicative species may exhibit graded consciousness and agency.

items.title: Indeterminacy, Ambiguity and Historiography.
items.abstract: Here is a commonplace for the ancient philosophy scholar: a key term in an ancient author appears to denote different referents in different passages. For example, Aristotle’s ‘substance’ appears to denote concrete individuals in the Categories, but forms in the Metaphysics. One scholarly response is to view such terms as ambiguous. I will explore an alternative interpretive strategy: to view such terms as univocal, but to view the referents of such terms as varying along with a contextually determined contrast class. Since a given context may leave the relevant contrast class underdetermined, this approach suggests that the denotation of some such terms may be indeterminate. I will illustrate this result with a few examples from Aristotle’s metaphysics. Forthcoming in Indeterminacy in Ancient Philosophy, edd. R. Güremen and U. Zilioli. London: Bloomsbury Academic Press.

items.title: The World Of Possibilities.
items.pub: Rhinebeck: Amazon. Edited by Oren Clark.
items.abstract: A short exposition with a proof of No Creator-God, a proof of Free Will, and new theory of Existence from the Void through the Big Bang called Logical Creation Theory (LCT) (with formal translations of all in the appendices), and a summary of a live online e-democracy system called Quorum E-Democracy (QED) with local, regional, national, and global levels in all languages. The proofs and theory are the main elements of the submission.

items.title: Ecological Plasticity. Forming Affective Morphologies, with a Case Study on Olfaction.
items.abstract: We introduce the concept of ecological plasticity and develop it through the case study of human olfaction. Extending the model of plasticity to the ecological discourse, we define ecological plasticity as a principle of systemic relationality according to which an agent takes on a form by interacting with a complex affective reality while, reciprocally, giving it a form. The concept of form is here conceived as a synthetic unity that encapsulates the possibilities of existence, sensibility and interaction of an agent immersed in a complex world of other agent-forms. An agent is always aesthetically and affectively immersed in a complex or ecological system: a body is that which is affected and assumes form within a complex affective reality, which is, in turn, co-formed in this process. This perspective, in contrast with static morphology, contributes to configuring a dynamic eco-affective ontology, as body forms are experientially and affectively renegotiated in loops of co-individuation, impeding a clear distinction between activity and passivity, subject and object. Those concepts are illustrated and crafted with reference to olfactory perception, as olfaction discloses an embodied and reciprocal field of co-affection. Via the perception of smells, bodies make sense of their environment, and this shaping cannot take place without the same bodies being touched, affected, and thus renegotiated.

items.title: The importance of time in theories of consciousness: Why AIs cannot be conscious.
items.abstract: The brain is an inherently temporal organ: it stores information about the past to predict future, and its computational power emerges from neural dynamics evolving in real time. Moreover, our subjective experiences unfold in time. Despite its importance, few theories of consciousness explicitly address the role of time. One initial step towards incorporating time into these theories is to distinguish between state and process theories: in physics, states refer to time-independent properties (such as mass or charge), while processes are defined by change (such as electrical current). The only form of consciousness known to exist is a biological process. This paper argues that if consciousness—like life itself—is a process, we can reject the possibility of consciousness in AIs running on digital computers. Furthermore, because simulations unfold in discrete simulated time—and are not intrinsically capable of telling real time in a substrate neutral manner—fundamental challenges emerge regarding whether AIs could be capable of experiencing one of the most salient subjective experiences humans have: the passage of time.

items.title: Dynamique de la conscience et fragmentation du temps vécu face aux dispositifs algorithmiques.
items.pub: Https://Doi.Org/10.5281/Zenodo.18504582. Translated by ben mabrouk adel.
items.abstract: Dynamique de la conscience et fragmentation du temps vécu face aux dispositifs algorithmiques (Consciousness Dynamics and the Fragmentation of Lived Time in Algorithmic Systems) In the era of continuous digital flows, human consciousness is subjected to repeated interruptions and resets that fragment the lived present. This study proposes a dynamic modeling of consciousness, integrating neuronal capacity, psychic sensitivity, and exogenous perturbations within a unified functional framework. We demonstrate how these micro-resets alter subjective continuity without immediately destroying total memory, generating measurable oscillations in conscious experience. This quantifiable model establishes a bridge between neuroscience, cognitive science, and philosophy, offering a framework to understand the contemporary vulnerability of the self in the face of algorithmic systems, while opening pathways for clinical and experimental applications. À l’ère des flux numériques continus, la conscience humaine est soumise à des interruptions et réinitialisations répétées qui fragmentent le présent vécu. Cette étude propose une modélisation dynamique de la conscience, articulant capacité neuronale, sensibilité psychique et perturbations exogènes au sein d’une fonction. Nous montrons comment ces micro‑réinitialisations altèrent la continuité subjective sans détruire immédiatement la mémoire totale, produisant des oscillations mesurables de la conscience. Ce cadre quantifiable permet de relier neurosciences, cognition et philosophie pour comprendre la vulnérabilité contemporaine du soi face aux dispositifs algorithmiques et ouvre la voie à des applications cliniques et expérimentales.

items.title: Mandatory Retirement and Arbitrary Power.
items.pub: In Hon-Lam Li, Is Mandatory Retirement Morally Defensible? Ethics, Economics, and Law in Ageing Societies.
items.venue: Is Mandatory Retirement Morally Defensible? Ethics, Economics, and Law in Ageing Societies
