items.abstract: Since 2022, genetically modified pig organs have been transplanted into both deceased and living human subjects, and first-in-human clinical trials began in 2025. Yet, little is known about the experience of performing such procedures. The first kidney xenotransplant studies involved human brain-dead recipients, with graft function ranging from hours to months. Interviews were conducted with one of the first surgeons with experience in performing a pig-to-human kidney xenotransplant and analysed using interpretative phenomenological analysis. Following analysis, four personal experiential themes were identified: Desiring a more equitable patient future; Being changed by bonding with the family; Crossing a boundary without feeling the difference and Everything changed when the pig kidney turned pink. As the first exploration of a surgeon’s lived experience of xenotransplantation, the study highlights how motivations, uncertainties and ethical commitments influence engagement with emerging biotechnologies. While uncertainties remain, the findings provide insight into how a surgeon interprets and navigates the conceptual and emotional terrain of crossing into first-in-human xenotransplantation.

items.title: Alienation and Political Action, Revisited.
items.abstract: In this paper, I challenge our thinking about affect, and its relationship to politics, agency, and action, through a close reading of the concept of alienation in the fiction of Harlem Renaissance thinker Nella Larsen. Larsen’s phenomenological account of the experience of alienation offers two novel perspectives on the relation between “negative” affect and politics. First, it offers a framework of non-sovereign political action which makes a rad-ical claim: politics is not the way we get free from such feelings but is, in fact, the product of their existence. Our efforts to overcome or elide painful feelings can unexpectedly pull us out into the world and drive our worldly political projects. Second, it makes a methodological case for theorizing affect from the ground up, “staying with the trouble” of our feelings rather than seeking grand interpretive theory which pathologizes, diagnoses, and seeks to cure.

items.title: Information-Centric Unification of Quantum Mechanics and Relativity - an Interpretive Framework.
items.abstract: This paper introduces NORMeOLi’s information-centric philosophy-of-science framework that unifies quantum mechanics and relativity without proposing new physical laws. By reframing reality through an on-demand conditional rendering architecture, the framework provides a single operational logic for wave-particle duality, state reduction, time dilation, light speed invariance, and mass. Within this model, quantum mechanics is explained through "use-case" rendering, where the wave function acts as a dynamic catalog of unrendered possibilities (potentia) employing wave logic for probabilistic outcomes. Special relativity emerges from a fundamental master clock (the Outside Observer’s Universal Perspective and Time, or OOUPT), where c serves as the invariant presentation rate and time dilation reflects varying frame-sampling densities. Furthermore, mass is reinterpreted as a relational coherence invariant; the rules of local observation are mathematically extrapolated outward until reaching terminal presentation boundaries where the models break down - specifically at the Planck scale (quantum granularity) and extreme cosmological scales (black hole event horizons). Maintaining consciousness as ontologically fundamental rather than emergent, NORMeOLi provides mechanistic grounding for concepts like Heisenberg’s potentia and Deutsch & Marletto’s Constructor Theory, offering a parsimonious, simulation-based contribution to philosophy of science. The framework’s significance lies in its capacity to integrate physics with metaphysical reflection, situating quantum phenomena and relativity within a broader vision of reality as a context for conscious participation and evaluative choice. The approach also resonates with, and in some cases extends, themes developed in the works of Gödel, Penrose, Elitzur, Barandes. As such, it invites further exploration of the simulation perspective as a legitimate and potentially fruitful contribution to foundational debates.

items.title: Physics of Process: Reality as Prohibition of Fixation.
items.abstract: Special and General Relativity, together with Quantum Mechanics, constitute theories that are mathematically rigorous and empirically validated. Their predictive power is unquestionable. However, their ontological interpretation — what they implicitly claim about the nature of reality itself — remains fundamentally flawed. This paper proposes a radical re-foundation of physics through Metamonism: a methodological framework grounded in a foundational axiom — the prohibition of identity (or indifference). Reality is treated not as a collection of entities but as a continuous process of actualization that intrinsically prohibits fixation. Within this framework, space, time, energy, particles, and fields are understood not as primary constituents of being but as secondary modes of a single process — the actualized Monos. We demonstrate that the invariance of the speed of light, gravitation, and the so-called quantum collapse acquire coherent explanation when reality is understood as pure becoming, while fixation appears as a cognitive artifact produced by the limitations of Logos.

items.title: A Systems Approach to Vehicles.
items.abstract: Vehicles, the carriers of representational content, are an important, if somewhat undertheorized, posit in cognitive science. In this paper we argue that generating and maintaining representational vehicles is not a trivial problem, even more clearly so when we are dealing with cognition in complex systems such as brains, or brain-body-environment aggregates. We discuss various vehicle-building operations and strategies that can be applied to complex systems (such as underutilizing and enlarging encoding space), all of them connected to what information theorists call channel coding. We then show how these strategies map onto various prominent vehicle candidates in neuroscience.

items.title: An Autonomy-Based Argument in Favour of Plant-Based Diets for Children.
items.abstract: In this paper, I argue that respecting a child’s autonomy requires feeding them a plant-based diet, at least until they develop the capacity to formulate their own judgments about the morality of animal consumption. Drawing on the independence view of autonomy, I begin with the premise that a child’s autonomy is violated when their parents enrol them into particular moral, religious, or philosophical doctrines before they are capable of independently examining those doctrines. I then argue that feeding children animal products constitutes such a violation, as it presupposes a contested view about the morality of animal consumption and involves forcing children to participate in a practice that is based on that view.

items.title: AI preference prediction and policy making.
items.abstract: Democratic decision-making is difficult. Representatives often fail to represent the preferences of their constituents, and directly consulting members of the public can be costly. Inspired by these difficulties, several scholars have discussed the use of artificial intelligence (AI) models to support democratic decision-making. One such particular application is the use of AI to represent public policy preferences by predicting them. In this paper, we perform an analysis on the different ways AI models can be used to represent public policy preferences. We make distinctions between using AI as epistemic tools and for procedure; group and individual predictions; and predictions about preferences and inferences about values. We also describe how AI models can help policymakers screen policies for potential worries and objections, double-check any beliefs they have about the acceptability of their policies, and justify policy proposals. We also consider a number of worries about the use of AI in policymaking. We argue that these worries, while legitimate, can be mitigated or avoided in the way we have proposed the use of AI.

items.title: From Theory to Implementation: CCF Applied Philosophy and the Sal-Meter Proof of Concept.
items.abstract: This document presents the applied philosophical and conceptual bridge between the Consciousness Civilization Framework (CCF) and its first operational measurement prototype, the Sal-Meter. -/- It explains how a consciousness-centered civilizational theory can be translated into a measurable architecture through CAIS (Consciousness–Aptamer Interface System)–compatible design, non-coercive state-based measurement logic, and proof-of-concept implementation principles. -/- Rather than proposing a medical, diagnostic, or predictive system, the work articulates why consciousness measurement must be governed before it is optimized, and how philosophical constraints map directly onto engineering boundaries such as openness, non-monopolization, and post-experience state observation. -/- The document serves as an applied philosophy reference, a conceptual technical proof-of-concept, and a canonical connector within the CCF document constellation, linking foundational theory to downstream technical and governance standards without redefining any canonical specifications.

items.title: Why Contemporary AI Is Not Sentient: A structural argument from constraint, normativity, and first-person contact.
items.abstract: AI can now speak as if it has an inner life. It can report feelings, intentions, and self-understanding with impressive coherence. This paper argues that such fluency is not evidence of sentience. The reason is structural: sentience is not a style of language but a condition of contact. A sentient system is bound by an interior “hard floor” where reality is met as non-optional constraint; it is organized by norms that matter from within; and it encounters the world with consequence in a first-person field. Contemporary AI lacks these conditions. It can imitate the forms of experience without bearing the costs that make experience real. The paper closes by proposing an epistemic posture suited to the AI era: treat AI outputs as candidates for truth that require audit under contact, rather than as testimony from a subject.

items.title: Revisiting computer authorship: a longitudinal perspective.
items.abstract: Despite the proliferation of computer-generated texts, the concept of AI authorship remains ambiguous. This paper investigates evolving public perceptions of authorship pertaining to computer-generated texts through review of an international survey distributed in 2024/2025. Comparing results of this survey to those from the same survey distributed in 2017/2018, this paper offers what we believe to be the only longitudinal empirical consideration of AI authorship pre- and post-LLM boom. Even with dramatic technological advancements in natural language generation, this study suggests that societal understandings of authorship have only seen minor change since the survey’s first distribution. Participants continue to hold ambivalent opinions of AI authorship, perhaps partly due to the cultural and historical weight of the term ‘authorship’ itself. This ambivalence raises broader questions about the persistent usage of ‘authorship’ as a default term for describing computational text production. Through an interdisciplinary analysis represented by humanities and computational researchers, merging both quantitative and qualitative data, this paper interrogates whether the concept of authorship remains viable in discussions of computer-generated texts via feedback from survey participants.

items.title: When AI meets AI: analyzing AI bills using AI.
items.abstract: With the rapid advancement of Artificial Intelligence (AI) technology and its pervasive integration into society, governments worldwide have introduced a range of AI-related policies. In the United States, the use of AI technology has surged significantly since 2021, driven by the emergence of generative AI and its transformative potential. In response, the U.S. Congress has proposed numerous AI-related bills, reflecting growing legislative engagement with AI governance. This study examines 204 AI-related bills introduced during the 117th and 118th Congresses (2021–2024) through computational text analysis, employing topic modeling to identify recurring legislative themes and sentiment analysis to assess congressional attitudes toward AI policies. The findings reveal distinct variations in legislative focus and tone across chambers and political parties, offering a nuanced understanding of how AI-related issues are framed within U.S. policymaking. In addition, the results highlight how AI is connected to broader opportunities and concerns, including national security, technological innovation, and public service delivery. By applying machine learning techniques to legislative texts, this research provides a systematic and scalable approach to understanding AI policymaking. The study contributes to broader discussions on the partisan and institutional dynamics shaping AI legislation in the United States, offering insights into how emerging technologies are shaped by legislative priorities, regulatory attitudes, and broader political contexts.

items.title: Why Theaetetus Wonders: The Protagorean and Mathematical Background to Theaetetus 155c8-d5.
items.abstract: Many commentators struggle to explain why thauma is a fitting response to the dice and height comparisons in Plato’s Theaetetus. I argue that Socrates employs these comparisons to test the cogency of Protagoreanism and remind Theaetetus of his mathematical lesson with Theodorus. In this way I align Theaetetus’ wonder with the various senses in which Plato typically employs thaumazein and its cognates. Theaetetus is surprised that the comparisons validate Protagoreanism; he desires to know whether this implausible metaphysics can be squared with more intuitive principles; and he is ultimately led to marvel at the irrational length, an extraordinary measure.

items.title: The Summoning of Soul: To Reclaim Uncertain Freedom.
items.abstract: This is an article meant to vanish upon reading. To engage with it may leave you intellectually dizzy and unsettled, yet to pass it by might mean forgoing a crucial moment to awaken into your own sovereign thinking. It begins with the fundamental paradox of cognition, weaving through ethics, political philosophy, aesthetics, philosophy of language and mind, philosophy of science, and even the metaphysics of divination—all threaded by a single, unifying ontological-epistemological concept: being as verb and the relativity of description. From philosophy to commerce, from Socrates to まつした こうのすけ, from scientific revolution to fortune-telling, it appears to speak of everything, yet in the end articulates nothing definitive. It is, instead, a pure summons to spiritual independence. Therefore, its true reader is not the academic specialist, but every existing individual. As for why it was written, even the author does not know—yet written it was. （These articles are just records of places I’ve passed by. Don’t take them too seriously, my friend — they may be full of mistakes. Trust yourself. If you want to find my recent location, please check the pinned post or updates on my homepage.）.

items.title: What? Consciousness, the Self, and the Question of Being.
items.pub: London: Liminal Way Scriptorium. Edited by James Cullinane.
items.venue: Liminal Way Scriptorium. Edited by James Cullinane
items.abstract: What? is a philosophical inquiry into the nature of consciousness, selfhood, and existence, approached through a synthesis of analytic philosophy, phenomenology, cognitive science, and speculative thought. Rather than advancing a single doctrinal theory, the work examines the question “What am I?” as an unresolved and structurally open problem, one that resists reduction to biological, computational, or metaphysical accounts alone. Across a sequence of conceptual investigations, the book explores issues including personal identity over time, the relationship between mind and body, the emergence of moral experience, the role of language in shaping thought, the limits of introspection, and the implications of artificial intelligence for theories of awareness. Classical problems such as the observer’s paradox, the continuity of self, and the nature of subjective experience are revisited alongside contemporary questions concerning machine consciousness, distributed cognition, and systems theory. The work adopts a cumulative structure in which thought experiments, metaphors, and interdisciplinary perspectives are used not to resolve philosophical uncertainty but to clarify its contours. Consciousness is treated as a process rather than an object, and the self as a dynamic pattern rather than a fixed entity. In doing so, What? argues that uncertainty is not a failure of inquiry but a fundamental feature of any honest engagement with the question of being.

items.title: Computational Analysis for Philosophical Education: A Case Study in AI Ethics.
items.abstract: This paper explores what computational methodologies can tell us about philosophical education, particularly in the context of artificial intelligence (AI) ethics. Taking the readings on our AI ethics and responsible AI syllabi as a corpus of AI ethics literature, we conduct an analysis of the content of these courses through a variety of methods: word frequency analysis, term frequency–inverse document frequency (TF–IDF) scoring, document vectorization via SciBERT, clustering via k-means, and topic modelling using latent Dirichlet allocation (LDA). We reflect on the findings of these analyses, and more broadly on what computational approaches can offer to the practice of philosophical education. Finally, we compare our approach to previous computational approaches in philosophy, and more broadly in the digital humanities. This project offers a proof of concept for how contemporary natural-language processing techniques can be used to support philosophical pedagogy: not only to reflect critically on what we teach, but to discover new materials, explore conceptual gaps, and make our courses more accessible to students from a range of disciplinary backgrounds.

items.title: Fractals, Synchronicity, and the Metalogic of a Generative Reality.
items.abstract: This essay presents a unified theory of reality as a generative, fractal process. It synthesizes four conceptual pillars—fractals, synchronicity, simulation, and metalogic—into a cohesive model where phenomena emerge through a recursive cosmic double-pass: an encoding-decoding mechanism operating on a primordial information substrate. This process generates “fractal twins”: structurally isomorphic events separated by space, time, or modality. Synchronicity is the conscious recognition of these twins, serving as a pattern-readout of the underlying generative grammar. Metalogical events, such as the UFO phenomena documented by Jacques Vallée, are treated not as supernatural interventions but as anomalous artifacts that expose the model’s operational layer. Contemporary AI systems provide a potent technical analogue, demonstrating how compression-decompression architectures can produce isomorphic outputs, artifacts, and confident hallucinations. The pervasive “simulation feeling” arises not from external imposition but from the direct perception of recursive rendering in action. The model is grounded in a cosmological framework of informational decompression (Carboni 2026), wherein cosmic expansion is driven by the lossy unpacking of information from a maximally compressed singularity. The mathematical formulas discovered by science are not timeless Platonic forms, but human approximations of this compressed, unified informational structure. This substrate defines a “possibility-space”—the fundamental rules and constraints for what can manifest. Decompression is the playing-out of this constrained game, a collaborative unfolding where information and energy interact to generate physical structure, from galactic forms to biological life. Consciousness emerges not as an epiphenomenon, but as the phenomenological appearance of information when decompressed into living, self-observing systems. The brain is neither primary producer nor passive container, but an integral component of the cosmic unpacking process itself.

items.title: Intuizioni morali. La giustificazione come problema.
items.abstract: Cosa succede quando un’azione ci sembra giusta o sbagliata? Possiamo fidarci di questa impressione e confermarla nei giudizi e nel comportamento? Il libro cerca di rispondere a queste domande partendo da un’analisi del fenomeno in questione, che prende il nome di intuizione morale. L’autrice presenta una teoria dell’intuizione morale come una «presentazione» o «impressione» relativa a oggetti o situazioni moralmente rilevanti e ne indaga la relazione con le intuizioni non morali, le credenze e le emozioni. Vengono poi esaminate obiezioni classiche e recenti all’appello alle intuizioni in etica, che contestano in particolare la pretesa di oggettività in quest’ambito e il realismo morale. La tesi difesa è che le intuizioni morali possono giustificare giudizi e atteggiamenti e che i loro limiti, messi in luce da studi empirici riguardanti le influenze irrilevanti sulle valutazioni morali, possono essere superati con lo sviluppo e l’esercizio di virtù epistemiche.

items.title: Four Views of the First-Person.
items.abstract: I argue that all experiences are my experiences.

items.title: When algorithms sell: rethinking consumer behavior in the AI-enhanced marketplace.
Beyond the attention economy, towards an ecology of attending. A manifesto.
items.abstract: We endorse policymakers’ efforts to address the negative consequences of the attention economy’s technology but add that these approaches are often limited in their criticism of the systemic context of human attention. Starting from Buddhist philosophy, we advocate a broader approach: an ‘ecology of attending’ that centers on conceptualizing, designing, and using attention (1) in an embedded way and (2) focused on the alleviating of suffering. With ‘embedded’ we mean that attention is not a neutral, isolated mechanism but a meaning-engendering part of an ‘ecology’ of bodily, sociotechnical and moral frameworks. With ‘focused on the alleviation of suffering’ we mean that we explicitly move away from the (often implicit) conception of attention as a tool for gratifying desires. We analyze existing inquiries in these directions and urge them to be intensified and integrated. As to the design and function of our technological environment, we propose three questions for further research: How can technology help to acknowledge us as ‘ecological’ beings, rather than as self-sufficient individuals? How can technology help to raise awareness of our moral framework? And how can technology increase the conditions for ‘attending’ to the alleviation of suffering, by substituting our covert self-driven moral framework with an ecologically attending one? We believe in the urgency of transforming the inhumane attention economy sociotechnical system into a humane ecology of attending, and in our ability to contribute to it.

items.title: Причинная неадекватность неодарвинизма: от информационного вызова к семиотическим, кибернетическим и телеологическим барьерам.
items.abstract: Данная работа представляет собой Главу 3 монографии «Кризис классической диалектики как основание для смены научной парадигмы» и завершает её Часть I («Диагностика кризиса: пределы классической парадигмы»). В рамках общего анализа трёх классических объяснительных схем (диалектика, физикалистский редукционизм, неодарвинизм) глава фокусируется на критике причинной достаточности неодарвинизма. Проводится тезис о том, что механизмы случайных мутаций и естественного отбора принципиально неадекватны для объяснения происхождения фундаментальных атрибутов жизни, упираясь в три концептуальных барьера: 1) Семиотический (проблема абиогенного скачка от химии к символическому коду); 2) Кибернетический (проблема возникновения нередуцируемо сложных систем управления); 3) Телеологический (проблема источника имманентной способности систем к эволюции — «эволюционируемости»). На основе операционализации концепций специфицированной сложной информации (CSI) и нередуцируемой сложности демонстрируется статистическая и причинная ограниченность неодарвиновской парадигмы. Делается вывод о необходимости выхода за её рамки и рассмотрения телеологически обогащённых исследовательских программ как шага к построению полной причинной теории биогенеза. Таким образом, глава вносит вклад в общую цель монографии — диагностику кризиса классических парадигм объяснения развития. -/- .

items.title: Truth Is Acognative.
items.abstract: Truth is typically framed as a cognitive property: something grasped in propositions, evaluated by minds, or justified through reasoning. This paper argues that truth is more basic than cognition. Acognitive biological systems—such as sperm cells navigating chemotactic gradients—succeed or fail according to objective environmental structures that distinguish correct from incorrect movement without requiring beliefs or concepts. These cases show that truth functions as a structural constraint embedded in the world, not as a product of mental activity. Cognition refines access to these constraints but does not generate them. Reframing truth as acognitive restores its fundamental role: marking alignment or misalignment with the way the world is.

items.title: DIÁKRISIS — A Contrastive Braking Corpus for AI.
items.abstract: DIÁKRISIS — A Contrastive Braking Corpus for AI is a final, closed, non-authoritative interpretive reference work presenting a contrastive corpus (BAD / MIMICRY / GOOD) designed to increase interpretive braking—hesitation, scrutiny, consistency pressure, and reversibility—in AI-related decision contexts. -/- The work is non-operational and non-binding. It provides no enforcement, certification, governance, monitoring, or guarantees, and makes no claims of prevention or control over AI systems. -/- DIÁKRISIS is intentionally closed and read-only. No extensions, amendments, successor doctrines, or compliance claims are permitted under the DIÁKRISIS name. Quotation, critique, and descriptive discussion are permitted.

items.title: Perceptual abstraction.
items.abstract: Perception puts us in touch with highly determinate properties of objects, such as fine‐grained color shades and detailed surface shapes. However, most of our immediate perceptual judgments concern more abstract properties, such as the property of being a dog, or of being red simpliciter. So, how does perception attune us to abstract properties despite its evident determinacy? This paper argues that perception can be sensitive to abstract properties in multiple, fundamentally different ways. We articulate a distinction between implicit and explicit perceptual abstraction and explore its ramifications for debates about the role of concepts in perception, the richness of perceptual content, and rationalist versus empiricist views of our innate representational repertoire. We also propose an empirical test for differentiating implicit from explicit perceptual abstraction. Finally, we outline a version of Conceptualism built on the implicit/explicit distinction, on which explicit perceptual abstraction involves the use of concepts, while implicit abstraction can occur non‐conceptually. We argue that this form of Conceptualism is both empirically viable and unscathed by prominent Non‐Conceptualist arguments.

items.title: Epistemic Authority: What Ontology Leaves Unresolved.
items.abstract: Even when consciousness-first metaphysics is accepted at the level of ontology, physicalist epistemic privilege does not automatically dissolve. This essay examines the structural problem that emerges: physicalist assumptions about what counts as legitimate knowledge can survive the very inversion that was supposed to displace them. Earlier work in this project exposes physicalism as an unjustified default at the level of ontology. But a subtler asymmetry persists at the level of epistemology — in which forms of consciousness states are permitted to “know,” where first-person access sits in the hierarchy of explanation, and whether contemplative evidence carries weight or merely illustration. The residue is specific: meta-consciousness is still assumed to require neural substrate; third-person description retains authority over first-person experience even when the subject matter is experience. This essay diagnoses that persistence and argues that ontological inversion without epistemic revision is incomplete.

items.title: Anomalous Phenomena and Consciousness: A Diagnostic Stress Test of Explanatory Frameworks.
items.abstract: Contested phenomena — from psychedelics to mediumship — have resisted clean integration into physicalist frameworks for decades. The resistance is not coincidental; it is diagnostic. This essay tests both physicalism and analytic idealism against ten such phenomena, organized by evidential maturity (Tiers 1–3) and argumentative role (Groups A–C). The central conceptual move is the distinction between mechanistic explanation — a constrained causal pathway specifying why this experience, this content, this timing — and dismissive labeling — “hallucination,” “coincidence,” “noise” — that classifies a phenomenon as unreal without explaining it. Where physicalism has genuine mechanisms, the essay credits them; where it relies on labels masquerading as explanations, the essay names what the labels do not do. The constraint theory enabled by analytic idealism — that the brain shapes consciousness rather than producing it — makes falsifiable predictions, and the essay states what would break the model. Group C phenomena (psi, mediumship, reincarnation) are the test case for whether the project’s central diagnosis — that asymmetric restraint produces evidential gaps which are then cited as evidence of unreality — applies where prejudice is strongest. The argument does not establish idealism; it establishes that physicalism’s apparent explanatory coverage often conceals refusal to explain.
