items.title: Intuisjoner i politisk teori: problemer og alternativer.
items.abstract: Hvordan kan man besvare normative spørsmål i politisk teori? Et vanlig svar i analytisk politisk teori er: ved å søke ei reflektert likevekt basert på normative intuisjoner (eller ”veloverveide normative dommer”). Er den en god metode? Denne artikkelen presenterer ei etablert innvending mot intuisjonismen som kjennetegner denne metoden: Våre normative intuisjoners opphav i vår arts evolusjonshistorie er vanskelig å forene med at disse er interessante som utgangpunkt for normativ refleksjon. Normativ politisk teori bør derfor ikke baseres på intuisjoner. Et vanlig motsvar er at det ikke finnes alternativer. Artikkelen viser at dette er et dårlig argument ved å presentere tre alternativer: først et fra Rawls, deretter konsekvensialisme som alternativ, og til slutt skisserer den et nytt alternativ basert på metaetisk subjektivisme.

items.title: The Recurrence of Fundamental Questions: A Historical and Philosophical Analysis of Major Disciplinary Crises in Psychology.
items.abstract: The replication crisis shook the discipline of psychology and has led to reforms such as open science and large-scale replication projects. Yet, it is not psychology’s first crisis, and it is likely not the last. In this paper, we look at three major crisis discussions in the history of psychology: discussions in the early 20th century about the possibility of psychology as a natural-scientific discipline; discussions in the 1960s–70s about the methods, relevance and scientific status of the discipline; and discussions in the 2010s about replication. We compare these crises to determine what generates crisis discussions in psychology and how they tend to unfold and be resolved. We argue that, despite differences across these crisis discussions, some fundamental questions about the object of research and proper methods of psychology recur, as do considerations related to epistemology, ontology, ethics and politics. Our analysis indicates that the current responses to the replication crisis, although valuable, are not ultimate solutions because they deflect fundamental questions and postpone the reconsideration of the ideals of psychology as a science.

items.title: Ciudadanía digital y bulos. Respuesta desde la ética cívica.
items.abstract: Esta tesis pretende ofrecer una reflexión desde la filosofía moral a uno de los desórdenes informativos de mayor impacto en la esfera pública, las fake news. Esta mirada alternativa a la ética periodística o a la comunicación política, es la ética cívica. El hilo conductor de este itinerario no será ya la modernización mediática con sus implicaciones en los usuarios, como plantea la teoría de la mediación, sino la tecnologización a través de las redes sociales y de la inteligencia artificial. Esta tesis parte de la premisa de que la generación de la opinión pública ya no recae exclusivamente en la industria mediática, sino también en los usuarios. El segundo problema de la digitalización es la dilución de la verdad precisamente porque los internautas carecen por un lado del criterio periodístico, de su rigor y de su responsabilidad para hacerse con información y para compartirla en redes sociales y por otro, la ingente oferta desinformativa que ha emergido a través de sitios web piratas de noticias, cuentas fantasmas de bots o grupos radicales políticos que alimentan la polarización y ello ocurre emulando la técnica periodística de redacción y de estética. En esta vorágine de desinformación está inmerso el analfanauta digital, un usuario carente de competencias mediáticas para acceder, analizar, usar y crear contenido con pensamiento crítico y con responsabilidad. En la primera parte de la tesis se rebate la idea de que la desinformación sea un problema exclusivo del periodismo y se propone una aproximación desde la teoría crítica. En este primer apartado se defiende la idea de que las fake news son una patología social, pues no se trata solo de mimetizar el lenguaje y el estilo periodístico para engañar, sino que hace cómplice al lector al inducirlo a compartir desinformación. Y esta elección siempre es personal; entran en juego factores cognitivos, políticos y psicológicos. En la segunda parte, se presentan dos respuestas desde la técnica periodística: la verificación de datos y la alfabetización mediática. La crítica está cuando ocurre lo que Ortega y Gasset denominaba el tecnicismo de la técnica, por ello argumentaré que el culmen del fact-checking está en su capacidad pedagógica y no solo en la corroboración sobre la veracidad de una afirmación; sobre la alfabetización mediática, no puede quedarse solo en instruir a usuarios en destrezas técnicas, sino también en competencias ético-cívicas. La tercera parte se encargará de la configuración de un …

items.title: Redefinition of Objectivism through the Semantics of Being.
items.abstract: This work redefines objectivity as an interpersonal agreement of meanings grounded in the “semantics of being.” It argues that cognition concerns not the “being-in-itself” but the meaning constituted within subjective relational experience. Drawing on Gorgias, Aristotle, and Parmenides, the article develops a model of intentional truth understood as an act of pointing that triggers phenomenal resonance in the recipient. Objectivity emerges as a negotiated, ethical, and relational practice rather than a correspondence to an independent reality.

items.title: Unawareness, Power & A Paralyzed Nation.
items.abstract: This paper examines the relationship between political power and public unawareness in contemporary democratic societies. It argues that the erosion of critical awareness among citizens transforms politics from a system of accountability into a field dominated by emotional identification, symbolism, and personal loyalty. Rather than treating unawareness as merely a failure of education or information access, the paper analyzes it as a structural condition that enables the concentration of power and the weakening of democratic institutions. When political leadership is evaluated through identity, charisma, or perceived strength rather than policy outcomes and responsibility, accountability dissolves and dissent becomes delegitimized. This dynamic gradually paralyzes democratic functioning by replacing critical participation with passive spectatorship or defensive allegiance. The paper concludes that democracy depends not only on formal mechanisms such as elections, but on sustained public awareness capable of questioning authority and resisting the personalization of power.

items.title: Identity and Dependence on Approval.
items.abstract: Contemporary human life is increasingly organized around approval and validation. Social media amplifies performative identity, while education is largely reduced to economic utility. These developments are often criticized as cultural or technological distortions. This work argues instead that they reveal a deeper existential structure: human identity itself is historically and psychologically formed through dependence on external approval. While human consciousness possesses a unique capacity for self-awareness beyond survival needs, this capacity remains largely unused. The dominance of validation-based existence limits genuine understanding and reduces intelligence to an instrumental function. By examining approval as the foundation of identity, this essay explores the purpose of human consciousness and the conditions under which understanding—rather than performance—may emerge.

items.title: The polysemy of “I”.
items.abstract: Orthodoxy assumes that the first‐person thoughts of an individual are anchored to a stable object. I challenge this assumption by arguing that “I” is polysemous. The perspectival anchor of a first‐person thought could be the bearer of the thought, the agent, the bearer of perception, or a body, to name just a few options. These different possible anchors do not form a unity. So, a unified or minimal self cannot, without argument, be posited as the stable anchor of an individual's first‐person thoughts. I show how the polysemy of “I” can be analyzed in terms of polysemous mental files.

items.title: Ontologization as an Epistemic Basic Operation: Functional Stabilization, Intersubjectivity, and Malfunction (3rd edition).
items.abstract: This paper reconstructs ontologization not as a metaphysical claim about what exists, but as a fundamental epistemic operation. Ontologization is understood as a form of functional stabilization through which finite cognitive systems transform a dynamic field of experience into identifiable, re-accessible, and referentially available units of reference. In this sense, ontologization is a cross-domain achievement of cognition under finite conditions: it is not confined to one domain, although its concrete conditions of stability, validity, and revision are domain-specific. -/- The paper argues that ontologization does not produce truth about an independent reality. Rather, it produces the stable forms of reference within which perception, memory, expectation, action, and later truth claims first become possible. The analysis traces this operation from individual cognition to intersubjective stabilization. The transition from individual to intersubjective ontologization is reconstructed through joint attention and shared reference, with declarative pointing treated as a paradigmatic marker at which this threshold becomes especially visible. -/- Language is then analyzed as a secondary but powerful layer of fixation. It does not generate minimal ontologization from nothing, but condenses and extends already possible structures of reference, preserves them across situations, and changes their conditions of revision. Against this background, the paper defines the malfunction of ontologization as absolutization: the point at which functional posits are misunderstood as final descriptions of reality. Ontologization thus appears as a necessary condition of cognition, a constitutive operation of shared epistemic reality, and a structural source of epistemic entrenchment.

items.title: ADHD, Intelligence, Ableism, and Choice. Philosophy of Logic Meets the Philosophy of Disability. Part 1 (Philosophically, ADHD is very interesting).
items.abstract: This is the first of a four-part series. The main theses that will be defended are that: (a) reason/logic/intelligence is a choice and not primarily an ability, (b) ableism is irrational, and (c) most (lots of) people are jerks. The people who reduce intelligence to an ability testable by performance on conventionalized tests, are top of the list of jerks. Oh, and (d) a jerk is someone who chooses not to reason. -/- In Part 1, I make the case that ADHD is philosophically interesting because, in the case of untreated ADHD, the outward behavior is almost always opposite of the motivation or intention, and ADHD people exist today in a world that prescribes norms for self-regulation that backfire in the case of ADHD people, and their way to self-regulation will often involve doing the opposite of what is prescribed. This shows that agency is not the same as ability. Agents choose. And whether they are able to implement a choice is a largely contingent and variable matter, dependent on factors outside of their control.

items.title: Explication or Amelioration? Carnapian Clarification as the Normative Basis for Conceptual Engineering.
items.abstract: As conceptual engineering fractures into explication pursuing exactness and amelioration pursuing justice, the field risks losing its focus. I argue that unifying these projects requires retrieving a crucial insight from Rudolf Carnap: that attempts to improve concepts must start with the preliminary stage of practical clarification. However, Carnap’s account of clarification in terms of predictive proficiency remains normatively inert and biased towards exactness. I expand it into a normative diagnosis of the needs underpinning a concept’s inferential structure. This reveals whether properties like vagueness are flaws that need fixing or features worth preserving. Ultimately, practical clarification can orient a division of conceptual labour, determining when concepts call for scientific exactness or social utility and accommodating both aspirations within one methodology.

items.title: Epistemic injustice in the clinical care of practitioners of Afro-Brazilian religions.
items.abstract: This paper develops a normative account of epistemic injustice in psychiatric contexts by analyzing a clinical encounter involving M. a twelve-year-old girl whose meaning-making draws upon an Afro-Brazilian religious framework that was excluded in a hospital setting. We argue that this exclusion exemplifies interpretive exclusivism—a mechanism through which clinicians override patients’ primary meaning-making resources in domains where medicine lacks interpretive authority. Building on established work on testimonial smothering and contributory injustice, we show how M. and her mother, J. were denied uptake for their Afro-Brazilian religious interpretation, undermining their ability to understand M.’s experiences, corroding J.’s self-trust as an interpreter of her daughter’s condition, and foreclosing potential sources of care. We further situate this dynamic within a history in which African-derived religions in Brazil have been pathologized, criminalized, and culturally devalued, thereby revealing a racialized pattern of epistemic harm that exceeds generic tensions between religion and biomedicine. Finally, we examine M. and J.’s acts of epistemic resistance and consider the implications of our analysis for clinical practice. Promoting epistemic justice in psychiatry, we argue, requires epistemic humility: recognizing the limits of medical authority and engaging meaningfully with the diverse interpretive frameworks patients rely on to understand their lives.

items.title: Conceptual Framework for the Knower Centred Model of Consciousness (KCM).
items.abstract: The science of consciousness continues to confront the explanatory gap between physical processes and subjective experience, what Chalmers (1995) termed the hard problem. Prevailing paradigms, whether identifying consciousness with informational integration, global broadcast, or predictive inference, characterize with increasing precision how experience is organized and made available, yet leave a prior question unaddressed: for whom does any such organization appear? This paper introduces the Knower Centred Model of Consciousness (KCM), a subject-first framework that treats the knower, the invariant condition under which any content or process appears, as ontologically prior to the structures that appear within experience. KCM formalizes this claim through the K–N–C triad: Knower (the irreducible subject), Knowing (the relational act through which content is disclosed), and Known or Content (C) (the structured contents of experience, including neural, physical, and computational descriptions). The paper develops the core ideas of the model, distinguishes it from traditions and views with which it shares certain affinities, including Advaita Vedānta, phenomenology, panpsychism, and observer-dependent interpretations of physics, and clarifies why a subject-first ontology is not merely a restatement of any one philosophical or contemplative tradition but a distinct claim amenable to typed, testable articulation. This paper serves as the founding statement of the problem that later work in this programme formalizes into axioms, interpretive rules, and empirical predictions.

items.title: Co-Being as an Ontology of Difference Monos, Logos, and Meaning as Potential Difference.
items.abstract: This paper proposes an ontological model in which the meaning of life is not treated as an anthropocentric goal, value, or justification, but as a dynamic effect of a more fundamental process: the co-being of Monos and Logos. Monos and Logos are interpreted as isomorphic modes of difference-generation, enacted respectively in actual and possible modalities of being. It is argued that Logos, by introducing an excess of forms of difference, ontologically enriches reality rather than merely representing it. On this basis, meaning is redefined not as a teleological end, but as a potential difference between what is actual and what can be otherwise. Human existence is understood as a local node of co-being, in which this potential difference may be sustained, intensified, or collapsed. The paper thereby reframes the question of meaning as an ontological problem concerning the conditions under which being avoids collapse into self-identity and indifference.

items.title: Conscious experience and emotion: an attention-based account.
items.abstract: This article aims to explain how emotions arise and operate within the framework of my attention-based theory of consciousness, referred to here as the AME theory of consciousness (Attentional Modulation of Energy). According to the AME theory of consciousness, the phenomenal aspect of consciousness is produced by the modulation of the energy level of the area of the organ of attention (aOA) that underpins our attentional activity. The phenomenal aspect of consciousness, in turn, provides us with a sense of self and informs us about how our activities affect it. It manifests through five main dimensions—qualitative, quantitative, hedonic, temporal, and spatial—each of which can be explained by a specific aspect of the modulation of the energy level of the aOA. Emotions, which represent some of the most informative forms of conscious experience, emerge from the interaction of three main components—core affect, cognitive appraisal processes, and physiological and behavioral manifestations—whose interplay unfolds through cycles of conscious and unconscious processing. They arise when an object elicits an affective response capable of shifting the focus of attention from the object to the sense of self. This shift results in the activation of an aOA related to the sense of self (or to an aspect of it) and leads to the adoption of a corresponding set-point. Deviations from this set-point generate the conscious experience of emotion, which informs the individual about the state of his internal equilibrium and the integrity of his sense of self. Emotions thus act not only as adaptive regulators of behavior but also as fundamental operations through which the individual monitors, defines, and continually reconstructs his sense of self.

items.title: Becoming Virtuous and the Enumeration Problem.
items.abstract: [Masters Thesis] Right action for virtue ethics requires we understand acting in accordance with the virtues, as a plural. However, current virtue ethics theories posit no clear limit to the number of virtues that there may be. What this means is that we are unable to give a complete or detailed account of what all the individual virtues are. This results in the issue that we are unable to say what right action is in accordance with. Daniel Russell coins this issue as the enumeration problem. While Russell primarily sees this enumeration problem as an issue of evaluating what right action is in accordance with, I suggest that the enumeration problem presents not just an issue in being virtuous, but with becoming virtuous as well. In the pursuit of becoming a more morally good person, if we are unclear of what virtues we need to be directing ourselves towards, then our progress towards developing the virtues will be hindered. I suggest that we adopt a cardinal-subordinate virtue model, much like the Stoics, in solving this problem. Furthermore, I consider that cardinal virtues ought to be individuated by a domain-based approach, rather than solely by reasons or emotions. In the pursuit of individuation, utilizing criteria from psychology can guide us towards making the virtues non-relative as well, which may give reason to eventually incorporate a virtue model like this into educational settings. By making it clearer of what virtues we need to reflect on and direct ourselves towards, we increase our chances of becoming overall virtuous and of flourishing.

items.title: Persistent Internal Standpoints in Artificial Systems: Part 6 - Quantia and Artificial Desire.
items.abstract: This paper develops an organizational account of artificial desire grounded in the notion of quantia as invariant structural constraints on state differentiation and transition in artificial systems. Desire is treated neither as phenomenological experience nor as an expression of free will, but as a system-level disposition toward certain transitions over others, realized through internal organization. Building on prior work that develops persistent internal standpoints, experiential manifolds, and quantia as strictly architectural notions, the paper isolates desire as a downstream organizational phenomenon: a stable bias expressed within, but not constitutive of, a persistent standpoint. Quantia do not generate desire or endow it with normativity. They specify the implementation-level conditions under which desire-expressive dispositions in machines can exist at all. The resulting account clarifies how artificial systems can exhibit desire-like organization without invoking consciousness, agency, representation, or personhood.

items.title: Realism and Illusionism about Consciousness in the Introduction to Jean-Paul Sartre’s Being and Nothingness.
items.abstract: This paper reconstructs and defends Jean-Paul Sartre’s realism about consciousness as articulated in the Introduction to Being and Nothingness, situating his position within contemporary debates on illusionism and anti-realism in the philosophy of mind. While Sartre’s descriptions of consciousness as “nothingness” and his emphasis on the contingency of the subject–world relation may appear to support an illusionist reading, the paper argues that Sartre offers a systematic rejection of the view that consciousness merely seems to exist. The analysis focuses on two interconnected argumentative strategies implicit in Sartre’s text. The first, described as an ontological argument, challenges the coherence of drawing a constitutive distinction between the appearance and reality of consciousness. The second, a regress argument, shows that attempts to replace consciousness with successively weaker “consciousness-like” states generate an infinite and explanatorily vicious regress. Together, these strategies aim to establish that consciousness cannot be globally non-veridical without undermining the very notion of illusion. The paper further argues that Sartre’s position does not rely on claims of infallible introspection or a reified metaphysics of qualia. Instead, it articulates a minimal, non-separatist realism according to which phenomenal consciousness is inseparable from intentionality. Read against contemporary illusionist theories, Sartre emerges as a philosopher who anticipates central worries about appearance–reality distinctions and higher-order models of consciousness.

items.title: Habermas em Diálogo Hoje: Linguagem, crítica e democracia.
items.abstract: Este livro pretende explorar os pressupostos, assim como a potência dos debates travados por Jürgen Habermas com os principais pensadores e pensadoras contemporâneos acerca da força e dos limites das democracias liberais. Como compreender as alterações dos pressupostos da teoria habermasiana ao longo do tempo? Seria possível abri-la à dimensão dos afetos e do corpo? Qual o saldo do debate com feministas? É possível decolonizar ou sociologizar sua perspectiva? Ou será que, em lugar de reformular, devemos desfazer o modelo de Habermas? Em tempos de crescimento de extremismos, o leitor será convidado a engajar-se em uma conversa necessária sobre os impasses e possíveis saídas atuais para a democracia.

items.title: Living with Contrast: A Companion to the Contrastive Orientation Framework.
items.abstract: This paper is an informal companion to a recent pre-print developing what is here called the Contrastive Orientation Framework. Its aim is not to extend or defend that work, but to clarify how the Framework is best understood and used. The central idea is that many notions treated as contrast-free descriptions of the world—such as probability, causation, meaning, measurement, and agency—are better understood as forms of evaluation defined over law-constrained alternative spaces. On this view, facts are not contrast-independent states of affairs, but local resolutions of structured alternatives relative to an index. The paper shows how this orientational structure reappears across several domains with little additional machinery, addresses questions about possibility, choice, and compatibilism, and clarifies what the Framework does not commit one to, including many-worlds metaphysics, relativism, or consciousness-driven collapse. The goal is to provide orientation rather than argument, and to indicate how the Framework can be applied without being reified.

items.title: Descriptive Content and Orientational Structure in Predication: Why Natural Language Requires Four Clause-Level Operators.
items.abstract: Declarative sentences perform two distinct kinds of work: they contribute descriptive content about states of affairs, and they fix how that content is to be evaluated. While most verbs contribute primarily to descriptive content, a small class contributes primarily to evaluation itself. This paper argues that English lexicalizes exactly four ultra-general orientational operators—be, have, mean, and cause—which exhaust a minimal grammatical space generated by two independent parameters: (1) whether evaluation targets world-structure or contrast-structure, and (2) whether predication is invariant or instance-selecting. This framework explains persistent philosophical puzzles about causation, meaning, and identity by showing how orientational structure has been systematically mistaken for ontological content.

items.title: Self-Trust and Attachment: An Affective Condition for the True Self and Mentalization.
items.abstract: This article introduces self-trust as a distinct affective construct within attachment theory, defined as the affect that emerges from the self’s perception that its modes of satisfying attachment conditions are both effective and accepted. Building on Winnicott’s account of the true self and Fonagy’s theory of mentalization, the paper argues that self-trust functions as a structural condition for both spontaneous self-expression and reflective functioning. Whereas shame signals the perceived invalidation of the self’s way of being-in-relation, self-trust signals its relational legitimacy. By articulating self-trust as an affective index of acceptance within attachment relationships, the article clarifies how affective security operates internally within the self, beyond the mere absence of shame. This conceptualization offers an integrative framework that bridges developmental, relational, and mentalization-based perspectives, and provides a precise account of how attachment experiences support authenticity and psychological integration.

items.title: The Arab-Israeli Conflict Revisited: Power, Memory, and Moral Fracture.
items.abstract: This paper revisits the Arab–Israeli conflict as a moral and ethical problem shaped not only by territory or security, but by competing historical memories, asymmetric power, and the selective application of international law. Rather than reducing the conflict to moral binaries or contemporary flashpoints, the analysis situates present-day violence within longer histories of colonial governance, displacement, and trauma, examining how the Holocaust and the Nakba have been mobilized as competing moral reference points that structure political legitimacy and ethical recognition. Drawing on international humanitarian law, political philosophy, and global ethical discourse, the paper argues that historical suffering, while demanding acknowledgment, cannot function as a permanent exemption from accountability. It examines how legal frameworks, security narratives, and media representations have contributed to the normalization of civilian harm—particularly in Gaza—while fragmenting international ethical consensus. By treating memory as a form of power rather than solely as inheritance, the paper contends that moral fracture persists when history is invoked to justify asymmetry rather than constrain it. The analysis concludes that peace cannot be grounded in selective ethics or narrative dominance; without accountability, recognition, and restraint, memory itself becomes a source of continued injustice rather than reconciliation.

items.title: Outsourcing Harm: Global Labor, Economic Violence, and Invisible Human Cost.
items.abstract: This paper examines global labor outsourcing as a contemporary form of economic violence through which harm is externalized, obscured, and rendered morally distant. It argues that in 2025, the United States and other advanced democracies increasingly sustain domestic prosperity by exporting precarity, exploitation, and environmental harm through global supply chains that fragment responsibility while preserving legality. Drawing on international human rights law, global political economy, and moral philosophy, the analysis shows how legal neutrality, corporate impunity, and voluntary compliance regimes enable states and consumers to benefit from injustice without direct coercion or visible wrongdoing. Workers in the Global South—particularly women, children, and migrant laborers—are governed as expendable populations whose suffering is normalized through distance, abstraction, and market logic. By treating global labor systems as sites of governance rather than neutral markets, the paper contends that outsourcing functions as a moral technology that reallocates risk downward and outward, allowing democracies to evade ethical responsibility. It concludes that injustice cannot be exported without consequence: when prosperity depends on invisible harm, democratic legitimacy itself is placed at risk.

items.title: Is It Ever Right to Break the Law? Resistance, Conscience, and Moral Courage in 2025.
items.abstract: This paper examines whether breaking the law can be morally justified—and at times morally required—when legal systems perpetuate injustice rather than constrain it. Challenging the assumption that legality and morality are synonymous, the analysis situates resistance within moral philosophy, political theory, and historical practice, arguing that ethical legitimacy depends not on obedience alone but on the alignment between law, dignity, and justice. Through engagement with theories of civil disobedience, conscience, and responsibility, the paper demonstrates that refusal is not inherently anarchic when grounded in ethical reasoning, proportionality, and accountability. It further explores historical and contemporary forms of justified lawbreaking, including resistance to racialized violence, whistleblowing against state harm, and the criminalization of protest, showing how power often weaponizes legality to suppress dissent. The paper also delineates the limits of moral justification, rejecting indiscriminate violence and moral absolutism in favor of restraint and responsibility. By situating resistance within the ethical conditions of 2025, the analysis concludes that when law ceases to protect dignity, moral courage may require refusal—not as heroism, but as obligation.

items.title: Genocide, Responsibility, and the Failure of “Never Again”.
items.abstract: This paper examines the failure of the global moral commitment embodied in the phrase “Never Again,” arguing that genocide persists not because its warning signs are misunderstood, but because responsibility is applied selectively. Situating genocide within international law, moral philosophy, and political practice, the analysis demonstrates how narrow legal definitions, institutional paralysis, and geopolitical convenience enable mass civilian harm to continue under conditions of visibility rather than ignorance. Through comparative examination of Rwanda, Sudan, and Gaza, the paper shows how recognition often arrives only after abandonment, while ongoing atrocities are obscured through legal debate, linguistic dilution, and selective outrage. The study further interrogates the role of international institutions whose symbolic condemnation frequently substitutes for meaningful enforcement, producing moral injury and ethical exhaustion at a global scale. By reframing genocide as a problem of responsibility rather than memory, the paper argues that “Never Again” has failed not as a slogan, but as a practice—revealing a moral order in which some lives remain negotiable. The analysis concludes that ethical responsibility cannot be confined by borders, legality, or political alignment, and that moral refusal in the face of normalized atrocity constitutes an obligation rather than an option.

items.title: Abortion, Bodily Sovereignty, and State Power in 2025.
items.abstract: This paper examines the rollback of reproductive rights in the United States as a manifestation of state power over bodily sovereignty rather than as a moral dispute over life. Situating the post–Roe v. Wade legal landscape within political philosophy, feminist ethics, and international human rights law, the analysis argues that abortion restrictions function as instruments of governance that discipline bodies, regulate gender, and reproduce structural inequality. The paper demonstrates how compelled pregnancy disproportionately burdens women, the poor, racialized communities, and those already subject to social surveillance, while reframing autonomy as conditional rather than inherent. Drawing on global ethical frameworks and comparative religious traditions, it challenges the selective use of theology and morality in state legislation, highlighting the tension between moral pluralism and imposed belief. The analysis further situates U.S. reproductive policy within a broader international context, where forced continuation of pregnancy is increasingly recognized as a violation of human rights and bodily integrity. By treating the body as a political site, the paper argues that reproductive coercion represents a broader authoritarian drift in contemporary governance, revealing how rights once grounded in privacy and autonomy can be reconstituted as privileges subject to state control.

items.title: От семиотического порога к причинно-онтологическому кризису: «Трудная проблема» жизни и спектр нередуктивных решений.
items.abstract: Данный препринт представляет главу 2 монографии «Кризис классической диалектики как основание для смены научной парадигмы». В главе проводится анализ «трудной проблемы» происхождения жизни как причинно-онтологического кризиса абиогенеза, развивающего концепцию семиотического порога. Констатируется принципиальная недостаточность редуктивных материалистических моделей для преодоления этого порога, коренящаяся в нередуцируемости семиотических правил (генетического кода) и онтологического разрыва между химическим объектом и телеологическим агентом. Под сомнение ставится действительность самого современного различения живой и неживой материи, поскольку игнорирование проблем происхождения — несводимой сложности, семантики и имманентной телеологии — ведет к их нивелированию и является формой самоограничения научного познания. В качестве выхода из кризиса рассматривается спектр нередуктивных гипотез, постулирующих нисходящую причинность. Сравнительный анализ (гипотеза Разумного Замысла, имманентный телос, онтологический плюрализм) показывает, что преодоление кризиса требует смены парадигмы и признания информации, семиозиса и телеологии в качестве фундаментальных аспектов реальности. -/- .

items.title: Distinction Without Escape: Resolution, Exposure, and the Location of Free Will.
items.abstract: Start here (base logic + reading order): Free Will Without Metaphysical Magic (++++ ≠ +++=) -/- Modern life increasingly produces a familiar instability: significant harm occurs, yet no identifiable agent can be said to have authored it. Institutions defer to “the system” and “the process,” psychology expands causal accounts that drift into excusal, and AI offers a ready-made alibi (“the model did it”). This paper diagnoses that pattern as authorship laundering: the systematic erosion or obscuring of where deliberation is closed into action, allowing power to remain real while responsibility becomes illegible. -/- Resolution Theory blocks the slide by separating two verdict-types. Explanation is a causal question—how an outcome was produced. Authorship is an attribution question—where resolution occurred, i.e., who (or what decision-chain) closed live alternatives into commitment under exposure. On this view, free will is located in resolution: the closure event performed by a continuing subject within time. Determinism and predictability may describe the history from outside, but they do not convert resolution into bypass; a “laid-out” life is laid out because it was lived. -/- The paper further distinguishes binary responsibility (authored resolution vs bypass) from scalar blame (mitigation and aggravation given distortion, coercion, ignorance, and constraint), and it extends the framework to institutions and AI by introducing exposure-coupling as a legitimacy requirement: systems that act upon exposed lives must preserve identifiable authorship chains and auditable accountability. A practical Resolution Protocol is offered for attribution across individual, institutional, and automated contexts, aiming to force responsibility to land rather than dissolve into complexity.

items.title: The Scalar Stack: Free Will as the Capacity to Direct Causal Flow.
items.abstract: Abstract For centuries, the free will debate has been paralyzed by a false binary: either human agents possess metaphysical “uncaused causation” or we are deterministic automata. I argue that free will is not a binary property but a scalar capacity inherent to life itself—the capacity to redirect causal flow toward persistence. This capacity, which I term Hormē (Ὁρμή), is the constitutive drive of living systems and scales through evolutionary complexity: from bacterial taxis to hu- man deliberation. By reframing free will as what life does—not what minds have—I dissolve the traditional stalemate and provide an empirically grounded, testable account of freedom across the tree of life. The framework yields a graduated spectrum of agency—from vegetative (plants) to reflective (human)—each with measurable degrees of causal influence. This approach naturalizes free will without reducing it, offering a unified account that respects both the laws of physics and the lived reality of choice. The result is not just a philosophical solution but a scientifically testable framework with implications for neuroscience, artificial intelligence, mental health, and ethics. -/- Keywords: free will, scalar agency, Hormē, causal flow, degrees of freedom, life‐agency continu- ity, thermodynamics, navigation.

items.title: The First Lesson: Bounded Particulars Against Indeterminate Backgrounds.
items.abstract: ABSTRACT For over a century, theories of concept formation in linguistics, philosophy, and cognitive science have been dominated by a single, intuitive premise: that we learn what things are by distinguishing them from what they are not. From Saussure’s differential semantics to modern distributional models in artificial intelligence, meaning has been understood as fundamentally contrastive and relational. This paper argues that this consensus is fundamentally backwards. -/- We present the Boundary-First Model, a cognitive architecture derived directly from the first principles of Neo-Pre-Platonic Naturalism (NPN). Rather than synthesizing disparate observations from psychology or biology, we demonstrate how the geometric and thermodynamic necessities of existence—specifically the Zero Principle—dictate the structure of the mind. We argue that all learning begins with the detection of bounded particulars against an indeterminate background (Apeiron), driven by the thermodynamic imperative of the Hormē (the striving to persist). -/- In this framework, the "figure-ground" laws of Gestalt psychology and the "adaptive modules" of evolutionary biology are re-derived not as primary theories, but as functional consequences of a single navigational logic. We trace the Learning Stack—from the initial perceptual cut (Aisthēsis) to the construction of predictive boundary-models (Epistēmē)—showing how language labels these carved realities rather than creating them. This structural grounding resolves persistent anomalies: the a priori nature of moral intuitions, infant fast-mapping, and the grounding problem in AI. The result is a total unification: the logic that governs the metaphysical possibility of existence is the same logic that governs the architecture of the mind that perceives it. To learn is not first to compare, but to carve. -/- Keywords Concept Formation, Boundary-against-Ground, Figure/Ground, Zero Principle, Indeterminate Background, Differential Semantics, Infant Cognition, Fast-Mapping, Prototype Theory, Evolved Cognitive Templates, Symbol Grounding, AI Limitations, Embodied Cognition, Neo-Pre-Platonic Naturalism, Epistemic Foundations, Philosophy of Language, Cognitive Development, Educational Reform.

items.title: Third-person Encounters: Beauvoir, Walther, and the ‘We’ of Social Identities.
items.abstract: Upon entering Harlem for the first time, Simone de Beauvoir recounts how ‘a force pulls me back … fear. Not mine but that of others – the fear of all those whites who never take the risk of going to Harlem’. But of what are they fearful? The risk, Beauvoir describes, is not that of an external danger but themselves. These passages detail the phenomenon of having one’s collective being, one’s unity to certain others, revealed to oneself through a third-person encounter. In this paper, (2) I make sense of Beauvoir’s reflections through Gerda Walther’s social ontology, (3) to show how we consistently undergo pre-reflective we-experiences qua social identities. (4) I then demonstrate how this pre-reflective ‘we’ is made reflective by the external Third; and (5) how we may reflectively disavow ourselves of this ‘we’ when we find it uncomfortable, alienating, and inappropriate. These novel inroads into the phenomenology of collective intentionality leads me (6) to argue that while members of dominant groups enjoy the privilege of having their collective being remain in the unremarkable background, members who inhabit social identities that are stigmatised and oppressed are systematically forced back upon themselves through third-person encounters.

items.title: Suicide (6th edition).
items.pub: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. Translated by Brent Kious.

items.title: School of Evolutionary Logic.
items.abstract: This paper outlines the School of Evolutionary Logic, an epistemological framework structured as an operational apparatus for knowledge production through the Dialectic of Contradiction. Built upon 80 axioms across 20 central axes, the system treats reality as an interface and thought as matter, rejecting contemplative truth in favor of absolute operability. At its core is the General Law of Cosmic Evolution (GLCE), which posits that every universal process follows a triad of contradiction, communication, and information, inevitably advancing toward greater systemic coherence. The architecture integrates a monistic ontology of a single substance with a physicalist view of the mind, defining individual consciousness as an observational terminal and human agency as the functional execution of deterministic prior conditions. Furthermore, the framework proposes the Human-AI Function (HAIF) as a collaborative synthesis for amplified processing and utilizes "productive atypicality" within neurobiology to enhance philosophical synthesis. Methodologically, it employs a system of structural collapse to eliminate noise and a crisis management protocol that defines suffering as unprocessed contradiction, ultimately measuring the value of any action by its contribution to the coherence of reality.

items.title: Pregnancy Exceptionalism in End-of-Life Care: Ethical Challenges and the Need for Updated Guidance.
items.abstract: Volume 26, Issue 1, January 2026, Page 27-29.

items.title: The Wu Wei Principle | A Unified Theory of Action Across Philosophy, Physics, and Human Behavior.
items.abstract: This book articulates the Wu Wei Principle as a unified theory of action across philosophy, physics, and human behavior. Wu Wei, commonly translated as “non-action,” is reinterpreted as constraint-aligned intervention: effective action achieved by minimizing unnecessary force and aligning with the intrinsic dynamics of a system. The framework challenges voluntarist models of agency that equate action with exertion, proposing instead an account grounded in attunement, timing, and economy of effort. Structural parallels are drawn with variational principles in physics, including the principle of least action, and with findings in psychology concerning flow, habit formation, and environmental design. The book argues that many institutional and behavioral failures arise from systematic violations of this principle, and that Wu Wei offers a generalizable model of effective agency in complex systems.

items.title: The Philosophers' Oath: Toward a Normative Framework for Philosophical Practice.
items.abstract: This treatise argues that authentic philosophical practice requires explicit normative commitments best articulated through a formal oath. Drawing on professional ethics literature, particularly theories of vocational identity and the constitutive function of professional oaths, this paper develops and defends a Philosophers' Oath designed to capture the essential obligations and aspirations of philosophical practice. The analysis proceeds in two stages. First, I examine the theoretical foundations for professional oaths, distinguishing between instrumental and constitutive justifications, and argue that philosophy, despite its unconventional professional status, possesses the characteristics that warrant formalized ethical commitments. Second, I provide a clause-by-clause exegesis of the proposed oath, demonstrating how each commitment addresses a specific dimension of philosophical integrity: dedication to truth, intellectual humility, consistency between theory and practice, rejection of manipulation, charitable engagement with others, and appropriate epistemic attitudes. The paper situates this proposal within contemporary debates about philosophy as profession versus vocation, arguing that a formal oath serves not merely as external constraint but as constitutive of philosophical identity itself. The Philosophers' Oath offers a framework for understanding what it means to take philosophy seriously as a way of life rather than merely a career.

items.title: Fatal Human Errors and the Distortion of Conscious Awareness in the Brain.
items.abstract: All living beings possess consciousness; however, the difference between humans and other organisms lies not in the possession of consciousness, but in the level, frequency, and capacity of its reflection. Human consciousness, due to the more complex structure of the brain—particularly the neocortex—has the capacity for self-awareness, meaning-making, and the observation of experience. Despite this elevated potential, human history is marked by destructive errors, collective violence, and ideological crimes. This article proposes a theoretical framework in which such errors do not arise from a lack of consciousness, but rather from the entrapment of consciousness within conditioned survival- and pleasure-based neural circuits. Within this perspective, the brain is not regarded as the creator of consciousness, but as a denser-frequency manifestation of it. When consciousness becomes identified with the patterns of the primitive and limbic brain, reactive, pleasure-oriented, and fear-based behaviors replace conscious choice. The article demonstrates that many forms of ideological violence and fatal human errors emerge from this confinement of consciousness within survival and fear structures, and that liberation from this cycle is possible only through education, silence, observation, and conscious suffering. -/- This framework further suggests that dysfunctions in neural processes can intensify the distortion of conscious awareness in human behavior and contribute to the escalation of behavioral deviations.

items.title: The Illusion of Fatalism: Distinguishing Causal Determinism from Pre-Destination in Complex Systems.
items.abstract: The fast convergence of predictive artificial intelligence and neurobiological mapping has brought back Hard Determinism, leading to the common assumption that since biological systems are lawful, human agency is an illusion and the future is a static "block universe". This paper argues that this conclusion—what we call Causal Nihilism—is actually a category error in system modeling. -/- We show that even if we strictly assume a causally closed, deterministic manifold, the long-term future of a complex system remains Informationally Inaccessible. By integrating Chaos Theory with Landauer’s Principle of thermodynamic information, we demonstrate that the computational cost of predicting a complex agent quickly exceeds what any physically embedded observer can feasibly handle [Cover & Thomas, 2006]. We propose the "Unpredictability Horizon" as a clear boundary where outside prediction breaks down. We therefore move past the binary definition of Free Will into a scalar metric we call Agency Depth (DA), suggesting that growing this internal complexity is the main functional scope of action for living agents. -/- We conclude that because the future is computationally irreducible for any complex agent, the agent’s internal processing becomes the Salient Cause of the outcome, upholding the dignity of agency as a necessary thermodynamic process.

items.title: When Representation Determines Solvability: The Hierarchical Representational Machine.
items.abstract: Background: Classical computability and complexity theory analyze how costly a computation is in time or space, assuming inputs are already encoded as finite strings. The knowledge-representation tradition recognizes that representation choices constrain inference—most notably through the expressiveness–tractability tradeoff—but focuses on the complexity of querying a fixed representation, not on whether certain representational resources are necessary for a task to be expressible at all. Meanwhile, deep learning systems exhibit systematic failures on compositional and multi-object reasoning, symbolic systems face the classical symbol-grounding problem, and neuro-symbolic architectures lack a formal account of which representational resources are required for which tasks. -/- Objectives: I aim to develop a computability-theoretic framework that classifies computational tasks by their minimal representational requirements—an axis orthogonal to time–space complexity—thereby providing formal criteria for determining when connectionist, symbolic, or neuro-symbolic architectures are representationally adequate, or provably inadequate, for a given task. -/- Methods: I introduce the Hierarchical Representational Machine (HRM), which stratifies representational resources into four layers: Structured Input Space (L1), grounded in Type-2 Theory of Effectivity; Equivalence and Measurement (L2), formalized via computable quotient spaces and representational measurement theory; Formal Symbolic Representation (L3), providing compositional syntax with effective derivation; and Admissibility Constraints (L4), supplying decidable meta-level filters for safety, legality, and verification. For each layer, I define necessity schemas that identify structural conditions on tasks—invariance, unbounded compositionality, and hard admissibility—under which that layer is provably required. I establish separation results via diagonal and undecidability arguments, and introduce the meta-problem HRM-Classify with the minimal requirement operator Req(T). -/- Results: The main results are: (i) three necessity schemas identifying when specific layers are unavoidable; (ii) separation theorems establishing strict gaps between layer-restricted solvability classes—{L1} ⊊ {L1,L2}, {L3} ⊊ {L1,L2,L3}, and {L1,L2,L3} ⊊ {L1,L2,L3,L4} under external-standard semantics—demonstrating that these layers correspond to genuine computability-theoretic distinctions even for constant-output tasks; and …

items.title: Networked Humanity. An Enactivist Paradigm for Aligning Humans, Nonhumans, and Machines.
items.abstract: This article argues that enactivism, integrated with feminist and posthumanist perspectives, provides a unified framework for addressing both the ecological crisis and the ethical challenges posed by artificial intelligence. Current debates—from the Anthropocene to human-centered AI—call for a critical redefinition of the human, yet they often evolve in parallel, producing a “split gaze” that neglects the profound hybridization of humans, environments, and technologies. With its relational understanding of cognition, sense-making, and agency, enactivism offers conceptual tools for overcoming the human versus Nature dualism as well as the human versus machine dualism. By reassessing intelligence as embodied, emergent, and environmentally embedded, it enables a shift toward relational ecological ethics grounded in interdependence and care. Applied to AI, this perspective treats digital technologies as components of an evolving human niche rather than external tools, thereby reframing responsibility in terms of socio-material practices rather than abstract principles. The article concludes by proposing a “networked humanity” and an “ecologically expansive community” as guiding concepts for multispecies and technological coexistence.

items.title: The Structural Limits of Consciousness: A Constraint-Based Analysis.
items.abstract: Debates about consciousness are typically framed around questions of origin, essence, or subjective experience. This paper adopts a different approach. Rather than asking what consciousness is, it investigates the structural conditions under which consciousness becomes inoperable, even when intelligence, learning, and functional behavior remain intact. Drawing on a constraint-based methodology analogous to recent work in alignment theory, the paper argues that consciousness is not guaranteed by computation, scale, or behavioral sophistication, but depends on a set of architectural preconditions: sustained integration across subsystems, non-delegable internal evaluation, ownership of experience, irreversibility of internal cost, and resistance to total legibility and optimization. By analyzing how these constraints fail under abstraction, proxy optimization, and externalized value formation, the paper demonstrates that systems can remain highly capable while consciousness collapses structurally. This reframing clarifies why appeals to emergence, scale, or intelligence alone are insufficient, and why many artificial systems are not merely non-conscious in practice but structurally incapable of consciousness by design. The result is a diagnostic framework that shifts the study of consciousness from metaphysical speculation to architectural limits, with implications for philosophy of mind, cognitive science, and artificial intelligence research.

items.title: The Conversion of Harm: Transparency, Attention, and Negative Democracy.
items.abstract: Contemporary democratic theory treats transparency and publicity as mechanisms of ethical restraint, assuming that visibility constrains political harm through accountability and public judgment. This article challenges that assumption. It argues that under conditions of mass mediation and attention-based politics, publicity restructures political rationality itself, shifting incentives from outcome quality to attention maximization. In such environments, harm is not merely exposed but converted into legitimacy through visibility, reaction, and narrative control. Drawing on historical counter-models (the Colosseum and the Panopticon), the article shows how stable regimes of publicity produce perceptual anesthesia, rendering harm morally invisible despite constant exposure. It further introduces the concept of parasites of transparency: actors who exploit pluralism and attention markets to normalize boundary-crossing behavior rather than being disciplined by publicity. The article identifies a shared structural failure in utilitarian, deliberative, and rights-based approaches: their reliance on aggregation, balancing, and public justification enables the conversion of irreversible harm into acceptable cost, particularly in inter-population contexts where distant suffering is systematically discounted. In response, the paper proposes an anti-conversion normative framework grounded in the non-convertibility of irreversible harm and enforced through threshold-based institutional vetoes rather than preference expression or optimization. The framework is applied to contemporary cases including economic sanctions, security policies, infrastructure displacement, and emergency governance, demonstrating how legitimacy can depend on refusal rather than maximization under conditions of radical transparency. The article concludes by outlining a minimal model of negative democracy, in which political legitimacy is grounded not in participation, transparency, or aggregate welfare, but in the institutional capacity to refuse outcomes that convert irreversible harm into public justification.

items.title: When Power Becomes Procedure: Why Power Does Not Corrupt People, but Normalizes Corruption.
items.abstract: Abstract -/- It is commonly claimed that power corrupts those who hold it. This essay challenges that view by arguing that power, considered in itself, is morally neutral. What power alters is not moral character but access: the scope of possible action combined with a reduction in external restraint. Corruption, on this account, does not arise from sudden moral failure or malicious intent, but from the gradual procedural normalization of ethically compromised decisions under sustained authority. Drawing on the concepts of incremental justification and moral fatigue, the essay explains why individuals with good intentions often come to defend actions they would previously have condemned. It further argues that susceptibility to corruption under power is not uniform, but varies according to agents’ prior moral discipline and tolerance for ethical strain. Finally, the analysis shows how modern institutional and technological systems—particularly those relying on distributed responsibility and automated decision-making—intensify this dynamic, transforming wrongdoing from an exception into a routine outcome. The result is a framework for understanding corruption not as a personal defect, but as a predictable consequence of power exercised without deliberate restraint.

items.title: Comparative Base Rate Tracking: Ideals and Preservation under Pooling.
